items.title: Protests begin across France, with shops, businesses and tourist sites closed – Europe live
paragraphs: Several of France’s leftwing political leaders have already shown up at the rallies in Orléans protesting against Marine Le Pen and her anti-immigrant party.
The demonstrations against “racism, fascism and imperialism” are being held as the National Rally’s congress takes place this weekend and Le Pen launches her presidential campaign.
“It was important for me to come here to Orléans,” said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis, saying he was there to stand up against racism and the hate speech spread by the right.

He also directly referenced the “close link” between hateful rhetoric from parties like Le Pen’s, and the drive-by shooting outside of Paris on Friday morning which the town’s mayor had said appeared to be targeting people of African origin.
Sophie Binet, General Secretary of the CGT union, also began her address to protesters by addressing the Trappes attack.
double quotation markI want to express our support and condolences to the victims, their families, and all the residents of Trappes.
This violence does not come from nowhere, it comes from speeches that convey racism, anti-Semitism, violence, which essentially come from the speeches of the far right.
The Socialist party leader, Olivier Faure, has also been seen in the crowds, marching behind an “All united against fascism” banner.
Italy police raid homes in Milan ahead of protests
Paris protest route moved away from Bastille and pushed back to afternoon
Some protest bans overturned in last-minute court challenges
Drive-by shooting outside of Paris targeted victims on skin colour
Counter-demonstrators expected at Le Pen rally
Police in Italy have raided 150 homes in Milan and other cities as the country braces for more protests on Saturday afternoon.
The searches were conducted in the homes of those, including 51 minors, suspected of intending to cause trouble during the demonstrations.

The events, organised by the Movimento 17 October and due to take place in Milan, Turin, Rome, Bologna, Naples and other cities and towns, are targeted at various issues, from the high cost of living and underfunding in schools to support for Palestine.
They follow protests last weekend which escalated into violence, especially in Milan, where hooded youths vandalised and looted shops in the city centre.
Many stores in Milan, Naples and other cities have covered windows with plywood over fears of further violence on Saturday.
Late last night, Paris police also ordered a change in the route for the main march that’s been organised by trade unions.
Originally, protesters had been given the green-light to march from Bastille to Nation squares in the centre, with the rally to commence in the late morning.

However, in their decree banning the route, police said such a procession presented “serious risks of public disorder, particularly due to the high density of businesses similar to those targeted during the 17-18 October weekend.”

Demonstrators can now only march from Porte de Vincennes and Porte d’Italie from 1pm to 7pm. Organisers had scrambled a legal challenge but that has failed, and groups are now preparing for a 2pm start.
The new route is on the outskirts of the Parisian ring, through the 13th and 12th arrondisements.

Paris’s streets are pretty quiet at the moment. Police are out in full force guarding the main squares and government buildings, metro stations are closed, and most retail shops are closed or about to shut up shop.
Following last weekend’s unrest, authorities across France moved to try to restrict demonstrations, limiting gathering numbers and march routes and issuing blanket bans in some cities.

That led to groups seeking permission for “authorised” protests with mixed results. For example, in Paris, the leading trade union was granted permission for their march while the Yellow Vest demonstrators were denied.
The bans have also sparked last-minute legal challenges from civil rights groups.

And now in the past hour, courts have overturned two protest bans – in the Bouches-du-Rhône prefecture and its capital Marseille and also in the city of Limoges, which saw its centuries-old city hall set on fire last week.
Other cities that have bans in place for “unauthorised” demonstrations include:
Paris, Lille, Strasbourg, Mulhouse, Grenoble, Toulouse, Amiens
Of course, many protesters – from students to union groups – have said they will march anyway regardless of the bans or rules around where and when they can demonstrate.
The mood in Paris was heightened by fear and horror after what the government said was “racist, terrorist attack” in two towns west of the city on Friday.

A 26-year-old, well-respected martial arts star from a club outside Paris was killed and five other people were injured, including a 12-year-old girl shot eight times as a gunman pointed an automatic weapon from his car.
The French president, Emmanuel Macron, said they were targeted because of the colour of their skin.

“These people were targeted because of their skin color or perceived religion, and for no other reason,” he said during his visit to Trappes, one of the affected towns, on Friday afternoon. “There is no place for this in France.”
“There are no words,” wrote the sports club of the 26-year-old victim, the ATCH Academy. “Nothing could justify a life being torn away like this.”
Several of France’s leftwing political leaders have already shown up at the rallies in Orléans protesting against Marine Le Pen and her anti-immigrant party.
The demonstrations against “racism, fascism and imperialism” are being held as the National Rally’s congress takes place this weekend and Le Pen launches her presidential campaign.
“It was important for me to come here to Orléans,” said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis, saying he was there to stand up against racism and the hate speech spread by the right.

He also directly referenced the “close link” between hateful rhetoric from parties like Le Pen’s, and the drive-by shooting outside of Paris on Friday morning which the town’s mayor had said appeared to be targeting people of African origin.
Sophie Binet, General Secretary of the CGT union, also began her address to protesters by addressing the Trappes attack.
double quotation markI want to express our support and condolences to the victims, their families, and all the residents of Trappes.
This violence does not come from nowhere, it comes from speeches that convey racism, anti-Semitism, violence, which essentially come from the speeches of the far right.
The Socialist party leader, Olivier Faure, has also been seen in the crowds, marching behind an “All united against fascism” banner.

Tension was also high in the city of Orléans on Saturday as Marine Le Pen’s far-right, anti-immigration National Rally party gathers for its annual congress and the official launch of her presidential campaign.
The police presence in the city has been stepped up as around 5,000 party members and officials gather on Saturday and 10,000 attend Le Pen’s first campaign rally on Sunday.
A protest march by the left has been organised against “racism, fascism and imperialism”. Between 20,000 and 30,000 people are expected to demonstrate against the far right in the city.

Several political personalities on the left were to attend the Orléans march including the leader of the Socialist party, Olivier Faure, the head of the leftwing CGT union, Sophie Binet, and the mayor of Saint-Denis, Bally Bagayoko, from the party La France Insoumise.
The capital’s authorities have shut down the stations in a bid to contain crowds and curb movement throughout the city today.

The affected stations are: Argentine, Assemblée Nationale, Bel Air, Champs-Elysées – Clemenceau, Charles de Gaulle – Étoile, Cluny - La Sorbonne, Concorde, Daumesnil, Dugommier, Franklin D. Roosevelt, George V, Mabillon, Maubert – Mutualité, Miromesnil, Odéon, Picpus, Rennes, Rue du Bac, Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Saint-Sulpice, Sèvres - Babylone, Solférino, Tuileries and Varenne.

We’ve seen other attempts by authorities to restrict movement in cities across France for this weekend; Marseille authorities earlier this week said they would suspend public transport services on Saturday; they were forced to reverse the decision following outcry.
In Orléans, which is hosting the far-right National Rally congress, the tram lines are suspended and bike-sharing rentals have been removed from the city centre.

All through the night in neighbourhoods in the centre and east of Paris, the sound of sawing, drilling and hammering rang out as wooden boards were hastily secured into place to cover windows and shop-fronts.
Businesses being boarded up included opticians, supermarkets and pharmacies as well as trainers and handbag stores.
Hundreds of shops were smashed and looted over two nights last weekend in Paris, and thousands more in cities across France, including Marseille and Bordeaux.
At a public meeting at Paris city hall this week, some shop-owners had cried as they spoke of their fears of businesses being smashed and looted again this weekend.

“I’m afraid there isn’t enough wooden board left to protect shops and the demand is making it so expensive to board up shops,” one optician near Châtelet in the city centre said. “We’ll close up and take all our stock of glasses out of the shop.”
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of events in Europe – we will be closely following protests across the continent today.

In France, hundreds of thousands are expected at rallies across the country, with high school students, unionists, “yellow vest” demonstrators and others turning out for a fourth weekend of protests demanding more government funding for schools and measures to help with housing and the cost of living.

Desperate to avoid the looting and property damage seen on the fringes of some protests last weekend, French authorities have ramped up restrictions on where protesters can march and which groups are “authorised” to do so. They’ve increased policing 20%, mobilising 70,000 police officers and soldiers to the streets, including both elite units and trainee officers.
Many of Paris’s metro stations and major museums and tourist sites are shut today, while across the country, shops and businesses have been urged to close their doors.

Community tensions are also high following a deadly shooting on Friday west of Paris where the gunman targeted non-white people, killing one person and injuring five others including a child. The French president called it a “racist terrorist attack”.

Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen’s anti-immigration party is also due to hold its national conference in the central city of Orléans. The far-right National Rally’s meeting is expected to draw up to 30,000 counter-demonstrators.
Protests are also being held in Italy, Spain, Austria, Portugal, Albania and Ireland today.

items.title: Infantino tells BBC Sport he is backed by 'vast majority' of world football
paragraphs: Fifa president Gianni Infantino insists he has the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football, as he laughed off questions about whether he had considered resigning over the World Cup sell-off debacle.

In a rare interview, he struck a defiant tone to BBC Sport about his own position in the wake of the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, and said it was not always easy to bring different points of view "under one roof".

"There is nothing bad in disagreeing," he said. "We see it every day in so many countries in the world. It's OK to disagree. It's OK to have different points of view, but then we need to be able to move on."
Two months ago, Infantino was facing mounting calls to stand down as president of the organisation he has led since 2016.

The heads of European football's governing body Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America, signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".

Last week Uefa demanded that Fifa release all key documents relating to FFE by 2 November, with Uefa general secretary Theodore Theodoridis saying that the organisation had failed to address "a number of fundamental questions".
Under FFE, which Infantino scrapped within days, a portion of the commercial rights of football's world governing body would have been sold to a private investment firm.

Since the delivery of the letter, Infantino has been travelling the world, appearing in Morocco, the Dominican Republic, Cape Verde, and Japan, managing to shore up support to the point where his re-election as president for a fourth term next year now looks inevitable.
He has also proposed to increase the amount of money handed out for football development across the world by $3.4bn (£2.6bn).

During the interview he reflected on having been "fully endorsed" by the Asian Football Confederation - following a U-turn by its president Sheikh Salman - and having the backing of "all African countries".
But only last week, he apologised to the Fifa Council over the "communication and consultation" regarding FFE.
He was told by Council members in that meeting that he was not "fit to be Fifa president" if he did not give them the documents they have asked for, including the rationale for FFE.
Yet, when pressed on when he would be providing the requested papers, he did not give a clear answer, saying they had to follow a "legal process" and that they were "working on it".
"We'll answer of course all the questions that are asked as far as the process allows, as far as we can," he said.
Speaking from the first Under-15 World Cup in Azerbaijan, he said he and the Fifa administration were doing "as best we can" but admitted they have done "some things which are maybe less good".
He also said that they need to have dialogue "more often" with Uefa, in an effort to repair their strained relationship.

Asked by the BBC if he was fit to be Fifa president, and whether he had considered standing down, he laughed, before saying: "Well you know I was elected by 211 member associations from all over the world.
"I think what is important is that in an organisation like Fifa, there can be different views, different points of view.

"But if we are serious about democracy, about the democratic process, about believing that everyone has the same vote and the same voice all over the world, that football belongs to everyone, if we are serious about that, then we need, to respect as well the views of the vast, vast majority.

"I'm just coming back off Tokyo where the Asian Football Confederation has fully endorsed me. I was in Cape Verde where all [Confederation of] African [Football] countries have endorsed me. I'm speaking to all associations everywhere in the world."

He continued: "There are different points of view it's not always easy to bring them all under one roof but we need to respect and I do respect all opinions all views and then it will be up to the Fifa member associations to decide who they want as a president and how they want Fifa to be run."
The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino for the election in March is 18 November - although none have yet filed and he could stand unopposed.
Infantino arrived in Baku on Friday for the Fifa Under-15 World Cup and Festival, which is being held in Azerbaijan and features teams from 189 member associations.

England, Spain, France, Argentina and Brazil are all taking part. Russia have also sent a team, marking the country's first appearance in a Fifa-sanctioned tournament since the world governing body, and Uefa, suspended Russian teams from international competitions in February 2022 following the invasion of Ukraine.
This tournament is only for boys, with next year's tournament being girls only, and then from 2028 Fifa's plan is to have boys and girls competing in the tournament annually.
Matches are played in an 8v8 format, on smaller pitches and with 20-minute halves.
"It's just beautiful to bring the world together at such a young age to create something like this," Infantino said.
"When some of these boys participate in a World Cup 10 years, 20 years from now, they will all remember that their first World Cup was here."

items.title: Suspect arrested over fire at Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ retreat in Bavaria
paragraphs: German police have arrested a suspect after a fire ripped through Adolf Hitler’s former mountain retreat in Bavaria, leaving the historic Nazi meeting place – known as the Eagle’s Nest – largely destroyed.

About 200 firefighters were deployed on Friday night to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator’s remote, purpose-built Kehlsteinhaus residence, a protected building on the peak of Obersalzberg in southern Germany.
Flames rose high into the air as firefighters approached the scene to find the building “completely ablaze”, police said.
“A suspicious person was taken into temporary custody,” they said in a later statement, adding that nobody was injured in the fire.
Lisa Maier, a police spokesperson, said firefighters struggled to tackle the blaze due to its location at an altitude of 1,834 metres (6,000ft).
The building, which was one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hitler era, was only accessible with “heavy breathing apparatus”, she said.
Built by the Nazis and formally inaugurated by Hitler on his birthday in 1939, the Eagle’s Nest has been preserved as a monument to “the insanity of the regime”, according to its website.

It is only accessible via a road cut into the mountain through previously impassable terrain. Nazis would enter a tunnel and take a 124-metre brass lift buried in the mountain to get inside the building.

Authorities were alerted to the fire when a smoke detector triggered a fire alarm at about 9.15pm, police said. When firefighters arrived on the scene at about 9.50pm, the entire building was engulfed in flames.

No reason for the fire was given, but German media reported that investigators suspected it was the result of arson. Firefighters found no one inside the building, which was reportedly still burning at 7am on Saturday.
Fire departments from six municipalities sent emergency personnel to tackle the blaze and the Bavarian Red Cross, the local mountain rescue service and the police also attended.
The blaze appeared to be out later on Saturday morning, although smoke continued to rise from the building.

A police spokesperson told the German tabloid Bild: “It is damaged to a large extent. The house is unlikely to be saved.” Officers blocked access to the road leading to the retreat, according to an Agence France-Presse photographer.
Maier said police were still investigating and would hold a news conference later on Saturday.

According to Bild, a motorcyclist whom local police officers came across on their way to the scene had been arrested, but his involvement in the fire remains unclear and a police spokesperson declined to release information about his identity.

The Eagle’s Nest was constructed between 1937 and 1938 and forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler’s Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews as well as Roma, LGBTQ people and communists in the Holocaust.
It became legendary in the postwar period and was often depicted as an essential meeting place in US war films, although in reality Hitler rarely visited the complex.
Since 1952 the building has housed an exhibition by the Institute for Contemporary History recounting its Nazi history, and a restaurant.
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

items.title: Bayern Munich coach Vincent Kompany's recovery will take 'weeks' after collapse
paragraphs: Kompany was taken to hospital after collapsing as he watched the club's second team train.
He had been unwell with a virus and missed the pre-match news conference on Tuesday for Bayern's Champions League game against Arsenal.
Kompany was on the touchline for Wednesday's match and Eberl questioned whether he "should have put the brakes on him earlier".
"The fact is, we protect our coach wherever we can," he said.
"If a coach says he feels ready to do something, then we're not going to say 'we won't allow that' if we don't know what's going on.
"It's also everyone's own responsibility to say, 'I can't carry on now'.
"Vinnie's a hard worker. If you don't listen to the subtle signals your body sends, eventually it will scream out in pain.
"Vinnie will be given that time [now], and we'll continue to try, even more than before, to protect him from himself."
Kompany spent 11 years at Manchester City as a player, winning four Premier League titles, two FA Cups and four League Cups, before going into management with Burnley.
After guiding them to the 2022-23 Championship title, Kompany was unable to keep the Clarets in the Premier League.
He left to take over at Bayern in May 2024 and has led them to successive Bundesliga titles.
Kompany's assistant Aaron Danks has spoken with the Bayern boss in hospital.
"I explained to him that we would be having no football conversations," said Danks. "It was just checking in on his health and making sure he's OK.
"All the football operations are in our hands and we'll work together as a team to keep the club moving forward."

items.title: England thrash France to keep alive World Cup hopes
paragraphs: Tries: Farnworth 3, Young 3, Lewis 2, Ashton, Williams, Radley, Litten, Welsby, Brimson Goals: Savala 13
After losing their opener, then watching Tonga and Samoa rack up huge victories, England knew only a massive win over France in Perth would keep alive their World Cup dreams.
Mission accomplished: 82-0. But they still require a lot of work and a pinch of luck to reach the semi-finals.
England needed this margin of victory following their 30-12 defeat by Tonga last Saturday.
They must do the same against Papua New Guinea in Wollongong on Friday - then hope Tonga beat Samoa next Sunday.
After a nervy opening quarter, in which England looked weighed down by expectations and permutations, they finally got going with three tries in four first-half minutes.
By half-time, England had six converted tries on the board including a Herbie Farnworth hat-trick. Come full time, Dom Young also bagged a treble and England had 14.

After 23 minutes, England found their breakthrough as captain George Williams - overwhelmed by Tonga last week and initially nervy here - broke the line before a clever behind-the-back pass set up Young to score in the corner.

England had, belatedly, arrived at this World Cup as a force to be reckoned with. Soon after, full-back AJ Brimson - whose direct runs pierced France time and again - led a breakaway before finding Matty Ashton.
The wing had knocked on over the try line early on to spill a seemingly certain England opener, but made no mistake here for his seventh try in six Tests.

Harry Smith spotted the gap before setting up Farnworth for his first try on 27 minutes. And after a period of defence against a France side - who threatened sporadically but made too many simple mistakes - Farnworth scored again nine minutes later.

Williams powered over under the posts for 30-0, and then came England's best move of the World Cup just before the break - slick through the hands to the right before Young set Farnworth back in for his third.
Eight minutes after the break, Young chased down a grubber kick to bring up 40 points - before Jez Litten and Williams cut through a tiring defence and Victor Radley scored unopposed.

England needed to repel another French siege, before overpowering at the other end for Litten - who impressed as an interchange - to score. Another Brimson surge led the way for try number 10, scored by Mikey Lewis.
A dreadful short kick-off was caught by Young, who raced through for his hat-trick. Jack Welsby got on the act for try 12, a third score in four minutes, as the French surrendered.
The 13th try - scored by Lewis who broke through two weak tackles - ensured England surpassed Samoa's 74-point winning margin against the French.
After a frustrating few minutes where they had to defend deep for their clean sheet, England finally reached 80 as Brimson scored a deserved try.
Hugo Savala was also a key figure with superb kicking. He only missed one goal from 14 attempts, adding 26 points.
England are far from perfect. They made six errors in the opening 20 minutes - and a better side than France, who haven't reached the semi-finals since 1992, would have taken advantage.
But it all comes down to points on the scoreboard - and England must hope they have enough.

After Samoa thrashed Papua New Guinea 62-6 earlier, England were a massive 150 behind the Samoans on points difference - which, if Tonga beat Samoa next weekend, would be the deciding factor between the teams as to who reaches the semis.
A hefty win here helps the English cause, but they still need work and luck to avoid missing the World Cup last four for the first time ever.

items.title: A theatrical dancer on a pristine limestone mountain in East Java: Mohammad Nur Nasikin’s best phone picture
paragraphs: Early this summer, in a pristine, limestone mountain range in the East Java province of Indonesia, Mohammad Nur Nasikin met with the father and son pictured here. His aim was to capture a character from a treasured Indonesian theatrical dance and art form called Reog Ponorogo.

“Bujang Ganong is one of the characters in the dance; a young regent who is agile, skilful and clever,” Nasikin explains, “Mr Hanafie, on the left, is a true artist, skilled in many Javanese arts. He’s wearing the traditional costume worn by a Bujang Ganong dancer: a wooden ganong mask, and a bright red waistcoat, a shoulder cloth known as a sembong, and loose‑fitting trousers called katok panji. At his feet is his drummer – his son Tirta, which means ‘water’ in Javanese.”

The energetic movements of the character made it easy to capture a range of shots, Nasikin notes. When he returned home, Nasikin showed his own 12-year-old son, and explained the importance of preserving culture passed from ancestors.

“We must continue to safeguard it for generations to come,” he says. “My hope is that viewers will be interested in learning more about this art form, and our culture, and in that way I will have formed a link between the past and the future.”

items.title: Is your Medicare Advantage plan ending next year? Here's what to know
paragraphs: Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6014612/nx-s1-9964380" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Medicare chief Dr. Mehmet Oz speaks at an event announcing the artificial intelligence website, America.gov in Washington, D.C., last month. Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
A slew of Medicare Advantage plans are disappearing for next year, leaving seniors in many areas with fewer options. In 193 counties across the country, no plans are offered at all.

Medicare's annual open enrollment period kicked off October 15 and runs until December 7, and seniors enrolled in those privatized Medicare plans that are closing in certain markets should carefully review their options.

Medicare Advantage means private insurers run Medicare for older Americans who choose it over traditional Medicare, where the federal government itself administers the program. More than half of the 70 million Americans in Medicare choose Medicare Advantage. It's popular because it covers services like vision and dental, often with lower premiums than traditional Medicare. It also often folds in the "Part D" drug benefit, simplifying that decision.

But a downside of Medicare Advantage is that companies can pick and choose where they offer plans. If a certain community is not profitable, a company can leave that market. And that has been happening on an increasingly large scale the last three years, according to research published in JAMA.
Big swaths of rural America are losing Medicare Advantage choices and so are some major metro areas.

Last year, 2.9 million seniors were in Medicare Advantage plans that closed up shop, according to JAMA. This year, an analysis of insurance company announcements by An Arm and A Leg podcast, shows at least 2 million people will be affected. Other preliminary estimates range from 3.2 million to 5 million seniors. About 35 million people are enrolled in Medicare Advantage.

According to an analysis of federal data by the health policy research organization KFF, the 193 counties that will have zero Medicare Advantage plans are mostly rural. Last year that number was about 120 counties without a plan offered.

KFF's numbers also show that there will be far fewer plans offered in some metro areas. Dallas, Minneapolis, Seattle, Houston and Portland all have between a quarter and a third fewer Medicare Advantage plans for seniors.

If your plan is ending, and you don't choose another, the insurance company will assign you to another Medicare Advantage plan or the government will enroll you in traditional Medicare — but without a supplemental or drug plan.

If you want to switch from Medicare Advantage to traditional Medicare and your plan is ending, you can enroll in a Medicare supplemental plan — also known as Medigap — without the same restrictions that you would normally have. If you have a pre-existing condition that has prevented you from enrolling in Medigap before, that could be good news.
Another wrinkle this year is that insurance companies can cap enrollments on some of the Medicare Advantage plans that they do offer.
Which means: If you wait to sign up, a plan you want might already be full.
The companies are supposed to enroll people on a first-come, first-serve basis — and not cherry-pick customers based on health conditions, age, or demographics.
Another reason not to delay is that with so many people on the hunt for new plans, it may take longer than usual to get help.
Here are some tips for navigating Medicare open enrollment this year:
Emily Pisacreta is the senior producer for An Arm and a Leg, a podcast about the cost of healthcare produced in partnership with KFF Health News and distributed by KUOW, Seattle's NPR member station.

items.title: U.S. birth rate drops to record low, but older women are having more babies
paragraphs: Fewer women in their 20s are choosing to become mothers, leading to an overall birthrate decline in the U.S. But the birth rate among U.S. women age 30-45 is rising according to the latest federal data. CHARLY TRIBALLEAU/AFP hide caption

Sarah Harris was 37 years old when she gave birth to her daughter Bridget last year. She describes motherhood as equal parts joy and exhaustion. "When you have a baby in your mid-30s, what you gain in wisdom and experience you also lose in terms of energy," Harris says with a laugh.

Harris, who lives in Vermont, was laid off from a job four months after Bridget was born. She says she's still figuring out what her career and her life will look like with a child. Harris thinks a lot of women are like her. They're wrestling with financial uncertainty and waiting much later to choose pregnancy.

There's also the high cost of raising a child, which Harris said convinced her that one is enough. "I think in another era or another life or another scenario, I might have had more children," Harris says. "I think we're in a difficult societal moment and so that's absolutely affecting people's reproductive choices."

Harris is, in fact, part of a slow revolution in what motherhood and parenting look like in the United States The latest report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found the general fertility rate for women fell by 1% to a new record low in 2025. That continues a two-decade trend toward fewer children.

The one-year drop for 20-somethings was even more eye-catching. "Certainly the 6% decline in the birthrate for women age 20 to 24 is noteworthy," said Brady Hamilton, a demographer at the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics who co-authored the report. He noted that women in their late teens also saw a 7% decline.

A separate study released last month by the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta found Gen Z women, in their late teens and twenties, "are dramatically less likely to want children" compared with U.S. women of previous generations.

"Several factors have been identified as contributing to this lower desire to have children, such as increased labor market opportunities and agency among women, rising financial costs, changing priorities, and [concerns about] maternal mortality," the study found.

Dr. Tanise Branche, medical director of labor and delivery at Temple Health, a health, research and training network in Philadelphia, told NPR more of her younger women patients are following a different life script.
"They're starting to focus not necessarily just on what they can bring to kids, but what's going to be best for them," she says.
Meanwhile, the latest CDC data shows a small but significant increase in older women, ages 30 to 45, who are choosing to become pregnant.
Branche says more women, including herself, are building careers and stable lives before becoming mothers.

Branche is currently pregnant with her fourth child. "I will be 43 with my last delivery and I started this reproductive journey at 37," she said. "I see the net positive being that we have a choice."

As a consequence of this shift, there are fewer children now in the U.S. The population under age 18 is falling steadily, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, dropping by more than 1 million from 2010 to 2020.
Some experts also believe women would choose to have more kids if they could afford them and had proper supports that include affordable housing, daycare and health insurance.

"The fact that there are a lot of people who still say they want families, but don't feel like they're able to have them [is a concern]," says Anna Louie Sussman, author of a new book on parenting choices called Inconceivable. "Young people say, I can barely take care of myself I can't imagine taking care of someone else."

Sussman herself is part of the trend toward delayed motherhood. Because of her own concerns about affordability and her career, she froze her eggs and waited to have her child until she was in her early 40s.
"I do feel lucky that I'm a little further along professionally than I would have been in my 20s or even 30s," she said.

As women build different lives and birthrates keep falling, the U.S. is changing. The median age is rising rapidly, reaching 39.4 years old in 2025. More states, including Vermont where Sarah Harris lives, are seeing actual population decline, according to the Census Bureau.
"I think about it a lot because I live in a very small place where we're hoping to keep the doors of our elementary school open for as long as we can," she says.

items.title: Cloud House by Peter Morris brings "fairytale flamboyance" to London
paragraphs: Marshmallow-pink walls, sweeping arches and turquoise detailing influenced by a trip to Miami animate architect Peter Morris‘s self-designed home in Gospel Oak, London.
Named Cloud House, the eccentric project combines two offset residences, one for Morris and his partner, producer Emily Kennedy, and a second for a neighbour who shares their love of colour.
According to the architect, the goal of the project was to bring joy to passersby, while giving his “love of postmodernism a chance to reveal itself fully”.
“The key goal was to make a beautiful building which I hoped might create a little moment of joy for anyone walking past it on the street,” Morris told Dezeen.

“It’s easy to dismiss colour and pattern in architecture as frivolous, but there’s something about this visual language that triggers an emotional response that’s different from what you’ll get with elegant modernism,” continued Morris.

“For me, that alone tells us we should push for more variety in the built environment and be open – as Camden Council have been with this project – to the idea of more fairytale flamboyance on our streets,” he continued.
Cloud House occupies the site of a now-demolished Victorian home, adjacent to a distinctive church and school, where the couple have lived since 2016.
Its bold colour palette and cloud-like forms were inspired by the couple’s honeymoon in Miami and the city’s vast collection of art deco architecture.

“Emily and I honeymooned in Miami, where we loved the art deco curves of the buildings, and the pink and turquoise colours everywhere,” Morris explained. “In a way this building is an architectural love letter to my wife, so it felt appropriate to have some of that honeymoon spirit in the mix.”

According to Morris, the project also draws on the curved forms of the neighbouring Grade II-listed school and Grade I-listed St Martin’s Church, which Morris said are “fabulously eccentric buildings”.
“The school, which sits in St Martin’s Hall, has a frontage that looks like a Medieval castle,” he said.

“And the church – described by the historian Nikolaus Pevsner as ‘the craziest of London’s Victorian churches’ – has a knock-out interior, with a brightly coloured chancel ceiling and a nave with dramatic wooden arches.”
Cloud House’s main structure is composed of structural steel and blockwork.

This is clad in decorative arches made of polystyrene, sprayed with a waterproof layer and a textured top coat to match the bright pink render on the elevations, and positioned in place by the architect himself.
Morris’s home is the smaller of the pair, located on the right side of the plot. It measures 133 square metres.
The home is accessed from an entrance on its front elevation. It has a large, open-plan ground floor, comprising a lounge, kitchen and the architect’s studio.
Its two upper floors are each fitted with a bedroom and bathroom, while a roof terrace crowns the home, complete with an outdoor bathtub.
Next door, the adjoining 165-square-metre home is accessed by a side entrance and has an upside-down arrangement.
Its ground floor contains a home office with a kitchenette, and a guest ensuite bedroom at the rear. Above is the main bedroom.
The main bedroom has a dressing room and ensuite, and sits alongside another smaller ensuite bedroom.
Meanwhile, the social space with seating, dining and cooking spaces is on the top floor, with an adjoining terrace. A second larger terrace tops the home.
While the interiors of Morris’s house boldly match its vibrant exterior, the interiors for the neighbour’s home were left blank and ready for them to customise.
Interior highlights of the architect’s home include turquoise epoxy floors, colour-drenched bathrooms and an emerald-green striped kitchen.
Cloud House was featured on the TV show Grand Designs in September and has been shared widely on social media. Morris said the response to the project is sharply divided.

“I know that not everyone will love the Cloud House as much as we do – the reactions to it on social media have been either overwhelmingly positive or overwhelmingly negative, with nothing in between,” he reflected.
“My final goal, and hope, is that some of the people that do love it might one day be keen to commission me to create something colourful and joyful for them too.”
Other pink dwellings featured on Dezeen include a concrete “fun house” on the English coast by RX Architects and a guesthouse in the Azores contained within a converted stable.

items.title: Mum dies after trying to rescue sons swept away at sea
paragraphs: In a statement, posted on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said: "According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock.

"Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.
"Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
"In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.
"She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered.
"Foul play is not suspected at this time.
"An autopsy will be conducted to assist in determining the exact cause of death."
A spokesperson for the Foreign Office said: "Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.
"We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family."

items.title: British woman dies trying to save sons on Bahamas snorkelling trip
paragraphs: A British woman has died in the Bahamas while trying to rescue her two sons after a current swept them away as they were snorkelling.
The Royal Bahamas police force said it had launched an investigation after the death of a 36-year-old woman on Tuesday.
The force said they believed she was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island of North Bimini when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
The police said that in an attempt to rescue her boys, “the woman was also swept away”. The children were later rescued from the water.
The Foreign Office said it was in contact with the woman’s family and was providing support.
Bimini is a small island group between the largest landmass in the Bahamas, Andros, and Miami in the US. It is the closest point in the Bahamas to the US mainland.
The islands are best known for once being home to Ernest Hemingway and are also home to a world-leading shark research centre.

In a statementposted on social media, the Royal Bahamas police force said: “According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini ferry dock.

“Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.
“Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
“In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.
“She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered. Foul play is not suspected at this time.”
An autopsy would be carried out to help determine the exact cause of death, the statement said.
A Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.
“We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family.”

items.title: Kim Jong-un crosses over newly opened bridge into China
paragraphs: Kim Jong-un has travelled to China over a newly opened bridge marking the North Korean leader’s first known trip abroad in more than a year, South Korean officials have said.

A government source told the Yonhap news agency on Saturday that Kim had arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong, in Liaoning province, after taking a train from Pyongyang to Sinuiju and crossing the New Yalu River Bridge.
Yonhap also reported that the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, had travelled to the city. Kim’s trip was not announced in advance and had not been confirmed by Pyongyang or Beijing by Saturday evening.
China will mark the anniversary on Sunday of its entry into the 1950-53 Korean war on the North’s side.

Japan’s Kyodo news agency said on Saturday that traffic controls had been imposed around the bridge and near a museum devoted to China’s role in the war, and that hotel bookings nearby had been restricted.
Diplomatic sources told the agency the measures were linked to a visit by a senior North Korean official.

The 3km bridge opened in mid-October, 12 years after China finished building it, after being held up by delays on the North Korean side. In early September, North Korea and Russia opened the first road bridge across their own short border leaving Pyongyang newly linked by road to its main backers.

The trip is Kim’s sixth visit to China and his first since September 2025, when he attended a military parade in Beijing alongside the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin. Xi visited Pyongyang in June, his first trip there in seven years.

Relations with South Korea, meanwhile, have deteriorated. Kim’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, has issued about 10 statements criticising Seoul since late September, a frequency South Korea’s unification ministry has called unusual, and has also announced plans to resume loudspeaker broadcasts at the border within days.
Xi will host the Apec summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November, which has fuelled speculation about a meeting between Kim and Donald Trump.

items.title: No panic for England but Mitchell issues PWR warning
paragraphs: Before England's three-match series against Canada, few would have predicted this outcome.

A 2-0 series defeat for the Red Roses; their record 39-match winning streak and 41-match unbeaten run – stretching back nearly four years – ended; and consecutive losses for the first time since 2016.

Over the past 13 months, Canada have turned a 33-13 defeat in the World Cup final into a statement 31-22 win in Ottawa. And three years out from the 2029 World Cup, they have laid down an early marker of their title credentials.

More than that, they have proved England are not invincible – a reality which should hearten New Zealand and perennial Women's Six Nations bridesmaids France because both have beaten giant-killers Canada in the past 12 months.
For the second time in eight days, England captain Meg Jones has been called upon to take stock of a defeat. Once again, she opted for a message of defiance.
"It was a hell of a contest. We're not broken, we just need to grow," said Jones. "Do it together, use the lessons. We're playing the best teams, getting the best punches thrown at us.

"I genuinely believe we've got the best players in the world. When we're firing, generally we're unstoppable. We don't dwell on the past, we're not anxious about the future, we're focused on the present."

It's true, this is far from panic stations. In 2016, England were the defending world champions when they lost to France and beaten finalists Canada. Since then, they've been imperious, winning a second World Cup, reaching the final in 2017 and 2022, and lifting nine of the past 10 Six Nations titles.
This is only their third defeat in 74 matches, so perspective is required.
But England's performances throughout the WXV Global Series highlighted areas for improvement.

They have lacked their usual clinical edge in attack. In Ottawa, Sarah Bern was held up over the line and England conceded a turnover less than five metres out as they failed to make their dominance pay before the break.

Tellingly, they opted to kick a penalty early in the second half to close the deficit – perhaps a lesson learned from last month's 26-26 draw in Exeter, where they turned down a shot at goal to snatch the win in the dying moments.

In defence, they have conceded 18 tries across their past five matches in the WXV, compared to eight in six at the World Cup. They have trailed at the break three times, something they hadn't experienced since 2020.
Last week, ill-discipline repeatedly gifted Canada field position before a late handling error, which put a clearing kick under pressure, opened the door for the hosts' winning try.

On Friday night, Gabrielle Senft picked off a bouncing ball from a missed pass to set up Canada's second try. Minutes later, England were lucky not to concede a similar try when a pass bisected Jess Breach and Jones, who pounced on the ball just before Lizzie Gibson got to it.

"We were riding the waves, building phases, scrum, set piece, we were very strong. Sometimes it's the bounce of the ball or it doesn't swing your way. We couldn't execute when we got in their 22, that's a big one to reflect on for sure," said Jones.
Canada does not have a professional women's domestic league and their players had to launch a crowd-funding campaign before the last World Cup to cover the cost of their training camps.

It's unsurprising, therefore, that many of Canada's top talents play domestically in England's Premiership Women's Rugby, which offers a level of training and match experience they cannot find elsewhere.

Twenty-five Canadian players are contracted for the 2026-27 season, with 11 featuring in July's PWR final between Saracens and Trailfinders. Three Canadian coaches, including head coach Kevin Rouet at Saracens, are also involved in English domestic rugby.
PWR squads must have a minimum of 13 England qualified players in a matchday squad.
But England head coach John Mitchell has warned that too many overseas players in the PWR could be detrimental for future Red Roses sides.

"I think it's necessary to make sure that young English girls are getting enough PWR time," Mitchell said. "It's a critical pathway because Sevens is definitely gone. For players aged between 19 and 23, it's critical.
"We're just going to make sure we don't erode our depth as a result of [overseas involvement]. It's not so much about now. It will be the future that will suffer if we're not smart in that area."

Mitchell has been forced to call upon England's squad depth on multiple occasions in 2026 with Abby Dow and Emily Scarratt retiring after the World Cup, four players absent through pregnancy, and several big names – including Hannah Botterman, Alex Matthews, and Amy Cokayne – spending time on the sidelines because of injury.

He's handed out more than half a dozen debuts this year, with hooker Bryony Field particularly impressing during September's home internationals, played the likes of Abi Burton and Ellie Kildunne out of position, and brought Liz Crake back into the fold after several years away.

items.title: ‘Unlike anything we’ve experienced’: fans swarm San Francisco for BTS star’s art exhibition
paragraphs: Two years ago, RM of the wildly popular K-pop boyband BTS was serving as a soldier in the South Korean military when he received an offer from América Castillo, a museum curator in San Francisco: would he consider an exhibition of his private art collection?

“I loved it,” said RM (real name: Kim Namjoon) at the media preview of RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me, a new exhibition that opened in San Francisco earlier this month and is co-curated by SFMOMA’s Castillo and Hyoeun Kim. “There aren’t many things that show a person more honestly than a collection they’ve built over a long period of time.”

The result is a multi-dimensional exhibition of 142 works of RM’s private collection of mostly Korean works, including paintings, calligraphy, sculpture and even a Pokémon animation cel, in conversation with 36 of the museum’s pieces. The show has been a blockbuster success, with over 66,000 tickets sold and advance sales that were six times higher than any previous exhibition at the museum.

RM has been an evangelist for modern Korean art: a song from his 2022 solo album Indigo samples a conversational snippet from the Korean painter Yun Hyong-keun. At the SFMOMA show, Yun’s monochrome Umber-Blue sits juxtaposed next to Mark Rothko’s No. 24 in the show. There’s also an audio guide and playlist by RM.

“I’ve always dreamed of seeing different places, times, boundaries and backgrounds all mixed together in harmony,” RM said at the preview, before adding lightly: “It could be a mess – I never formally studied art history, and I’m not a curator.
“Sometimes an outsider can bring in a new breeze,” he added.

While his celebrity looms large over the show, the collection and the curation of the show are formidable. In South Korea, gallery owners and art dealers who have met RM have told me their nickname for him is “bakhsa” (professor) owing to the depth of his knowledge. “It is especially meaningful to bring the depth and richness of his collection to a wider audience,” says Kim, assistant curator of painting and sculpture.
Some of the art is displayed with a scholarly arc, while other curation feels more intuitive. One room is titled “I Don’t Know, But I Like It.”

“I started this with an innocent heart,” RM said at the preview. “I just didn’t know that this innocence would eventually make me write, erase and rewrite hundreds of labels.” His text that accompanies the pieces combines historical context with diaristic personal reflections, in a break from museum convention.

In a placard that accompanies a Lee Ungno painting of the Gwangju uprising in 1980, a brutal crackdown on protesters by a military dictatorship, RM writes: “He painted these crowds until the day he died. Strange, isn’t it. These people are not falling. Arms raised, legs wide, they are dancing.”

Last year, as US museums grappled with the lingering effects of the pandemic on attendance, funding challenges under the current administration and lower tourism rates in many cities, SFMOMA laid off 7.5% of its workforce amid a $5m deficit. Its new director Christopher Bedford wrote that the museum would adjust its programming and budget to reflect “a reduced annual attendance normal in the range of 600,000 visitors”.

Since the RM show opened, the museum has seen an undeniable financial boost. Its success, and whether it ushers in a direction toward celebrity exhibitions, is something officials and other museums seem to already be considering. In 2024, Brooklyn Museum staged a major exhibition showcasing the private collection of Swizz Beatz and Alicia Keys, while other recent shows have focused on art made by musicians like Jack White and Paul McCartney.

Yet the dedication of BTS fans, who call themselves Army, may prove to make this show a one-off. On the day of the media preview and opening reception, a couple hundred fans lined up outside the museum entrance, one holding a sign saying she came from London for RM. Another handed journalists small bags of gifts including custom-made bookmarks, key chains and cake pops along with thank you notes for covering the exhibition.

Exhibition merch available at the SFMOMA Museum Store and web store sold out within three hours. “It’s different in so many ways,” store director Shane Salvata says of the exhibition, adding that it is important for visitors to commemorate “how special it is that he curated this show”.
“It’s unlike anything we’ve ever experienced, and probably will experience ever again,” he says.

For Castillo, who originally conceived the show, success has a different measure. “To actually see it in the galleries … people are crying in front of you,” she says. “You’re never going to expect that. It’s a beautiful surprise.”
RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me is on view at SFMOMA until 7 February 2027

items.title: This decade has been missing its big-impact midterm
paragraphs: New speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., holds the gavel during the opening session of the 116th Congress at the Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 3, 2019. Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Given all that's happened in American politics since 2019, it may be hard to believe there's been anything missing.
But the decade of the 2020s has yet to see a midterm that mattered much — or that ranked among the impact midterms of past decades.
That sets the 2020s apart, as every other decade over the past hundred years has produced at least one midterm that made a big difference in Congress and in national politics more broadly.
These big-impact midterms have also shifted power in the statehouses, often signaling changes in state and national political landscapes that have mattered and lasted.

Midterms do not attract the same level of voter participation or voter interest as presidential elections. When the White House is not at stake, "low propensity voters" tend to tune out. Overall vote totals slide by about one-third.

But those voters who show up for midterms elect just as many members of Congress and fill just as many state legislative seats as voters in presidential years. Moreover, midterm voters determine about two-thirds of the nation's governorships.

The big midterms have tended to come in presidents' second terms, when their popularity and political energy may be waning. And just because a president is not on the ballot does not mean he's irrelevant. Historically, each president's detractors have seen midterms as an opportunity, while his supporters have often been complacent — or at least less motivated.
All this contributes to the general expectation that the midterms arriving Nov. 3 will be important, and perhaps momentous.

Because this is a decade with three presidential cycles (2020, 2024 and 2028), it is also a decade with just two midterms. One went by in 2022. Some expected at the time that a "big red wave" would sweep then-President Biden's majorities out of Congress.

It did not happen. Democrats held on in the Senate, and the House shifted from barely Democratic to barely Republican. That did bring an end to House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's second (and last) turn with the Big Gavel. But the GOP would spend much of the next two years struggling to unite behind a speaker of their own.
That's a far cry from the big midterms that have at times rivaled presidential elections for responding to the mood of the times and rearranging the landscape.

If we take the last hundred years as our sample, we can start with the midterms that followed the Wall Street "Crash of 1929." That financial panic set off a sequence of events that would be called the Great Depression, and the collateral damage included the closing of an era of Republican dominance in Washington.

That era ended with the midterms of 1930, which cost the GOP eight Senate seats and 52 seats in the House in November 1930. Although the GOP initially retained small majorities in both chambers, they lost it in the House with the results of a few special elections early in 1931.
The "Democratic New Year's Eve Cheer" cartoon from Dec. 31, 1931, reflects the Democrats' win of the House that year after special elections. National Archives hide caption

The Senate remained nominally Republican but featured a working majority of Democrats and progressive Republicans. A page had been turned, and Democrats would take control outright in 1932 and hold that majority through World War II.
After that war had ended, the period of Democratic hegemony under President Franklin Roosevelt also ended, and abruptly, with the results of the midterm of 1946.

Republican numbers in Congress had fallen so far in the FDR years (below 100 at one point in the 435-seat House) that it seemed impossible for them to return to power. But in 1946 they stormed back to majority control of both House and Senate in a single midterm cycle.

Midterms have continued to serve as political regulators in the generations since. Dwight Eisenhower won two landslide elections as president in the 1950s, but he lost the House in 1954 and needed the vice president to break ties in the Senate.
In his second term, the re-elected "Ike" did not control Capitol Hill, and in the 1958 midterms saw his party drop to just 35 seats in the Senate.

The Senate Democrats first elected in 1958 established a critical mass that would later drive the bipartisan super-majorities needed to break the filibuster and pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

In the same era, Democrats in Congress enacted a raft of social programs that would become part of the language, such as Medicare and Medicaid. It was all part of President Lyndon Johnson's "Great Society" program.
Demonstrators carrying signs against the war in Vietnam march in front of the White House in April 1965 in Washington, D.C. AFP via Getty Images/AFP hide caption
But by the midterm year of 1966, much of the energy from LBJ's landslide election in 1964 had been expended — and much more had been siphoned off by his escalation of the war in Vietnam.

Right on time, the midterm arrived, and while the Democrats only took a haircut in the Senate elections they lost a painful 47 seats to the GOP in the House. It gave the party a new lease on life and encouraged its new emphasis on winning in the South. The redirection would guide the party's 1968 presidential candidate, Richard Nixon, and remain a focus for the onetime "Party of Lincoln" for decades to come.
Also in the midterm of 1966, out on the West Coast, a first-time candidate named Ronald Reagan won the governorship of California. People were starting to use the term "Sunbelt."

But what the midterms of 1966 gave the GOP, the midterms of 1974 would largely take away. Nixon had been elected president in 1968, pursuing what was called a Southern Strategy, and was reelected in a resounding 49-state landslide in 1972.

But by 1974 it had all gone the other way for Nixon. The "Watergate" scandals emerged from his 1972 campaign's use of burglary and electronic surveillance among other unsavory tactics. An attempt to cover it all up blew back on the White House and forced Nixon to resign on the brink of impeachment in August of 1974 – just three months before the midterm for his second term.
The result was a crushing defeat for the GOP, the loss of 48 seats in the House and several more in the Senate (where the Democrats already had more than 60 votes).

While it is tempting to attribute these losses to Nixon's downfall, the country had — to some extent — rallied behind his vice president and successor, Gerald R. Ford. The underlying vulnerability of the GOP was the state of the economy, which was suffering from inflation and the hangover from the oil embargo of 1973 by Arab members of OPEC, the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries.

That embargo, a side effect of the Arab-Israeli "Yom Kippur War" of 1973, temporarily raised the price of crude oil from $3 to $12 and introduced Americans to the phrases "oil shock" and "energy crisis."

President Ronald Reagan waves beside his wife, Nancy Reagan, after being sworn in as 40th president of the United States by Chief Justice Warren Burger on Jan. 20, 1981, at the Capitol in Washington, D.C. Consolidated News Pictures/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Consolidated News Pictures/AFP via Getty Images

Reagan became the dominant political personality of the 1980s, defeating incumbent President Jimmy Carter in 1980 and winning a 49-state landslide reelection in 1984. He was able to carry in a majority for Republicans in the Senate and establish a kind of working majority in the House with the aid of conservative Democrats in that chamber.

On the strength of those elections, restrained only marginally by the midterm elections of 1982, Reagan began his second term on top of the world. But he soon learned how hard that height can be to hold. As he neared his second midterm, Democrats were on the march nationally and restoring their strength in the more populous Southern states.

In 1986, Democrats defeated six GOP senators who had been elected with Reagan in 1980. The net gain of eight Senate seats gave them a 55-45 majority. In the session of Congress that followed, the Senate would override Reagan's veto of a highway bill and reject his nomination of Robert Bork to the Supreme Court. Reagan was a spent force.

Reagan was able to see his vice president, George H.W. Bush, take the White House in 1988, but the party's hopes for momentum into the 1990 midterms were largely unfulfilled. The presidency was also lost in 1992, when Democrat Bill Clinton won a three-way race with just 43% of the popular vote, defeating Bush and independent candidate H. Ross Perot.

Clinton's lack of a majority and list of frustrations in his first term set the stage for a bruising first midterm election in 1994. But what came was beyond bruising. Republicans stormed to their first majority in the House (54 seats net) in 40 years and recaptured the Senate with eight new seats there as well.
The new GOP speaker, Newt Gingrich of Georgia, was a hard-driving partisan who had portrayed the chamber as a House of Ill Repute, the title of a book he and other House Republicans had published.
The use of a "Contract with America" theme promised lower taxes, less corruption and a healthier economy in a compact agenda that had voter appeal as well.

Gingrich explicitly rejected the go-along-get-along attitude of previous GOP leaders in the House and advocated confrontation. The strategy proved less fruitful once he had the Big Gavel, however, and Gingrich spent much of his time as speaker making deals with Clinton. Internal dissatisfaction with him forced him out late in 1998.

In the new century that followed, parties have continued to prosper when their presidential candidates win and give ground in the midterms. George W. Bush was an exception as the president after the terror attacks of September 2001. In his first midterm the following year, theGOP made gains across the board.

But the larger dynamic caught up to him in 2006, when he and his party took what he called "a thumpin'" in elections at all levels. Bush had initially gained popularity with his "War on Terror" and won a second term. But thereafter, his invasion of Iraq had become an albatross. And in 2006 he paid the historic price, losing both his party majorities in the House and Senate. The new majority in the House made Pelosi the first woman speaker in history.

That created an atmosphere of optimism for Democrats, who elected Barack Obama president in 2008 and gave him majorities in the House and Senate (the latter briefly reaching 60 seats). But Obama felt the sting of the midterms early — much as Clinton had. Republicans in 2010 capitalized on an economy still experiencing the recession that had aided Obama's win in 2008. The GOP also capitalized on fears and confusion surrounding the enactment of the Affordable Care Act, or "Obamacare," in 2010.
Echoing his predecessor, Obama called this setback "a shellacking," and settled in to work with a much diminished Senate majority and a Republican-dominated House under Speaker John Boehner.

President Barack Obama is greeted by House Speaker John Boehner and Vice President Joe Biden prior to delivering his State of the Union address in January 2011 at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C. Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Obama managed to thread the needle well enough to win a second term for himself in 2012, but the House remained Republican and the Senate followed suit in Obama's second midterm election in 2014.

That second midterm revealed continuing GOP strength across the South and Midwest and to some degree augured the Electoral College majorities that would make Donald J. Trump president in 2016 and 2024.
If the 2020s are to have a midterm with the kind of impact others have had, roughly once a decade for a century, the last opportunity for that to happen is Nov. 3.

If the once-a-decade rhythm has any rationale, in fact, the pressure for a meaningful midterm ought to be building substantially. And in fact most pollsters, pundits and other prognosticators now predict Democrats could flip control of the House and even the Senate as well.

Just as in the previous 10 cycles, the current cycle combines economic concerns (including energy prices) and negative stories about incumbents in various offices. It is the party perceived as being in power that is exposed in a midterm, and it pays a price when voters perceive that party to have lost its mandate — or at least its momentum.

items.title: Seven projects by RIBA award-winning Nakshabid Architects
paragraphs: Who is RIBA International Prize winner Nakshabid Architects? In this roundup, we get to know the Dhaka-based studio through seven of its key projects spanning Bangladesh.

Founded by Bayejid Khondoker in 2003, Nakshabid Architects’ extensive portfolio is concentrated in Bangladesh and encompasses both public and private projects – from residential blocks to mosques and museums.

Last week saw the studio’s Green Field Factory named the fifth winner of the biennial award, presented by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) to the world’s best new building outside the UK.

Praised for its focus on passive design principles and the prioritisation of employee wellbeing, the studio considers its latest award to be a recognition of Bangladesh’s architectural contributions at a global scale.
“We see the prize as a recognition of what architecture from Bangladesh can contribute to global conversations on climate and the dignity of labour,” the studio told Dezeen.

Alongside the award-winning Green Field Factory, recent projects undertaken by the 20-person studio include the government-commissioned renovation of the Bangladesh Military Museum in Dhaka, which reached completion in 2022 with a glass geodesic dome.
Central to its architectural approach, the studio said, is forging connections between a building and its “socio-ecological context” in a bid to reframe functional programmes as places of gathering.
“We believe that architecture must respond directly to its socio-ecological context, transforming ordinary programmes into meaningful collective experiences,” the studio said.
“We approach every project as a shared undertaking, listening closely to the people who will use it, the climate it sits in and the building traditions around it before we draw,” it continued.
“In this way even the most functional programmes become places of gathering, where light, air, landscape and everyday social life are woven into the architecture itself.”
Read on for a look at seven of the studio’s key projects:
The Green Field Factory, a rug factory in Rangpur, was designed by Nakshabid Architects to dismantle workplace hierarchies and is the fifth winner of the RIBA International Prize.
Fronted by a monumental green facade, the seven-storey building was informed by the traditional Bengali home, incorporating natural ventilation and biophilic design principles.
A pair of intersecting arches form an “invisible dome” that frames the interior of Aman Mosque, a cubic prayer hall completed by the studio in Narayanganj.
Set within a sunken circular courtyard, the mosque is defined by its solid concrete volume, which is adorned with triangular perforations that filter light into the space.
A concrete facade punctuated with square openings was designed to limit heat gain and control daylight access at the Shaptak Insignia apartment tower in Dhaka.
Comprising two blocks, the residential block contains 18 units on a 670-square-metre plot, with each apartment complete with a balcony and a stepped terrace.
A pair of slender, red-brick residential towers make up the studio’s Urban Legacy project in Dhaka.
Its jagged form is defined by cantilevered balconies, which are enclosed by horizontal louvres and complete with greenery intended to shade and cool the apartment interiors.
“Cascading vines and planters spill from every terrace and the brick-walled garden base, turning the building into a vertical green landscape,” the studio said.
Aman Cement Factory Mosque, Sirajganj, 2022
An arched entrance guides visitors beyond the tiered brick exterior of the Ullapara Mosque, which Nakshabid Architects completed on the grounds of a cement factory for its workers.
Spread across two storeys, the mosque was built using locally-sourced brick, concrete and glass in a bid to blend “tradition with modernity”.
“[The mosque] has become a place where factory workers and neighbours gather for prayer, social events and community life,” the studio said.
Looking to redefine museum culture in Bangladesh, Nakshabid Architects conceptualised its design for the Bangladesh Military Museum in Dhaka as a “vibrant civic destination”.
Its curving concrete structure contains cafes, galleries, an amphitheatre and an arena, which is sheltered by a 120-feet glass geodesic dome.
Nakshabid Architects intended for the Nurpur Graveyard, a Muslim graveyard in Rangpur, to also offer a place of leisure for the local community.
To do this, the site accommodates a healthcare facility and an education space – or madrasa – with future expansions expected to include a mosque.
“Nurpur Graveyard is a place that diminishes the typical boundaries of graveyards,” the studio said.

items.title: A censored library logo design just took the war on woke to a new level of weird
paragraphs: The weird 'war on woke' being waged in the US has already claimed some high-profile design victims. The most famous examples have been the Cracker Barrel rebrand, which was deemed too modern for conservatives, and the US State Department's use of the famously liberal typeface Calibri.

Several brands have held their nerve in the face of the onslaught. Mars refused to entertain Tucker Carlson's fetish for the green M&M, the Jaguar rebrand is starting to make sense, and Bob's Red Mill seems to be sticking to its decision to 'kill off' Bob.

Alas, it seems a library in North Carolina didn't have such guts. Farmville Public Library has reportedly ditched the logo design it had been using for the past 14 years because three people complained that it looked a little bit like a rainbow, which apparently reminded them of gay people.

THESE PEOPLE HAVE LOST THEIR MINDS!!! For 14 years, the Farmville Public Library's logo was an open book with each page in a different color. Now it's gone. Three residents complained that it "resembled a rainbow" and might suggest support for LGBTQ+ people. https://t.co/09sYGqk7jtOctober 23, 2026

According to Farmville mayor Alex Joyner, the town's library changed its logo after three complaints were made to a town commissioner. I won't comment on the choice of typeface, but the mark itself was perfectly serviceable for a public library: it was cheerful, it stood out, and it obviously depicted a book rather than a weapon of LGBT propaganda.

The mayor himself has taken issue with the decision. He pointed out that the iconic television series Reading Rainbow had made said climatic phenomenon a “significant symbol of libraries across the entire US”. He also complained that the logo was changed “in the dead of night behind a curtain” with no opportunity for public comment.

“The library is a symbol of inclusion and is supposed to be welcome to all. For a handful of people to be able to decide who is welcomed and who is not here is unacceptable in my eyes,” he said, as reported by ABC.

I'd also point out that the logo's seven colours don't even depict a rainbow and aren't the same colours as the pride flag. It's clearly an open book, with each colour depicting a different page. It's a nice way to show that books can contain a wide array of knowledge on diverse subject matters, like how colours are used to depict different subjects in Trivial Pursuit. Although admittedly, Trivial Pursuit is very woke.

The culture war, it seems, has now become a war on colour. Next, we'll be banning box sets of the best coloured pencils. Apple's iconic rainbow logo would never be allowed today, and I'd be surprised if Google doesn't soon receive complaints too: it's workmark contains red, yellow, green and blue. At this rate, everyone is going to have to dress in black, and any splash of colour will become the ultimate act of rebellion.
A public meeting to discuss he logo controversy will be held at Farmville Town Hall on 2 November at 5:30pm.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: Dónal Lunny, ‘colossus of Irish music’, dies aged 79
paragraphs: The Irish traditional musician Dónal Lunny has died at the age of 79 from cancer.

Lunny rose to prominence in the trio Rakes of Kildare alongside his brother Frank and Christy Moore. He went on to play in bands such as Planxty, Moving Hearts, the Bothy Band and Coolfin among others and toured the world.
A post on his Facebook page confirmed that Lunny died in St James’s hospital in Dublin on Friday morning.

“We are heartbroken to confirm that our beloved Dónal passed away peacefully this morning in Dublin following a short stay in St James’s hospital,” the post said. “Thank you for helping us to remember and celebrate his immense contribution to music, to culture and to so many people’s lives all over the world.”
The Irish president, Catherine Connolly, expressed her “deepest condolences to the family, friends and many musical collaborators of Dónal Lunny”.

In a statement, she said: “Dónal was one of Ireland’s greatest musical figures, a wonderfully talented musician and producer who was central to so many of the most influential moments of the last 60 years of Irish music.

“Dónal will be particularly remembered for his long partnerships with fellow musicians such as Christy Moore and Andy Irvine and for the innovative music he has left behind both as a musician in groups including Planxty, the Bothy Band and Moving Hearts and also as a renowned producer.

“This rich musical legacy, including his central role in the introduction of the bouzouki into Irish music, was appropriately recognised by his fellow artists in Dónal’s membership of Aosdána, as well as the well-deserved recognition which he received in being awarded a lifetime achievement award at the 2025 RTÉ Radio 1 Irish folk awards.
“Beyond his music, Dónal will be remembered for his warmth and the strong connection which he had with audiences all over Ireland and beyond. He will be deeply missed.”
The post ended in Irish, saying his likes will not be seen again: “Ní bheidh a leithéid arís ann.”

Lunny was born in Tullamore, County Offaly, and was a multi-instrumentalist but was best known for his mastery of the bouzouki. He was a talented melody writer and considered central to the revival of traditional music as he produced 17 albums under his record label Mulligan Records.
The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said he was “deeply saddened” to hear of Lunny’s death. “A colossus of Irish music, as a performer, songwriter and producer,” he wrote in a post on social media.
“Uniquely gifted, Dónal carried traditional and folk music to new audiences through Planxty and his many other endeavours.”

Sinn Féin’s president, Mary Lou McDonald, also paid tribute online, saying: “Deeply saddened to hear of the passing of Dónal Lunny. A giant of Irish traditional music, Dónal helped shape the sound of Irish music for generations, bringing our rich musical heritage to audiences at home and around the world. His contribution to Irish music and culture will never be forgotten.
“Ar dheis Dé go raibh a anam [May his soul rest in peace].”

items.title: Blue Planet III features cloudier footage to prove authenticity amid AI boom
paragraphs: The David Attenborough-narrated series Blue Planet III deliberately includes cloudier, less polished footage to counter AI fakery and assure viewers it is “authentic”, its producers have said.
