Nearly a decade after Blue Planet II shone a light on plastic pollution, and 25 years since the first Blue Planet aired, the hit BBC series is returning with more animal behaviour and cutting-edge technology, including the world’s first underwater CCTV camera – dubbed “stonefish” cam.

Since the first Blue Planet, TVs and cameras have evolved to give viewers sharper, higher definition pictures. But the combination of the rise in AI and the extraordinary sequences and fantastical creatures captured by BBC Studios’ natural history unit for this series led producers to include what they called more “organic” footage and less polished shots, to show that the animals were not AI-generated.

The executive producer, Elizabeth White, said AI, “makes us want to be even more authentic”, adding that the creatures filmed in the deep ocean “are probably more remarkable than AI could imagine and it’s completely real”.

She said that in the past “the amount of plankton and things that are in the water in the sequences” would usually mean they might be excluded, and previously, “we might have framed out a boat or a buoy or gone: ‘Oh, actually … the water conditions are not really good enough for this.’”
But now such things are being left in as “we’re really leaning into that authenticity … As AI booms we will probably lean more into the more organic”, murkier and less polished footage.

For the first time, the BBC’s specialist factual commissioning head, Jack Bootle, assured journalists at a press screening: “No gen AI was used in this series. Not a single frame. It’s all real photography.”
Bootle added that as we live in a “golden age of natural history-making … sometimes people feel like they’ve seen it all before [so] this series is bursting with novel behaviour”.

That includes never-before-seen action of dolphins using sea sponges to block holes in coral to trap fish, captured using underwater CCTV – developed by the programme’s producer and director, Yoland Bosiger.

Over the four years of filming across five oceans, BBC Studios “continually innovated”, said the series producer, Lara Bickerton, creating a “mini-dome” camera to follow an octopus, a “deep-sea selfie stick”, camera operators wearing leg-mounted scooters to create immersive TikTok-style diving footage and using lasers to film deep-sea creatures.

Other remarkable animal behaviour captured in the programme includes grouper communicating with another species of fish; 200,000 crabs lining up in formation to feed; sea urchins using shells as sun hats; and footage involving penguins that echoes the Planet Earth II, ‘iguana v snakes’ sequence.

Threats to the ocean as well as its resilience are addressed in the series. One episode shows how warmer seas caused by the climate crisis are killing off sea anemone where clown fish live and how they try to fix their homes, and the issue of plastics raised in Blue Planet II continues with a story about pollutants [and] forever chemicals, said White.
Bosiger said Attenborough, who is 100 years old, was “very much involved” and made changes to scripts.
White added: “What’s wonderful is he hasn’t lost his curiosity … he’s still that little boy … who gets excited … when you show him a new piece of footage.”

Asked if the BBC’s £500m cost-cutting drive would affect BBC Studios’ renowned natural history reputation, White said she could not comment on that but pointed out that Blue Planet III made savings by using more local crews on location than in previous series.
Blue Planet III starts Sunday 1 November on BBC1 and iPlayer

items.title: "Nobody has it figured out, and that’s the point": Radim Malinic on the power of creative risk
paragraphs: The confidence to be daring is a hurdle that many creatives will grapple with throughout their career, but for Radim Malinic it's an innate power that we all possess. In his latest book ‘Daring Forever’, the creative director and bestselling author dissects the human capacity for courage, curiosity and creativity, and the power it can hold.

From branding books to mindful practice guides, Radim's bestselling works have inspired creatives across the globe with his practical yet inspirational words. Yet another valuable curation of his industry knowledge, Daring Forever is a wonderfully human take on creative empowerment.

"‘Daring Forever’ begins at the edge of something – a blank page, a stage, a life we haven’t quite stepped fully into yet," the press release reads. "The rope feels unattached. The drop looks real. And still, something in us leans forward. The book is a love letter to that lean: to the body that carries us further than we believe it can, to the self we are still learning to accept, to the curiosity that refuses to sit still, and to the gratitude that brings us home to the present."

"After years of interviewing remarkable people, I noticed the same pattern. The ones doing the most daring work were often the most afraid. Nobody has it figured out, and that’s the point," Radim explains. “Your body is the vehicle, and you’re the driver. Most of us were never given the owner’s manual. This book is my attempt to write one.”
“Daring isn’t a personality trait reserved for the fearless. It’s a human capacity we all carry, and it’s never too late to use it,” he concludes.
Daring Forever is now available on Amazon in paperback, Kindle and audiobook form.

items.title: Drinking water supplies dwindle in Yemeni city besieged by Houthi rebels
paragraphs: FILE - Smoke rises after an attack by Houthi rebels on the city of Taiz, Yemen, on Oct. 21, 2015. (AP Photo/Abdulnasser Alseddik, File) Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP hide caption

Drinking water has been scarce for over a decade in Taiz, but the problem has reached crisis levels in recent weeks as Iran-backed Houthi rebels besiege Yemen's third-largest city in their escalating conflict with government forces.

The needs of Taiz's more than 1 million residents are now barely being met, humanitarian groups say, as access to wells is limited, desalination plants run low on fuel and water delivery trucks are largely prevented from entering the city.

Families are rationing every drop. Before Taiz came under siege, Hadil al-Shahid and her two young children used about 10 liters (about 2.6 gallons) of bottled water per day for drinking and cooking; now they are making the same amount last about four days.
"We stopped drinking coffee and tea, which we used to drink daily," al-Shahid said in a phone interview.
Families like al-Shahid's are paying as much as 75% more for bottled water than just a few weeks ago, and some have begun to buy water on credit.

The siege of Taiz — a strategic gateway to southern Yemen — isn't only constricting water supplies. Shortages of groceries have sent food prices soaring. Fuel is also in short supply, making it difficult to maintain basic services such as hospitals and sanitation, which compounds the public health risks.
Amnesty International has called on the Houthis to immediately open roads into the city, saying Taiz is being pushed to "the brink of a severe humanitarian disaster."
Houthis strangle Taiz, cut off residents' access to wells

Yemen descended into civil war in 2014, when the Houthis seized much of the country's north, including the capital of Sanaa, and forced the internationally recognized government into exile. Taiz has been a focal point of fighting ever since.

War-related damage to Taiz's aging water infrastructure magnified the pressures of population growth and frequent droughts that led to shrinking supplies of groundwater. Residents began paying for water delivered by trucks, a mostly reliable alternative — until recently.

By August, Yemen had become a widening front in the Iran war. The Houthis ramped up their advance on Taiz last month, after a lightning-fast capture of the port city of Mokha, an area about 130 kilometers (80 miles) away that is vital to controlling shipping through the Red Sea.
As Houthi forces took control of more land and roads surrounding Taiz, residents' access to nearby wells was cut off and deliveries of water from outside the city declined.
The truckers that have managed to ferry water into Taiz have in some cases tripled their rates to make the perilous journey.
As Taiz's fuel supplies dwindle, its water utility is struggling to maintain limited operations and desalination plants are running well below capacity.
The city is also enduring shortages of fuel and food

Since August, Taiz province, which includes the city and surrounding areas, has taken in roughly half of those displaced from other parts of Yemen because of the fighting — an estimated 124,000 people, according to the United Nations' migration experts. That is only compounding the pressure on Taiz's limited supply of water and other necessities.

Some displaced families are now living in makeshift shelters or tents and surviving on one meal a day, said Jens Laerke, a spokesperson for a division of the United Nations that focuses on emergency aid.

Fuel for cooking and transportation has also become scarce — and more expensive. The price of cooking gas has more than quadrupled, according to Hani Bafaqih, a water, sanitation and hygiene expert at the aid organization CARE in Yemen. To get by, some families are cooking over fires made by burning wood, charcoal or cardboard.
These fuel shortages have made it harder for community kitchens to provide free hot meals to families and have also forced waste-collection services to shut down.

"The shortages feed into each other. Without fuel, water pumps, hospital generators and solid-waste collection stop. With less clean water and waste piling up, the risk of disease, including cholera, rises," Laerke said. The health risks are exacerbated by thirsty families tapping into unprotected wells that could be contaminated with waterborne diseases, he said.
Food prices are also soaring. Flour and rice are about 50% more expensive than they were over the summer, according to aid groups, and fruits and vegetables are hard to find.

Ahmed Abdel Gaber is living with nine other family members in the ruins of another building after being displaced from their home by the fighting. He used to earn money hauling construction material, but that income is no longer steady and his family is barely scraping by.
"We heavily rely on assistance and donations from people to get food," he said in a phone interview.

Al-Shahid, a hair salon owner, said her income also dried up a few weeks ago. The salon was forced to close as former customers began to prioritize their spending on food and water. Her 10-year-old daughter and 5-year-old son now eat mostly rice, bread and cheese, she said.

While the Yemeni government still controls the center of Taiz, the siege is making it difficult to deliver supplies to its forces there. In the hills surrounding Taiz, the government forces are trying to repel the Houthis but face stiff resistance, especially east of the city.
Gaining control of Taiz city is vital to the Houthis if they seek to advance south toward Aden and Lahj, analysts say, but that won't be easy.

"Any Houthi attempt to seize parts of the city, let alone take it entirely, would likely require a prolonged and costly battle, with significant casualties among Houthi fighters," said Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group.

Three Houthi officials said the rebel group controls roughly 80% of the countryside surrounding Taiz and several key neighborhoods inside the city. The Associated Press couldn't independently verify the claims by these officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to brief the media, but Yemen's foreign minister, Afrah al-Zouba, has acknowledged the rebel group's tightening grip on the city.
The Houthis' fight for control of the city is made significantly more difficult because of its large civilian population, the officials said.
Earlier this week, missiles fired by the Houthis struck a residential area in Taiz, killing two teenage girls and renewing attention on the dangers faced by civilians.

Abdel Gaber said he can hear loud explosions every day from fighting that is happening roughly 5 kilometers (3 miles) away. The family isn't returning to their home in a mountain village out of concern for their safety.
Leaving Taiz is not an option for al-Shahid because the costs of travel and renting a home in another province are prohibitive.
"Staying in our home is inevitable — whether it be a matter of life or death," al-Shahid said.

items.title: Smith v Puello world title fight predictions
paragraphs: WBC light-welterweight champion Dalton Smith (left) has won all 19 pro fights with 14 stoppages
Dalton Smith will make the first defence of his WBC light-welterweight title on home soil when he faces former champion Alberto Puello in Sheffield on Saturday.
Unbeaten Smith, 29, returns to the ring for the first time since becoming world champion with a stunning knockout of Subriel Matias in New York in January.
Dominican Republic fighter Puello, 32, is aiming to become a three-time world champion, having lost his WBC belt to Matias on points last year.
Smith will have the backing of his home crowd at the Utilita Arena. Can he keep his dream of fighting at Sheffield Wednesday's Hillsborough stadium alive with another win?
Or will the tricky and experienced southpaw Puello, who has lost just once in 26 professional fights, ruin the homecoming?
BBC Sport spoke to figures from across the boxing world to get their predictions on who will come out on top.
"I think it's going to be a great fight, I think there will be a lot of close rounds, but I'm going for a majority decision win for Smith in a really tough fight."

"What a brilliant fight this is. It's such a terrific match-up with contrasting styles. You have a slick southpaw in Puello and the tough, rugged, well-schooled Smith. Puello being a southpaw will suit Dalton who throws a fantastic right hand.

"This is fine margins - high-level chess. I think Dalton will come through via decision, or perhaps a late stoppage, and he will have produced two back-to-back victories to cement his place in the top 15 pound-for-pound rankings."

"I think this will be an interesting fight. Both guys have a similar sort of style. Puello is a boxer-puncher who goes really well to the body. He throws that loopy left hand shot quite well that Dalton will have to be quite careful of.

"It will be cagey at the start and I think Puello will fall behind a little bit. Dalton is a better boxer than him and better at his game. Puello will then have to come forward and I think that will suit Dalton.
"So I see Dalton winning quite a wide points decision."

"It's a good fight and I think Puello is a good fighter but I'm Team Smith. He boxes well and his style has matured. Puello has fast hands and is good in close but Smith can find a way to beat him. If he knocks him out then it's a big statement, but I'll go for a Smith win on points."

"This is a harder fight for Smith than Matias. Matias was a monster, while Puello is a clever boxer who sits on the back foot and punches nice and long. He's southpaw which makes it awkward to adjust your feet and stance.
"Ultimately, I think the angles of attack will be the difference for Smith. I think it might be a bit of a frustrating night for him but I think he comes out on top on points.
"It will be relatively entertaining - not as exciting as the win over Matias, perhaps - but a good homecoming for the champion."
"I'm backing Dalton, he's been my guy since we were 12 years old. He was my roomate at every tournament and now is his time as WBC world champion."
"I'm backing Dalton Smith to beat Alberto Puello and retain his world title. Smith's power, accuracy and impressive stoppage win over Subriel Matias make him a dangerous opponent.
"Although Puello's experience and awkward southpaw style could make it a tough fight, I think Smith's power and work-rate will prove too much. Smith to win by unanimous decision."

"Puello can be awkward and disrupt rhythm as he did in wins over guys like now WBA champion Gary Antuanne Russell, but Dalton's a big light-welterweight and his boxing is on point as well as intelligent decision-making.
"His stoppage win over Subriel Matias was impressive but I see Dalton winning this one on points. Puello will complicate things in some moments, but Smith wins a comfortable decision."
"It's a big fight. I think the Utilita Arena - pound-for-pound - is the noisiest venue in the country. To use a football analogy, I think it will have to be a 12th man for Dalton.
"I think he's up against it. Puello is a very special talent, as is Dalton who put on a performance of a lifetime in January.
"Dalton has a lot of the advantages but Puello comes here with experience at the highest level at this division. He wants the belt back, which he thinks was robbed from him in his loss to Matias.
"I do edge towards the current champion because of home advantage, but I wouldn't be shocked if Puello walks away with the belt."
"Dalton is a real hero in Sheffield but Puello is very dangerous. He's a southpaw and a former two-time world champion.

"It's a very tough first defence but Dalton has home advantage, the age and the unbeaten record. He probably has plans A, B, C and D. He's a very clever boxer whose background has been perfect - an excellent amateur and a solid professional."
"I expect him to come through a very tough test."
"I think Dalton will stop him late on - round nine or 10. Dalton is just too good for Puello, he'll try to put pressure on but Dalton will just have his number."

"Dalton will have a little bit too much speed and a little bit too much flair. The one thing that Dalton has to watch out for is he cannot afford to slow it down to Puello's pace. He's decent with his jab, he likes his opponent to stand in front, he doesn't like it when they move.
"If Dalton is in and out with his feet, plays it tricky, he'll be able to beat him fairly comfortably as long as he doesn't stand and trade."
"I've got Dalton winning on points. I think it will be a competitive fight but Dalton will edge it."

items.title: The convicted £33m tax fraudster evading justice and living it up in Dubai
paragraphs: Arif Patel, who masterminded a massive VAT carousel fraud, remains on the run
One of the UK's most prolific fraudsters, described by a judge as a "breathtakingly arrogant" and "totally dishonest" man, remains on the run in Dubai after stealing more than £33m of public money.

Arif Patel, from Preston in Lancashire, was exposed following a complex investigation spanning years, led by His Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC), which established that he had tried to steal as much as £90m.
Patel, who skipped the UK in 2011 never to return, was eventually convicted in his absence and in 2023 was handed a 20-year prison sentence.
BBC File on 4 Investigates has been on the trail of the man who stole from all of us - and seemingly got away with it.

"Al Capone was brought down by the taxman. This is the same situation and 20 years was more than a satisfying result," said Rod Stone, a veteran investigator of large-scale tax fraud, of Patel's conviction and custodial sentence.
The judge at Patel's sentencing hearing described him as the leader of a "fraternal organised crime group" with his brothers Munaf and Faisal who were "truly high-level criminals".
The fact that Arif Patel has not served a single day of his 20-year prison sentence clearly rankles with Stone.
For him and the dozens of others who were involved in bringing Patel down, there remains a strong sense that justice has only been served on paper.
Former HMRC assistant director Rod Stone specialised in the detection of fraud and organised crime
In the early part of the millennium, Arif Patel appeared to be a businessman very much on the up.
His company, Faisaltex, headquartered in his home city of Preston, was known for manufacturing textiles, such as socks and nighties, which it supplied to retailers.
Patel was a fixture in the Sunday Times Rich List with his wealth in 2006 estimated to be £105m. He was also investing heavily in property across the city and beyond.

In 2007, his teenage son bought a minority stake in Preston North End Football Club. There was even a plan to build a £100m, 19-storey tower block - complete with botanical gardens and restaurant - in the centre of the city.
Behind the facade, though, something very different was going on.
In the early 2000s, organised crime groups had turned to large-scale attacks on the tax system through what became known as carousel fraud.
Chains of fake business transactions are created as a way of stealing VAT repayments from HMRC.
Goods move between different companies, into and out of the country, to generate false tax refunds.
The same shipments of goods are often moved around repeatedly, hence the name carousel fraud.
This type of fraud was costing taxpayers billions of pounds a year and experts like Stone were at the vanguard of the fightback.
This is how Patel's textiles empire appeared on his radar.
"When we started to look at them we did notice some very strange shipments of goods - a container load of hats to Switzerland seemed odd because they were actually Swiss hats," he said.
The fake clothes the gang were selling would have been worth up to £50m had they have been genuine
Most carousel fraudsters dealt in high-value, high-volume items like mobile phones or computer chips, for which investigators were on the lookout.
But Patel's enterprise had predominantly been dealing in textiles, making the scam harder to spot.
The team of investigators discovered Patel had successfully stolen more than £33m of taxpayers' money before HMRC cottoned on to what he was doing.
In total, he tried to steal more than £90m of public money - the rest of the payments were stopped.
Teams of investigators spent years working through vast chains of transactions until they were ready to make their move.
Patel was charged with a range of offences including conspiracies to cheat the taxman, money-laundering, false accounting and selling counterfeit goods.
But when he appeared at Bolton Crown Court in 2011, Patel asked the judge for permission to travel to Dubai on bail.
The judge agreed to this request and Patel left the UK, never to return.
In Dubai, he joined his brothers Munaf and Faisal, who had already left the country before they could be charged for their part in the conspiracy.
Over the next three years, 24 members of Patel's gang were convicted. Collectively, they were jailed for more than 116 years.
A judge ordered Patel's Ferrari Superamerica to be auctioned off
Efforts to have Arif Patel extradited back to the UK failed and he remained a free man in Dubai.
The BBC has heard claims he had been actively seeking to strike a deal with the UK authorities to settle the case against him.
"In my opinion, he thought he was above justice," said Graham Honey, another former HMRC investigator.
In 2020, he was working in the private sector when he said he was approached by Patel's representatives.
Honey said he was asked to open up a channel of communication with HMRC and the Crown Prosecution Service because Patel wanted to make a deal.
It soon became clear, however, that there would be a sticking point.
"It started to become apparent to me that Patel was not willing to come back," said Honey.
"He just thought he could get an agreement, pay some money, and this would all go away."
Honey claimed that while Patel was willing to admit his guilt and repay money, he was not prepared to face a criminal trial or the prospect of time behind bars.
He claimed it was not the first time that Patel had attempted to strike such a deal.

Honey said: "One of the officers told me that he had said 'I'm a tiger, not a caged tiger' meaning he was a big man, he'd done what he'd done, but in essence, he wasn't prepared to go to prison for it."
HMRC said it had seized more than £78m of the gang's UK assets
In 2023, Patel's trial got under way without him, something which is highly unusual and only done as a last resort.
He was found guilty of leading one of the UK's biggest carousel fraud gangs and received a 20-year jail sentence.
In 2025, he was subjected to a confiscation order to repay £90.5m through the sale of assets found to have been gained through criminality.
The funds raised were to be returned to the public purse.
But more than a year later, none of the money has been recouped because, despite being on the run overseas, Patel has been able to go to the Court of Appeal to object to the confiscation order.
So where is Patel now and what might he have done with his stolen millions?

The BBC has discovered that over the last few years, an increasing number of websites, press releases and social videos have begun to appear, celebrating the achievements of a businessman called Arif Patel in Dubai.

This Arif Patel is variously a business owner, an investor and a philanthropist. The photographs on the sites are often stock images or, in at least one case, belong to a different British entrepreneur.
Many of the pages also suggest Patel has links to Preston and worked in the textile industry.
A story was published in 2024 in which Arif Patel denies allegations of fraud by HMRC.
The article quotes a "Sam Mackenzie", who it said was a close associate of Patel.
Mackenzie spoke out in support of Patel, whom he described as a "pillar of integrity".
The piece also said he had received backing from an "Andrew Fox", who the article described as having reviewed the claims and deemed them to be "unfounded".
It just so happens that the deputy chief constable of Lancashire police is called Sam Mackenzie, while Andrew Fox is a senior prosecutor with the Crown Prosecution Service.
Both men had been quoted in the media following Patel's conviction.
Their names appeared in other stories too, including one which claimed Patel had made a sizeable investment in HMRC anti-fraud technology in Lancashire.

The BBC does not know for certain whether Patel is connected to these sites, but File on 4 Investigates has established some sites are linked to an online reputation management company based in Dubai.
Another story was published earlier this year, this time about a donation Patel had made to a charitable organisation which supports children with disabilities in Dubai.
It shared similarities with some of the other websites but had one key difference - it featured a genuine photograph of Patel.
With an up-to-date picture, facial recognition technology uncovered numerous other pictures of Patel posing at glamorous events in Dubai.
We showed everything we had learned about the case to the prime minister's anti-corruption champion Dame Margaret Hodge.
"I think this is a shocking story of somebody who deliberately acted fraudulently and laundered money and he should be punished," she said.
"He should not be beyond the reach of the British justice system.
"I think he is clearly abusing the justice system in a way that only rich people can.

"There's an intrinsic injustice in a system that allows those with money to delay the implementation of a punishment for a crime and to delay the confiscation of assets which was stolen as part of that crime."
The BBC contacted the Government of Dubai but did not receive a response.
The BBC also contacted Arif Patel via his Manchester-based solicitor - as well as his brothers Munaf and Faisal - but did not hear back.
You can listen to the File on 4 Investigates at 20:00 GMT on Tuesday 27 October.

items.title: Project to restore rare native trees with DNA testing
paragraphs: A project is aiming to help restore one of the UK's rare native trees across the Thames Valley using DNA testing.
Conservation groups have warned numbers of black poplar trees have fallen due to decades of felling, land drainage and habitat loss.

The Swindon to Oxford: Regenerating the Thames and Tributaries nature recovery programme is working with local conservation groups to regenerate the population along the River Thames and its flood plain.
Catrina Bass, from the Long Mead Foundation in Swindon, is involved in the project and said while the trees were "extraordinary survivors", there were just 50 recorded in Oxfordshire currently.
Describing black poplars as "Lord of the Rings" looking trees with "great gnarled trunks", she said they support other wildlife, including the poplar hornet moth.

The project secured initial funding from West Oxfordshire District Council and the Vale of White Horse Council but is now aiming to raise £20,000 for the work, which involves DNA analysis of existing trees, propagating new cuttings and planting them in suitable sites.
Oxfordshire County Council's Local Nature Recovery Strategy has committed to match fund the fundraiser up to £10,000.
Also involved in the project is the Trust for Oxfordshire's Environment, which works with community groups to fund local environmental projects.
Chief executive Benjamin Heaven Taylor said black poplars play an important role in reducing flood risk, by lining rivers and floodplains, holding water back.
He said the population that remained was "extremely fragmented", adding that it "needs a helping hand to recover".

items.title: Historic swimming pond to be restored
paragraphs: The aim is to create "a welcoming community resource"
Plans have been made for a historic swimming pond to be restored.

A new partnership between the Carew Pole Garden Trust, Torpoint Artists Collective and Rooted Futures said it was "taking the first steps" towards restoring a historic bath house swimming pond on the Antony Estate, in Cornwall, funded through the National Lottery Community Fund.
It said it hoped it would bring it into community use and improve access to nature.

In a joint statement, the partners said specialists at the garden trust had started to look at how the bath house pond "could be cleared, identify tree maintenance needs and better understand the tidal inlet and the movement of water through the site".
The bath pond and bathing house were built in the late 18th Century after being designed by Thomas Parlby.
Reginald Pole Carew, who had inherited Antony, wanted somewhere to swim in the stretch of woodland on the bank of the tidal River Lynher.
Sir Tremayne Carew Pole, who currently resides on the estate, said, when it was first built, it was used to swim in and the bath house, where the ladies would swim, had a sunken pool fed by the pond.

He said, over the years, it started to be used as a decorative pond for the garden as surrounding trees shed leaves into the pond and humus (soil organic matter) and mud formed at the bottom, making it not a great place to swim.
"I've always wanted to restore it to be swimmable and to share the benefits with those in the local community," he said.

In the statement, the organisations said this would help shape the next steps of restoration and it aimed to "create a welcoming community resource where people can connect with green and blue space, discover the natural environment and contribute to the long-term care of a valued local landscape".
It added "education, creativity and community participation" would be central to the project.
It said Torpoint Artists Collective would develop a programme of artist-led workshops including wildlife recording, photography and nature journalling.
Open-water swimmers, nature lovers and anyone interested in the pond's future have been invited to share feedback and volunteer by emailing Antony Woodland Garden.
The partners said a Friends of the Pond group would be set up to "help shape the next steps, bringing together local knowledge, practical skills and ideas for the site's long-term care and use".
Follow BBC Cornwall on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to spotlight@bbc.co.uk, external.

items.title: ‘It’s part of our history’: can the menú del día survive Spain’s changing eating habits?
paragraphs: A little before lunchtime each working day across Spain, evidence of one of the lingering, if less notorious, legacies of the Franco dictatorship is carefully traced in chalk, marker pen and printer ink.

Beckoning to hungry workers from blackboards, whiteboards and pieces of paper hastily taped to windows, the competitively priced menú del día, or daily set-price lunch, has been part of everyday Spanish life for more than half a century. But while 4m menús are still served each weekday, Spain is slowly losing its appetite for the familiar ritual.

Back in 2009, the country’s best-known chef, Ferran Adrià, went so far as to pronounce it dead – a victim of changing eating habits, economic downturns and bistro-style restaurants trying to charge €20-€30 (£17-£25) for what should be a simple starter, a hearty main and a choice of pudding or coffee … with bread and a drink thrown in.

Seventeen years later, however, the diagnosis seem a little premature. A new book by the Spanish food journalist Lakshmi Aguirre charts the history and evolution of the menú and argues that while the tradition is indeed in hot water, it hasn’t quite had its chips.

Her book – Menú del Día: Everyday Scenes of a First Course, a Second Course and Pudding – begins with the unpalatable fact that it all began with a tourist menu dreamed up in the mid-1960s up by the Spanish dictator Francisco Franco’s information and tourism minister, Manuel Fraga.

The regime was keen in the aftermath of the “years of hunger” that followed the Spanish civil war to show foreign visitors that food was plentiful, good and affordable. So it was that establishments serving food should offer “a starter of soup, a main course chosen from at least three options and based on egg, fish or meat and accompanied by a side dish, and a pudding based on fruit, something sweet, or cheese”.

The price was set at between 50 and 250 pesetas and, to stop unscrupulous restaurant owners watering down the drinks, the law stipulated that the accompanying quarter-litre of vino had to be “reds and whites from Spain that are pure, clean, pleasant on the palate and with an alcohol content of not less than 12%”.

In the early 1970s, the menú del día was rebaptised to make it look less like an attempt to woo – and sometimes gouge – tourists, but also to give ordinary Spaniards the idea that they, too, could indulge.

It is now so ubiquitous that many in Spain have no idea of its genesis. “When I was working on the book and people asked me about the menú del día, I’d mention Manuel Fraga and lots of them would throw their hands up in shock,” Aguirre said. “Some people know, but the vast majority don’t. It says a lot about us Spaniards; we forget very quickly.”
Researching the book, which includes personal reminiscences and a hefty selection of recipes, led Aguirre to consider the place of the menú in the popular consciousness.

“It’s part of our history, yet it’s changed over the years, reflecting the evolution of Spanish society,” she said. “It originated from something as terrible as a dictatorship, and today it has become a deeply ingrained custom. We feel a sense of nostalgia as we realise it’s fading away.”

The threats to the set lunch, whose average price today is €14.70, are many. Increasingly time-poor, many Spaniards now opt for a quick lunch, eating food from home at work or popping to a supermarket for a ready meal to microwave in a soulless canteen. Rising energy and food prices are making it harder for small, family-run restaurants to offer a rotating daily selection of starters and mains.

All of which explains the rise of the “dish of the day”, which offers restaurants a cheaper alternative to the traditional choice of three or four mains, and the increasing diversity of some menús, which now feature Latin American staples as a reflection of Spain’s changing demographics.

“The menú del día purists reject such options, but it has always been a reflection of the society that consumes it – and that’s exactly how it should be,” Aguirre said. “Spain today isn’t the same as it was in the 1980s, it is far more diverse and pluralistic, and as a result diners have changed as well. The menú del día exists for those who need it, for people who may come from many different backgrounds.”
Aguirre’s menú of choice would be a simple but well-cooked vegetable stew followed by hake in green sauce or baby squid in ink, and then leche frita (fried custard) or rice pudding.

But, as she points out in her book, the surroundings are almost as important as the cooking. Her benchmarks for a good menú del día spot include simple dishes, a regularly changing menu, chips that aren’t frozen, a chorus of regulars and “a chalkboard free of any trace of words such as avocado, burrata, tartare, truffle or sourdough bread”.
That chalkboard should, by preference, be written “by someone who’s never heard of lettering”, and bonus points are awarded if the child of the owners is doing their homework on a table down the end.
As it hobbles slowly towards what may be its demise, the menú del día has become something that transcends a filling and reasonably priced midday meal.

“What’s being lost is a meeting point,” Aguirre said. “A centre of community gravity where families with limited financial means can afford to eat out, and where those who live alone can find some company during a meal, which remains a deeply social activity.

“It’s a place where joys, sorrows and problems can be shared, or where you can simply enjoy a bit of breathing space, as well as a place for those who live far away or who don’t have the time to go home for lunch.”
The true privilege of the menú, she added, lay “not just in being able to pay for a meal, but also in having the time to enjoy it”.

items.title: The people on standby when a storm strikes
paragraphs: Tree surgeon Callum Kirk said preparing for severe weather involves checking and sharpening equipment
While most people are preparing to stay indoors as another storm approaches, others are getting ready to head straight into it.
Storm Boelo is expected to bring strong winds and disruption to parts of Northern Ireland this weekend.
For those tasked with keeping people safe and dealing with the damage, severe weather can bring long hours, dangerous conditions and calls for help at any moment.

In preparation for the storm, the Department for Infrastructure said their teams have been checking and clearing road gullies, monitoring river levels and tidal surges, and deploying a portion of temporary flood defences.
"Regional Community Resilience Groups have also been advised of weather patterns and to make appropriate preparations," a spokesperson said.
From rescue volunteers to tradespeople, being on standby means preparing for situations they cannot always predict.
With equipment checked and vehicles ready, they are prepared to respond whenever their help is needed.
The Belfast area commander for the Community Rescue Service said: "Don't underestimate the weather"
Darren Harper is the Belfast area commander for the Community Rescue Service, whose volunteers are preparing to respond to emergencies.
He said severe weather can bring heavy rainfall, rising water levels and flooding, with volunteers placed on standby to respond if needed.
"Our main concern is the safety of the public," he said.
Harper explained that preparations involve checking vehicles and equipment to ensure volunteers are ready for any call out.
"Being on standby, our volunteers are ready to mobilise at a short notice," he said.
"They're checking over vehicles, checking over equipment and they're ready to assist their partner agencies and emergency services as and when the call comes."
He said the risks associated with severe weather should not be underestimated, particularly around rivers and areas prone to flooding.
"Take weather warnings seriously, avoid flooded roads and paths. Stay away from swollen rivers and never put yourself at risk by entering any flood water," he said.
"Don't underestimate the weather - and stay away from riverbanks," he added.
Harper said taking simple precautions could prevent people from getting into dangerous situations.
Charles Howard advised homeowners to inspect their roofs before and after storms, particularly for loose or damaged tiles
For roofer Charles Howard, storms can bring an overwhelming number of calls from people needing emergency repairs.
"Normally years ago you would have loved the storms, because obviously you got the influx of work," he said.
"But now because the storms are so regular, I kind of hate it."
During a storm early last year, Howard said he received about 800 messages from people seeking help.
"It's hard to actually keep control of it," he said.
He explained that preparing for particularly bad weather usually involves stocking his van with spare roof tiles and clearing his schedule to deal with emergency calls.
"If it's going to be a bad, bad storm, you just pretty much go and load the van up with all the salvage tiles and stuff like that," he said.

He said his work can begin even before the worst of a storm arrives, with strong winds already causing damage to roofs, advising homeowners to inspect their homes before and after storms, particularly for loose or damaged tiles.
He added that dislodged ridge tiles can fall onto driveways and gardens, potentially damaging vehicles.
Tree surgeon Callum Kirk, who works in the Newtownabbey area and covers much of Belfast, said storms bring a different kind of working day.
Instead of scheduled jobs, he must be prepared to respond to fallen trees and potentially dangerous situations.
"Whenever there's a storm, we have to be on standby for any trees that could come down over someone's driveway or their property," he said.
He said preparing for severe weather involves checking and sharpening equipment, even when there is no guarantee of being called out.
"You haven't got planned work, you don't know, it's sort of a surprise, you're just more or less going to help people," he said.
Kirk explained that much of his work comes after the worst of the weather has passed, when fallen trees need to be removed from roofs, garages and other properties.
He said that work can be particularly hazardous.
"If you see a tree that looks like it's going to fall, get in contact with someone before it's too late."
He encouraged homeowners to keep an eye on potentially unstable trees throughout the year, particularly as the storm season approaches.

items.title: How Brazil's changing working class is reshaping the presidential race
paragraphs: A student at a rally for President Lula da Silva
Reporting fromSão Paulo and Rio de Janeiro
In the sprawling former industrial city of Osasco, shuttered factories have given way to a shopping malls and delivery app tech companies in what is now dubbed São Paulo's "Silicon Valley."

The municipality voted for Brazil's left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in 2022 but switched to the right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of Brazil's presidential election this month. Bolsonaro won that vote - and now the two men face a run-off on Sunday. Since 1989, every first-round winner has gone on to be elected president.
Like many of President Lula's traditional supporters, Gilberto Almazan, who leads a metalworkers' union here, is visibly worried.

He cries when he tells Lula's life story: a boy who grew up in hunger in the north-east, who became a metalworker, then a union leader, then a three-time president. But he's candid about how things have changed here and how the union movement that was so integral to Lula's support base is stuck in the "Middle Ages", and struggling to keep up.
"We had strong deindustrialisation here," Almazan says. "The profile of the working class changed. They are no longer predominantly industrial workers, they are service workers.
"Metal, chemical, textile factories disappeared. And five malls were built."

The word "change" comes up repeatedly among Bolsonaro supporters here. Many struggle to name specific Bolsonaro policies they like but know they want to try something different: frustrated by the economy, crime and corruption in politics – even though Flávio has been faced accusations of corruption too, which he denies.
Tairine says high prices are a problem for her
"He brings the hope of change, that we can have a different Brazil," says lawyer Gisele Bonfim in Osasco, who decided to vote for Bolsonaro after supporting Lula in 2022.

Lula's re-election campaign has been hampered by voters turning away from him. In some cases, their frustration drove abstention, which was higher than average this year, but others like Gisele actively wanted something new.
One major reason for that is Brazil's working class has transformed seismically in places like Osasco.
Near one large shopping mall lies an open-air market where this shift is noticeable. Everyone is touting products, armed with a portable card machine.

Tairine, who sells hot dogs, used to abstain from voting, even though - as voting is compulsory in Brazil - not going to the polls incurs a fine. This year, she plans to vote for Bolsonaro. She points to high taxes paid on "everything" she buys and says these make it "so difficult for a poor person" dealing with inflation, arguing "nothing has changed" since Lula became president again.
Flávio Bolsonaro has proposed cutting government spending, government ministries, and some taxes - though he has said he'd maintain some of Lula's flagship welfare programmes.

For his supporters, Lula is a working-class hero credited with advancing workers' rights through organising strikes and lifting millions of people out of poverty with generous social welfare programmes as president.

But across Brazil millions now work in the gig economy, a phenomenon Almazan calls "Uber-isation": driving for Uber, delivering food, or running small businesses from market stalls to providing at-home beauty treatments.
"There are a lot of workers who need more freedom, flexibility of days and hours," he says, rather than the welfare and collective action Lula offered.
Robson used to support Lula but has since switched to support Bolsonaro

Richard Lapper, who has written biographies of both Lula and Jair Bolsonaro – Flavio's father who was president from 2019-2022 - says the rise of individualised work and the decline of manufacturing caused by globalisation are not unique to Brazil. But because Brazil industrialised late and deindustrialised early, he argues, the effects have been sharper here. He calls Lula a "victim of his own success."

Unemployment fell to a record low, and Brazil was taken off the United Nation's Hunger Map during Lula's current presidency. But Lapper describes a crisis of "expectations" where people are now better off but don't feel it because prices have risen and household debt and interest rates are high.
Robson, 53, is a municipal civil servant in Osasco. Originally from Lula's north-eastern home state of Pernambuco, he grew up supporting him.

But he describes a country now running deficits and says its citizens are enduring the "worst phase" of its tax burden, which he blames on the Lula government's "mismanagement" of the economy and high public spending.
"Now you have to make choices: pay an instalment for your car, or put food on the table," he says.

In some areas, Lula lost votes compared to 2022, even though Bolsonaro did not gain more than his father did then: 33 million people did not vote in the first round, the highest abstention since 1998.

In response, Lula's campaign has focused on mobilising hundreds of thousands of people – particularly students – on to the streets to get the vote out for round two. It claims one rally in São Paulo attracted about a million people.
"A lot of people didn't vote, they thought it wouldn't change anything," says one supporter, Leila. "Our fight is to make those people believe their vote changes things."
Aerial videos of these huge demonstrations have been plastered across social media. An image of a topless man with a six-pack waving a Lula flag at one has been shared tens of millions of times.
The strategy is that their revolution will not be televised, but it should ideally go viral.

Lula, 80, has also been using social media to dismiss criticisms that he is past his prime: calling himself the "king of selfies" and posting videos showing him running from A to B on the campaign trail.
Some people who live in the favelas fear security forces entering if Bolsonaro is elected
In Maré, one of Rio's largest favelas which is controlled by rival gangs, abstention was higher than average.

This dented Lula's support, even though he still won here: among Brazil's very poorest, Lula's welfare initiatives clearly do still resonate. One 18-year-old mother in Maré, Vitoria, earns less than £300 a month and praises Lula's government for increasing the minimum wage, giving workers the right to two days off, and providing essential medicines for free.
She is sceptical of Bolsonaro's plans to designate the gang which controls this part of the favela, Comando Vermelho, as a terrorist organisation, which he lobbied the US to do earlier this year.

She thinks it will lead to authorities entering the favela to "kill, destroy, ruin families, leave blood and bodies on the ground", citing a police raid in Rio last year that killed more than 130 people.
Another resident, Andreza Dionísio, blames high abstention rates here on both last-minute changes to polling station locations, but also "a sense of hopelessness about the future."
Many Brazilians now worship in evangelical churches like the Assembleia de Deus Vitória em Cristo

Increasingly, that void of hope is being filled by the growth of the evangelical church: about a quarter of Brazilians are now evangelical. Its mega-churches offer not just a spiritual home but support with issues like childcare, employment advice and even food.
Its conservative pastors are some of Brazil's most powerful political operators.

Silas Malafaia, who has millions of followers on social media, leads the Assembleia de Deus Vitória em Cristo headquartered in the lower middle-class neighbourhood of Penha in Rio de Janeiro. He is being investigated for allegedly obstructing the coup trial of Jair Bolsonaro, which he denies and calls politically motivated.

At one two-hour sermon he preaches messages of self-improvement to an emotional crowd of hundreds, interrupted occasionally for live music interludes and breaks to collect money with card machines. The whole event is live-streamed on YouTube.

Afterwards, in his office adorned with a photo of him and the former president Jair Bolsonaro, at whose wedding he officiated, he told the BBC that without the evangelical church in working-class neighbourhoods the country would be "in a state worse than you can imagine".
"It gives these people meaning. To better their lives."
Pastor Silas Malafaia officiated at Jair Bolsonaro's wedding
He argues Flávio Bolsonaro shares the church's values: for family, and against gender "ideology" and abortion.

The church is driving some to actively vote for Flávio Bolsonaro, but among much of Brazil's new working class, the first round feels more like a rejection of President Lula than an endorsement of his rival.
"There will never be another Lula," Gilberto Almazan fears. He intends this as a compliment, but Brazil's changing world of work means it's also probably true.
While Lula's past story still stirs great emotion for people like Almazan, his political fate may depend on whether voters think he can now offer Brazil a new one.

items.title: From Wildwood to John Legend: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead
paragraphs: Wildwood Out now If Pixar was a chocolate bar, it would be a Mars, while Laika – whose new film Wildwood incorporates themes of war and child abduction – would be something like Green & Blacks. Darker and with more esoteric flavours, this stop-motion animation is not so much for the nursery school crowd, but for discerning pre-teens and adults alike.

Ghosts: The Possession of Button House Out now The beloved BBC TV comedy gets a big-screen outing, with Simon Farnaby’s trouserless Tory MP ghost, Jim Howick’s dead scoutmaster, shot by a member of his own troop, Ben Willbond’s closeted second world war officer and the other regular cast members all returning.

Fatherland Out now Joint winner of the best director prize at Cannes, Paweł Pawlikowski’s latest is set during the cold war, and sees an actor, writer and rally driver, Erika (Sandra Hüller), set off on a road trip across Germany with her dear old dad, the Nobel prize-winning writer Thomas Mann (Hanns Zischler).

Ali G: Who Iz I? Out now Twenty four years after Ali G Indahouse opened at No 1 at the UK box office, Sasha Baron Cohen revives his alter-ego for a followup, making his directorial debut in the process. Morgana Robinson also stars. Catherine Bray

Suede, Manic Street Preachers OVO Hydro, Glasgow, 28 October; First Direct Bank Arena Leeds, 30 October; touring to 12 November Christmas comes early for people of a certain vintage with a penchant for evergreen British rock bands in the shape of this co-headline tour. Expect a smattering of newer material – Antidepressants, the most recent opus by Suede is Mercury-nominated – and some undeniable classics from both. Michael Cragg

Jasmine Myra Norwich Arts Centre, 27 October; Earth, London, 28 October; St George’s, Bristol, 29 October Alto saxophonist-composer Jasmine Myra is on the rise within the cinematic spiritual jazz orbit of Manchester’s Gondwana Records, a visionary operation devoted to the soulful lyricism and storytelling she espouses. This tour will be a fascinating insight into just how far the very promising Myra is instrumentally ready to go. John Fordham

False Idols Halloween Drumsheds, London, 24 October Queer club night False Idols returns to London for a special Halloween blowout featuring Boo! Bitch! hitmaker Kim Petras. Other spooky banger merchants on the bill include Swedish alt-popper Cobrah, London’s Rose Gray and US rapper Cakes da Killa. MC

London Symphony Orchestra/Pappano Barbican Hall, London, 29 October The LSO is the latest major international institution to commission British composer Hannah Kendall, a distinctive, ambitious voice in contemporary classical music. Her new work I Have Discovered the Secret of Death features Grammy-winning mezzo Fleur Barron. Its world premiere is paired with Tchaikovsky’s impassioned Fifth Symphony. Antonio Pappano conducts. Flora Willson

Wilhelmina Barns-Graham Tate St Ives, to 3 May A big part of St Ives’s modernist boom in the early 2oth century, Barns-Graham (work pictured above) quietly became one of the UK’s most important artists of her era with an emotional take on abstraction, celebrated here with 170 works from throughout her career.

LS Lowry MK Gallery, Milton Keynes, to 28 February This big celebration of the life and work of one of England’s best-loved artists is the first institutional show of his grimy, gritty industrial painting for 13 years, and marks 50 years since his death.

The Rupture: No Condition Is Permanent Talbot Rice Gallery, Edinburgh, to 13 February Attempting to respond to a time of unprecedented political, social and economic change, this exhibition brings together a huge cast of international artists to reckon with our increasingly broken systems.

The Way We Live The Box, Plymouth, to 21 February This exhibition looks at the idea of the home, and what it means to a variety of artists including the likes of Do Ho Suh, Rachel Whiteread and recent Turner prize winner Jasleen Kaur. Eddy Frankel

The Lives of Others Adelphi theatre, London, to 9 January Director Robert Icke adapts the Academy award-winning film set in East Berlin, 1984. A writer and an actor are put under state surveillance – and a Stasi operative is inexorably drawn into their lives. Keira Knightley, Stephen Dillane and Luke Thompson star. Miriam Gillinson

Macbeth Liquid & Envy, Oldham, to 7 November While Oldham’s Coliseum theatre is being restored, it is staging work in imaginative locations around town. This site-specific take on Macbeth is set in a real-life nightclub, invoking a world of 70s gangsters, casinos and shifting social codes. MG

Hansel & Gretel and the Witch Northern Stage, Newcastle upon Tyne, 29 October to 1 November Choreographer Liv Lorent and her company BalletLorent have really cornered the market in fairytale family shows with a bit of edge and a lot of imagination. The latest is a new take on Hansel & Gretel that promises a brand new ending courtesy of its writer, the former poet laureate Carol Ann Duffy. Lyndsey Winship

Susan Calman Touring to 20 November The Glaswegian standup has presented a slew of TV programmes and done a Strictly shift in the decade since her last tour, but new show Tall Tales – which combines showbiz stories with meditations on grief and depression – proves this glam career pivot has done nothing to dent her twinkly misanthropy. Rachel Aroesti

Nocturne Apple TV, 30 October Stephen Graham is back in his most sinister role yet: a serial killer who is apparently able to murder from the confines of his underground cell. This psychological thriller (above) pits him against not one but two haunted detectives: Liev Schreiber’s ex-soldier Jonah and his protege Saga (Zazie Beetz).

A Course Called Ireland iPlayer & BBC Two, 25 October, 9.30pm As a genre, the celebrity travelogue has become tired and bloated, but this new series is fuelled by an unusual level of star power, as the one and only Bill Murrray embarks on a golf-based trip around Ireland. Extra craic comes courtesy of guests including Chris O’Dowd and Joanne McNally.

Minimum Wage Netflix, 25 October What started out as a micro-budget webseries about incompetent teens manning a pizzeria has been turned into a 28-part sitcom by Netflix, who will be hoping its cast – including newly recruited SNL cast member Grace Reiter – become comedy’s next big things.

Beat Luke Littler Netflix, 30 October Is darts really that hard? Find out this Friday, as 20 amateurs take on the 19-year-old world No 1 in Manchester in an attempt to win £501,000. The event will be streamed live, with Gary Lineker on hosting duties and Richard Osman contributing Pointless-style statistics. RA

Pardon My French Toast PC, Switch 2, out 29 October A brightly coloured 3D platformer, in which you’re a slice of anthropomorphic brioche toast able to cover himself in different spreads to gain a range of special abilities. Like a ZX Spectrum classic reheated for the 21st century.

Phantom Blade Zero PC, PS5, out 29 October An elite assassin is framed for murder and must prove his innocence while a fatal wound slowly kills him. Stylised martial arts in a dark fantasy realm? Hand me that sword. Keith Stuart

Michael Kiwanuka - Fudge Out now Originally due for release last autumn, this fifth album from the Brit-nominated Kiwanuka was delayed after he suffered a haemorrhagic stroke after returning home from a tour. While his recovery continues, the self-produced Fudge is a reminder of his immense talents, as showcased on opener Summer Clothes’ gospel-tinged swirl.

Sasha Alex Sloan – And the Crowd Goes Mild Out now The Boston-born singer-songwriter, who’s co-written songs for the likes of Olivia Rodrigo, Charli xcx and Karol G, returns with her fourth album. As the title suggests, Sloan’s own songs veer towards the doleful, with singles Glitter and Empty pairing rich melodies with soothing soft-rock flourishes.

Claud - Me and the Music Out now Co-produced alongside John Congleton (Alvvays, St Vincent), Brooklyn-based Claud’s third album marks a shift in their mindset. While 2023’s lauded Supermodel took things very seriously, Me and the Music finds a lightness in a heavy world, especially on She Doesn’t Love Me’s effervescent indie jangle.

John Legend - Muse Out now After dabbling in music for children with 2024’s lullaby-centric My Favourite Dream, the Egot winner returns to more grownup themes on this entirely Pharrell-produced 11th album. The soulful Daylight is an upbeat love song, while the more politically focused Fireflies fuses jazz and gospel. MC

The One About Matthew Perry Netflix, 27 October A moving film recounting the life and career of the late Friends actor charting his rise to TV stardom and lifelong battles with addiction, as well as the tabloid scandals that accompanied his fame.

How Houdini Made Magic Podcast TV’s favourite illusionist Derren Brown tells the story of one of magic’s most iconic figures, Harry Houdini, in this 10-part series. Brown builds a fascinating picture of how Houdini fashioned himself a modern celebrity image.

3ETV Somerset House Channel London cultural institution Somerset House is celebrating the 10th anniversary of its experimental interdisciplinary Studios space with this diverse online channel featuring archived performance pieces, documentary shorts and new commissions. Ammar Kalia

items.title: John Healey pledges to use budget to harness power of AI to bolster Britain’s security
paragraphs: John Healey has pledged to use Wednesday’s budget to harness the power of artificial intelligence to bolster Britain’s security and prosperity against the risks in the accelerating global technology arms race.

As he prepares for his debut budget, the chancellor said that Andy Burnham’s government would commit hundreds of millions of pounds to develop a “distinctively British” approach to AI that would capitalise on the benefits of the frontier technology.

At a fork in the road as AI developments pose both existential threats and transformative economic potential, Healey said he would be making the biggest ever investment to guard against cyber risks and the disruptive potential of the technology.

As part of the measures in his tax and spending statement, he promised fresh investment for Britain’s AI Security Institute and other critical institutions, alongside allocating public money to support the use of the technology for good.
“AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school and every aspect of our economy can benefit,” Healey said.

“I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI – one that doesn’t leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country.”

Three months into Burnham’s premiership, Healey is poised to deliver a budget against an increasingly volatile backdrop as the war in the Middle East sends shock waves through the global economy, putting pressure on public finances and reigniting the cost of living crisis.

The chancellor has vowed to use his first budget to provide households and businesses with “breathing space” as the global surge in energy costs triggered by the war hits millions of families this winter. On Friday, the latest tensions in the Gulf sent the oil price to its highest level for six months, rising above $117 a barrel at one point.

However he will also use the opportunity afforded by the critical speech to the Commons to flesh out Burnham’s policy priorities for government after he replaced Keir Starmer this summer, and to spell out a vision for Britain amid the increasingly turbulent global economic outlook.

Aiming to harness the opportunities of AI to raise living standards, back UK businesses and support economic growth, the chancellor said he wanted to seize the opportunities of the technology as a central plank of Labour’s plan for growth.

It comes after official figures show AI investment has helped the UK outperform gloomy economic forecasts as the Iran war pushes up inflation and drags down business confidence, powering the country to the strongest growth performance in the G7 in the first half of this year.

However, there are growing fears over the security of the nation and critical industries as the technology opens up the danger of cyber-attacks, IT systems turning rogue and devastating job losses as companies invest in machines rather than humans.

It comes as websites around the globe went dark this week after a serious vulnerability was found in a computer language used to build much of the world wide web, in a development made possible by rapid AI advances. It also emerged this week that Barclays is cutting 5,000 jobs as part of cost-saving plans identified by bosses as the rollout of AI across the bank helps it make efficiency gains.

Healey said he wanted to use his budget to protect against risks while also nurturing homegrown businesses and talent, in order to cut Britain’s dependency on other countries that were also making strides in AI technology.
New investments would be made in AI chip design capability in Edinburgh, alongside a new AI Centre of Excellence in Manchester that it said would enable the UK to harness the technology’s benefits.
The government would also spend £10m a year to lead the UK’s work on understanding how AI will reshape jobs and industry, aiming to address concerns about potential job disruption.

As part of the plan the Treasury said it would back up to £300m in public-private investment in a new AI Biosecurity Lab, designed to serve as a world-leading institution bringing together scientific expertise to protect people from emerging biological threats.
It comes after the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, warned on Thursday that UK households should make preparations against the mounting risks from weather, cyber or other serious emergencies.

The advice to stock up on supplies to last 72 hours, in a campaign called Be Ready, comes as Silicon Valley bosses sound the alarm over the increasingly existential threats AI could pose, and amid growing official concern over the impact of the climate crisis, technological dependency and hostile state threats.
Dan Jarvis, the security minister, said: “I’m proud the UK has repeatedly been at the forefront of global efforts to use AI for the benefit of humankind.
“Today’s investment will help the UK seize the opportunities AI presents to strengthen our national security, while staying one step ahead of those who seek to use AI to do us harm.”

items.title: This week we launched the new Dezeen website
paragraphs: This week on Dezeen, we unveiled the updated Dezeen website, which is “richer and more versatile” while better reflecting what Dezeen is today.

We worked with creative technology studio Made by On to refresh the look and feel of the site, building upon the foundation laid by designer Micha Weidmann, who designed the original Dezeen logo and layout. It is the first time the Dezeen website has been since 2016, after originally being launched as a basic WordPress blog by our founder Marcus Fairs in 2006.
“The new website is faster, richer and, we hope, more enjoyable to use,” Dezeen co-CEO Ben Hobson said. “It also better reflects what Dezeen is today.”
In China, international studio Snøhetta unveiled the landmark Shanghai Grand Opera House this week, which it designed to be “as much a civic destination as a performance venue”.
The striking building features a giant spiral staircase that guides visitors to the roof.

The historic town hall in the city of Limoges in France was set on fire, as an estimated 550,000 people in France took to the streets over the weekend to protest the rising cost of living and poor school conditions.
The fire destroyed significant parts of the 143-year-old Limoges Town Hall, with videos showing its slate roofs ablaze and its central bell tower collapsing.

Also in France, architecture studio OMA unveiled the Palais de Justice de Lille, a law court in northern France. The six-sided building has a pointy, hexagonal form, with each elevation finished in coloured glass.
It was designed to mimic a nearby star-shaped fortification, built in 1667 by the French military engineer Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban.

Design Miami.Paris took place in Paris this week, with technology brand Apple unveiling its Designers of Tomorrow. Among the pieces on show were a banana-palm-paper lantern and furniture with an acid-etched stainless-steel surface.
We also visited Dutch Design Week, which featured an installation that explored “hydrofeminism” and saw students protest against overcrowded workspaces.
Popular projects on Dezeen this week include a David Chipperfield museum for a single artwork, architect Diana Kellogg’s update of her Tribeca home and a textured home in Mexico.
Our podcast this week asked: has Tesla really made a flying car?
This week on Dezeen is our regular roundup of the week’s top news stories. Subscribe to our newsletters to be sure you don’t miss anything.

items.title: Arrest made after fire at Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat
paragraphs: Police in the south German state of Bavaria have detained a suspect during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.
Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 (19:15 GMT) on Friday, and firefighters found it engulfed in flames.
Difficult terrain was hindering efforts to extinguish the blaze and it was still burning early on Saturday, police said, with some 200 emergency personnel deployed. There were no reports of injuries.
The Nazi dictator used the retreat, which lies above the town of Berchtesgaden, as a part-time seat of government and met commanders there to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941.
A criminal investigation is under way to determine whether the suspect is connected to the fire.
Hitler also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.

items.title: Met investigates reports of letter detailing claims about Meghan's father
paragraphs: Instead, Scotland Yard has opened an inquiry to confirm the claim that the Met's royal protection unit passed on the letter to the Duchess eight years ago.
According to the Sun, the letter was sent to a Met Police unit tasked with dealing with individuals posing a threat to Royals and politicians - the Fixated Threat Assessment Centre.
A Met spokesperson said: "We are aware of media reports that officers from the Met's Royalty and Specialist Protection Command were involved in the passing on of a letter in 2018.
"We are undertaking inquiries internally in an effort to confirm this."
Thomas Markle moved to the Philippines in 2025 after a series of strokes.
He is reportedly now living in a rehabilitation centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk again, after having a leg amputated during surgery in December 2025.
In her statement on Friday, Meghan said that when she received the letter outlining allegations against her father in 2018, she was "given assurance that these were being investigated".
Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, told the Sun that he had allegedly found child abuse images at his father's home in the Philippines and reported it to the police.

The Undersecretary for the Philippines Department of Justice, Nicholas Ty, told the BBC that "the matter is currently being investigated" by an anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force in Cebu.
Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately told the BBC that national police had secured Thomas Markle Snr's computer to conduct a comprehensive digital forensic examination.

Investigators there are currently analysing the data to determine the full scope and extent of his alleged criminal activities, with the minister saying it would take one week to get the forensic results.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigations said it was "aware of the allegations", adding it would "provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities".
The FBI's statement continued: "We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of US law."
Meghan is the only child of Thomas Markle's marriage to her mother, Doria Ragland, but he has two other children - Samantha and Thomas Markle Jr - from an earlier marriage.
The relationship between Meghan and her father, a former TV lighting director, broke down in the run-up to her wedding in 2018.
At the time, Thomas Markle was found to have colluded with photographers, accepting payment to stage photographs of him preparing for the wedding.
It is understood that Meghan first learnt about the allegations against her father shortly after she married the Duke of Sussex Prince Harry.
Sources close to the Sussexes said Meghan could not speak publicly about the allegations when she first learned of them, in order to avoid jeopardising any future investigation.
Speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her, the sources said.

items.title: Second storm to hit UK with more wind and rain as thousands remain without power
paragraphs: Rough sea along the Dorset coastline on Friday
A second storm in as many days is set to batter parts of the UK, as thousands of homes remain without power following powerful winds and heavy rain on Friday.

Storm Boelo is forecast to hit on Saturday, with an amber weather warning issued from 21:00 BST across much of Scotland as well as parts of Northern Ireland and northern England where gusts of up to 80mph (128km/h) could lash exposed areas.
Travel chaos, power cuts and localised flooding are all possible as the storm sweeps in on Saturday.
The warning comes just one day after Storm Austen unleashed wind gusts in excess of 75mph, resulting in toppled trees, transport disruption and thousands of power outages.
Strong winds and heavy rain will persist over the weekend as Storm Boelo moves across parts of the country.

An amber weather warning for wind has been issued for across much of Scotland, excluding the Northern Isles, as well as the far north of Northern Ireland and England from 21:00 BST on Saturday to 21:00 BST on Sunday.
Wind gusts of 60-70mph are forecast, with exposed coastal areas potentially seeing speeds of up to 80mph.
The Central Lowlands could also experience periods of disruption as strong winds funnel through the region.
Travel disruption is expected - with ScotRail has confirming that some train services will be cancelled after 21:00 on Saturday - while damage caused by the winds could lead to additional power cuts.
An amber wind warning for Saturday covers much of Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England.

The second bout of bad weather comes after Austen, the first named storm of the season, brought strong wind gusts to large parts of southern England and Wales throughout Friday. Bad weather disrupted travel with fallen trees blocking railway lines and roads.
In Brighton, part of the iconic West Pier - an abandoned structure that first opened in 1866 - collapsed into the sea.
The National Grid said engineers had restored power to more than 60,000 properties since Storm Austen began - but more than 10,000 homes were still without power on Friday evening.
Storm Boelo is forecast to bring widespread heavy rain and gales across the UK
Yellow weather warnings for wind on Saturday cover Orkney, the rest of Northern Ireland and northern England.
Gusts of 55-75mph are possible in these areas, with isolated gusts potentially reaching 80mph.
While the worst of Saturday's weather is forecast to be felt in areas covered by warnings, heavy and persistent rain is expected across larger parts of the UK.
Spray and surface water could make driving conditions hazardous, while further downpours increase the risk of localised flooding.
Strong winds are forecast to continue into Sunday, although rain should gradually ease across most of the country.
Sunny spells and blustery showers are expected elsewhere, while north-east Scotland is likely to see the most persistent rainfall.
Watch: Homes without power as Storm Austen batters Britain
Once the weekend's stormy weather has passed, forecasts suggest another area of low pressure will develop over the Atlantic before deepening as it approaches the UK from the south-west.
This could bring a further spell of wet and potentially very windy weather to much of the country on Monday and into Tuesday.
Whether the system will be strong enough to be named remains uncertain.
Later in the week, high pressure is expected to build over the near continent, bringing a return to drier, calmer and more settled conditions.
It is not unusual for storms to arrive one after another – in fact, they often develop in clusters, particularly during periods of unsettled weather across the Atlantic.

A strong jet stream is needed to help rapidly develop powerful windstorms. The process involves warmer air being pushed northwards and colder air moving southwards across large areas of the Atlantic, creating a sharp contrast in temperatures.
These temperature differences provide favourable conditions for new low-pressure systems to form and strengthen.

If these systems are then steered beneath a developing, powerful jet stream, they can intensify rapidly, potentially becoming named storms capable of bringing damaging winds, heavy rain and widespread disruption as they move towards the UK.

items.title: Typhoon Champi kills one and injures more than 500 in Taiwan as it heads to China
paragraphs: Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.

Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).
The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.
Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan.
Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.
Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.
Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.
Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.

items.title: Embattled Greens senator Jordon Steele-John confirms leave from parliament after allegations against him made public
paragraphs: Jordon Steele-John has confirmed he will not attend parliament next week as the embattled Greens senator apologises for publicly releasing the letter outlining the claims against him.

On Saturday afternoon, Steele-John removed a social media post containing a three-page letter marked as “confidential” sent to Greens leader, David Shoebridge, earlier this month. The letter urged an investigation into allegations he had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025.
Jordon Steele-John has denied all allegations made against him.
The Western Australian senator said he’d heard the full letter had been circulating online and “didn’t want to be seen as hiding from it”.
“I’m now not sure that was the right call and I’ve taken it down. I am really sorry for any additional stress it caused,” he said on social media.
