After days of confusion following historical complaints about alleged misconduct were publicly aired in the media, the now-deleted statement posted to social media late Friday night said he considered attending Senate estimates virtually but was told it would be “unacceptable”.
He would instead focus on seeing through an independent investigation to its conclusion, he said.

“Over the past few days there has been a growing chorus calling on me not to attend parliament next week. I have explored attending digitally but have been informed that would also be unacceptable,” Steele-John said.
Steele-John said a precedent of keeping parliamentarians out of parliament after “allegations of allegations” are made had now been set.
“Had an allegation or complaint been made against me, I would have taken these actions immediately,” he said.
The 32-year-old senator’s attendance in parliament for the remainder of the year had been uncertain after a public stoush with Shoebridge, over whether he was on leave during the investigation.
The complaints are now subject to an independent investigation commissioned by the WA Greens and have been referred to the Independent Parliamentary Standards Commission.
Shoebridge claimed Steele-John had requested leave and he accepted it last week after seven party members penned a letter to the leader urging an investigation into the claims.

The three-page letter sent on 13 October, and first published by the Nine newspapers, said the authors had been “made aware of multiple allegations of serious misconduct” against Steele-John about his “behaviour in the presence of women”.
The letter referred to an allegation of sexual harassment at a Greens campaign event in 2024 that the alleged victim had not reported out of fear and backlash. The letter provided no further detail.

In another, the authors referred to an allegation of “serious sexual misconduct” in 2025. Steele-John later responded this was alleged by a former partner, and was investigated by Western Australian police with a finding of “no charges”.
Guardian Australia has confirmed the WA police told Steele-John the investigation was closed in May with no charges.
Also contained in the letter was a reference to a disparaging nickname for Steele-John – “feels on wheels” – which the authors said implied he had a reputation for acting inappropriately.

“To be clear, all signatories to this letter know that an allegation does not equate to a fact and/or guilt. We simply believe that it is in the party’s best interests to ensure that every allegation is investigated thoroughly, in alignment with community and member expectations,” the letter’s authors wrote.

Steele-John was defiant in a lengthy statement last Sunday, rejecting the allegations against him, denying he agreed to take leave from parliament and accusing an internal faction within the Greens of playing “nasty political games” in their decision to release the letter to the media.

Steele-John said any claims of his alleged behaviour should be investigated “fairly and thoroughly” but accused an “unofficial faction” within the WA branch had released the complaint letter to the media in a bid to oust him from the Senate.

items.title: Helen Haines’s condition improves days after losing both legs from alleged attack
paragraphs: Independent MP Helen Haines’s condition has been downgraded to serious but stable after she lost both legs following an alleged attack near her electorate office in north-east Victoria on Monday afternoon.
The Alfred hospital in Melbourne provided an update on Haines’s condition on Saturday morning.
“The patient is in a serious but stable condition at The Alfred on Saturday morning,” a spokesperson for the hospital said.

Haines, the federal MP for the Victorian seat of Indi, had been in a critical but stable condition after she was struck by a car in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon. Surgeons were trying to save her right leg but both legs had to be amputated due to the seriousness of her injuries.
The MP’s husband, Phil Haines, provided an update at the Alfred hospital on Wednesday, saying “both her heart and her mind are in good shape.”
“I think when we reflect and talk about and think about Helen, the two most important parts of Helen for us as a family are her heart and her mind,” he said.

“Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person. Incredibly supportive of all around her – her family, her community, anybody she comes across. And her mind. She has the sharpest intellect.”

Police on Tuesday charged Brendan Nugent, 43, from nearby Tarrawingee with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official. Police have since charged him with two additional offences – cultivating and possessing cannabis – according to court documents.
Nugent appeared at the Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday and did not apply for bail.
On Friday, an update on Haines’s social media accounts said her staff were working to reopen her electorate offices next Thursday.
“What happened on Monday has deeply affected Helen’s family and all of her staff. Many of us witnessed the incident and some were among the first to come to her aid,” the post read.

“As Helen takes the time she needs to recover, we will take time to look after ourselves and one another, too. Healing will take time, and we ask for your understanding as we navigate the days and weeks ahead.”

Haines’ staff said they had been overwhelmed with kindness shown by the local community in Indi and across Australia and the globe. They said more than $730,000 had been raised for Save the Children in Haines’ honour after her husband directed people to donate to the special appeal as his wife recovered.
“We are deeply moved by the extraordinary generosity of so many people,” the post read.

The alleged attack on Haines has reverberated through Australian politics, prompting conversations about the temperature of political debat, security risks for MPs and mental health services in regional Victoria.

WA Police charged a 56-year-old man after allegedly threatening staff and wielding nunchucks at the electoral office of the the state’s local government minister, Hannah Beazley, days after the alleged attack on Haines.
A community vigil was held for Haines in Wodonga on Wednesday evening after it was revealed the MP had lost both her legs following Monday’s alleged attack.
Haines’s predecessor as the federal member for Indi, Cathy McGowan, said on the sidelines of the event the community was grappling with “mixed emotions”.

items.title: Severe flooding hits Four Corners region, more expected through the weekend
paragraphs: Floodwaters surround trailers at the Fun Valley Family Resort campground and RV part in South Fork, Colo., early Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. South Fork Fire Rescue/AP hide caption

Looking out a window on Friday afternoon, Devin Neeley saw light, puffy clouds and a blue sky in San Juan County, N.M. The county's public information officer for emergency management called it "surreal."
Meanwhile, brown rainwaters were flooding homes in low-lying areas of the county and forcing sewage into the San Juan River.
"[The sky] belies really the danger that is coming down the river in historic levels," Neeley says. "We have not seen flooding like this in generations."

Neeley says, emergency responders rescued people on their roofs after floodwater inundated their homes. The county is under an emergency declaration and residents in susceptible areas were told to evacuate Thursday afternoon.
"These are communities that have beautiful riverfront places to live," Neeley says. "And unfortunately, that's a problem today."
Rare, heavy rainfall started to hit the Four Corners region — which includes New Mexico, Colorado, Utah and Arizona — on Wednesday.
Since then, severe, brown-colored floodwaters have led to road closures, mandatory evacuations and emergency declarations across the four states.
Areas of southern Utah, southwest Colorado, and the northern parts of Arizona and New Mexico were drenched with rain leading to rapidly rising floodwaters, Thursday and Friday.

In response to a post on X that showed brownish-red floodwaters in Hurricane, Utah, Gov. Spencer Cox, wrote on Thursday: "Our hearts are with the families whose homes and livelihoods have been impacted."
We are closely monitoring the flash flooding in Hurricane. Our hearts are with the families whose homes and livelihoods have been impacted.
Please follow all evacuation orders and local emergency guidance. We’re grateful to the first responders working to keep Utahns safe. https://t.co/8hDQ85T0Xz

The southern Utah city issued an emergency declaration on Thursday after flooding damaged more than 100 homes and Rvs. People were seen leading horses to safety through ankle-deep water, in a video posted by the National Weather Service.
In Farmington, N.M., at the center of the devastation, Police Chief Steve Hebbe said at a press conference on Friday that "this is singular and this is real."
"So far, we have not had any deaths that is very fortunate, but this is not something that should be played with," Hebbe said.
Colorado Gov. Jared Polis declared disaster emergencies for 11 counties. Polis also authorized the use of National Guard members to assist with rescue efforts in southwest Colorado.

The police department for the Navajo Nation, which spans across northeastern Arizona, northwestern New Mexico, and southeastern Utah, said on Thursday that authorities had rescued seven families, 30 people, from their flooded homes. The Hopi Tribe in northeastern Arizona declared a state of emergency on Thursday due to heavy rainfall damaging roads, bridges, homes and other infrastructure.
The Archuleta County Sheriff's office in Colorado warned residents to shelter in place Friday morning, and by the evening had issued an evacuation warning.
The flooding comes after extreme weather hit the Southwest throughout the week. Arizona saw baseball-sized hail and a possible tornado that injured at least one person Wednesday evening.
The region's mountainous terrain is conducive to flooding. In August, intense flash flooding in the Grand Canyon led to multiple deaths.

Severe thunderstorm warnings started earlier in the week, says Kris Sanders, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Grand Junction, Colo. The remnants of Hurricane Trudy, which was active from Oct. 15 to Oct. 18, in the Pacific Ocean formed into a slow-moving low-pressure system that worked its way southwest.

Sanders says a lot of the storms weakened as they came through the region, but the heavy rain did not. Portions of southwest Colorado and southeast Utah saw two to four inches, whereas areas with higher elevations, like the San Juan Mountains, got up to six inches. This caused small creeks and streams and rivers to flood.
"Those rainfall amounts are records in themselves," Sanders says.

While the amount of rainfall is rare, he says, these storms typically happen in the region at this time of year. An event last year caused major flooding in the same spots, "like a carbon copy" of this year, Sanders says.
The threat is not over, he says, and thunderstorm watches are active in many of the same areas through Sunday.

Daniel Swain, a climate scientist with the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, says the severe thunderstorms are fueled by the large amount of moisture in the air. He says that moisture comes from the record-warm waters off parts of the West Coast, which are driven by a strong El Niño event and a preexisting marine heat wave (which he attributes largely to human-caused climate change).

The flooding isn't a surprise, he says, pointing to a prediction he and others made in the spring — that if El Niño materialized according to forecasts, southwestern U.S. could see extreme precipitation events through October.
Now, "that is exactly what we've seen," he says, "because this isn't even the first event this fall."
Neeley, the public information officer in San Juan County, N.M., says his community will be on alert for more damage and safety risks throughout the weekend.
"People are concerned about their life and their welfare and their property," Neeley says. "This is going to be a long term impact to this community,"

items.title: Rubio tells Cubans ‘now is the time’ to act to see political change
paragraphs: Marco Rubio urged Cubans seeking political change in their country to act, saying “now is the time” moments after Donald Trump told a Friday rally for candidates in south Florida that US warships could intervene in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war.

The US secretary of state, in his social media post addressed “to those who seek to create positive change”, urged Cubans to capitalize on Trump’s plans. “The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA,” Rubio said.

The top US diplomat, whose parents left Cuba for the United States before the socialist revolution there, seemed to mistakenly use the word “discrete”, meaning separate, rather than “discreet”, meaning private or secret.

Trump first floated this idea earlier this year, but has not mentioned it in recent months. But he revived it in response to a shouted question from the crowd about the island nation. He was campaigning just days before midterm elections in which voters have expressed concern about the impact the US war on Iran has had on prices of goods from gas to groceries.

“We’ll do a little stopover,” Trump said. “Actually, what we’re going to do with Cuba is, we’re going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands. And then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”
Havana on Friday mocked the “desperation” of the US following the comments made by Rubio and Trump.
“Now the United States is resorting to public recruitment for the CIA,” Cuban deputy foreign minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossio wrote on X.
“There must be a great deal of desperation or misery within the agency for it to be forced to sell its services like a tube of toothpaste.”

Rubio and Trump have been bullish on action in Cuba, with Trump previously suggesting the country would “be next” in terms of intervention abroad, following the winding down of the Iran war he has long forecast but which has not yet happened.

In May, he and Rubio raised the specter of US military intervention in Cuba, a renewed threat that took on greater weight after the administration announced criminal charges against the island’s former leader, Raúl Castro. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that previous US presidents had considered intervening in Cuba for decades but that “it looks like I’ll be the one that does it”.

Rubio told reporters separately that Cuba had been a national security threat for years because of its ties to US adversaries and that Trump was intent on addressing it. While saying the Trump administration wanted to resolve differences with Cuba peacefully, Rubio voiced doubts that the US could reach a diplomatic resolution with the island’s current government.
Rubio has not addressed Cuba in depth in public for several weeks, with his last comments coming in a 29 September interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity.

“The truth is Cuba has already fallen. It doesn’t have a functional economy and it’s governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that’s never worked,” Rubio said, without alluding to any CIA operation.

“We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful … that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they’re facing. We’re never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear.”

Rubio and other top Trump aides have met with Cuban officials in recent months to explore possible improvements in relations. But the US side has come away unimpressed from those talks, leading to even more sanctions imposed on the Cuban government.

During his address to the United Nations general assembly last month, Trump said Rubio – son of Cuban immigrants, who has long taken a hard line against Cuba’s socialist leadership – was “deep into negotiations with Cuba”, saying he would “not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep”.
Days later, Trump told reporters that he anticipated that the two countries “will make a deal”, adding: “I don’t think we’ll need the military. Cuba is failing very badly.”

Earlier this week, the two countries clashed at the United Nations as the Trump administration sought once again to build opposition for an upcoming annual vote condemning Washington’s decades-long economic embargo against Havana.

Cuba has struggled since 2020 with an economic and energy crisis. Its gross domestic product has shrunk , and its 10 million residents have endured blackouts, food shortages and inflation. There have been waves of protests, and hundreds of thousands of Cubans have immigrated, many to the United States.

items.title: How does the UK state pension compare with other countries?
paragraphs: Getting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fund our later years, and how much we'll get, has been a hot topic.

The triple lock formula - state pensions increasing by the greatest of 2.5%, earnings growth, or inflation - means those benefits have risen far faster than the earnings of workers since its introduction in 2011.
But as housing costs have also been rising fast, pensioner poverty has actually increased slightly in the last decade.

Nevertheless, even if you take those costs into consideration, pensioners are less likely to be in relative poverty - that is, having to get by on less than 60% of the income of the typical household - than families with children or working-age people.

And funding the triple lock has already cost the state billions more than initially envisaged. With that cost set to balloon further, the debate over whether that is sustainable, or fair, has raged for a while.

Andy Burnham intends to start a new system in a few years, which would see the state pension increase by at least inflation or 2.5%, and remove the automatic annual link with average earnings. It will likely mean less generous increases, although it will keep track with earnings growth over the longer term.
But are pensioners being short-changed in other ways? How do we compare with other countries?
One way of measuring that is to look at how generous the typical pension is relative to workers' average earnings - the replacement rate.
The OECD considers the outlook for those born at the start of the millennium in different countries on average wages, and assumes the pension system as it existed in 2022 is in place.
On that basis, looking at the basic state pension, retirement benefits in the UK look low compared with other wealthy countries.
And that is even when you consider that our system compels workers to be automatically enrolled in occupational schemes.
If you consider both of those, then after tax, UK retirement benefits would be 54.2% of average UK earnings, compared with an average of 63.2% across wealthy countries.
But then there is income from other occupational and personal pensions, which are more prevalent in the UK. Include those and the gap narrows.
However, that does also mean that those relying on just the state pension for their incomes are a fair bit worse off than many retired people elsewhere.
So does that make the case for boosting spending on public pensions in the UK?
Well, the amount spent on the state pension is set to top £150bn a year, the single most expensive benefit to fund.
But other figures from the OECD show that the UK state spends a lower amount on total retirement benefits, relative to the size of its economy, than the average wealthy country.
Firstly, this is about political choices, and the UK chooses to dedicate larger amounts to items such as universal healthcare.
And secondly, with ageing populations, the OECD reckons the amount needed for pensions may be set to soar in many nations by 2060 (the exceptions largely being those that are deploying changes).
Its predictions for the UK are likely to rise by less under the revised triple lock system being put in place by Andy Burnham but it may still mean more borrowing.
As it is, £1 in every £13 the UK government spends is to pay the interest on existing debt. And countries with more generous pensions, such as Italy, have faced pressure to reform.

So in many ways, with auto-enrolment into workplace pensions, the UK appears to be ahead of the game in insisting on universal privately funded pensions for workers. But that system raises another issue: the gender pension gap.
The gender pension gap is the difference between the average pension income of men and women aged 65 and over, as a percentage of men's average pension income.
It found that the typical gap in most wealthy countries is around 22.8% in favour of men.

But in the UK women typically get a pension that is a third less than what a man gets - in the main, due to the reliance on private pensions - although it should be noted that the most recent data the OECD has for the UK is for 2021.
Women are more likely to have received lower pay over the course of their working lives, taken career breaks or worked part time. And the hit to pension pots can be stark.
So step back and look at the big picture and British pensioners - and those who have yet to retire - may feel others have it better elsewhere.
But the message from all of this isn't to dwell on outrage but to take action.
The state pension has become more generous over the years, but if you want to enjoy the same kind of retirement as those elsewhere, get saving.
That is - if you can, and if you haven't left it too late.

items.title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
paragraphs: The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.
As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit £100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms.
The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats.
"AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said.
"I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI.
"One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country."
The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge.

But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops.
"That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said.
"By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain's industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country."
The AI Biosecurity Lab's creation will also be supported by leading AI developers, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing £200m worth of AI model credits that can be spent on the use of their models.
The Chancellor's plans to boost AI spending will also see an additional £120m committed to the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI).

Established by the former Conservative government in 2023, the lab evaluates the risks of the most advanced and powerful models - and has been championed for its role in helping build a collaborative and open approach to AI testing.

The additional funding announced by the Chancellor will aim to help ensure the lab can continue its efforts and work, particularly amid growing calls for technical standards and guardrails for AI development.

It will come alongside a £60m investment in what it coined a "National Cyber Shield" which it said would use agentic AI to boost cyber-defences, and £70m funding towards a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.
This, it said, would harness AI tools to detect cyber vulnerabilities across the UK's critical infrastructure and economy.

It comes after the UK government revealed it was among organisations around the world to have taken some sites offline as a precaution after critical flaws were surfaced in a popular programming language.

Researchers who helped surface the vulnerabilities in PHP - a popular server-side scripting language used in web development for decades - warned platforms which use it could be exposed to potential hacks.
There have been no reports of any successful exploits of the flaw, coined php2shell, so far.
But experts have warned that the incident shows how quickly and easily bugs which have lain long dormant may be surfaced - and potentially exploited - using AI.

items.title: Before you crank up the thermostat, try these tips to keep your house warmer for longer
paragraphs: Cora Harrison says she saves money by only turning on heating in rooms her family is using

As the UK braces for a chilly weekend, with powerful winds and heavy rain hitting parts of the country, people are looking for ways to bring some warmth to their homes without cranking up the heating just yet. It is autumn after all.
But with rising energy prices making heating homes more expensive, taking action now could pay off in the long run.
Experts warn, though, that if you're elderly or vulnerable you shouldn't compromise your health.
To help you prepare for the chillier months, BBC News asked families and experts to share their tips for keeping your home warm and cost-effective.
When it gets cold, many people turn to hot water bottles and blankets - but there are other ways to warm your body.
The British Heart Foundation recommends wearing lots of thin layers, rather than one thick layer, to trap the heat in.
Natalie, 29, says she's replaced some of the clothes she wears round the house with supermarket thermal leggings and tops and says "it's made such a difference".
Amber Waring, 27, from Devon, says she eats warm meals like stews and pasta bakes, and dances round the kitchen with her toddler while they cook to help keep warm.
Amber Waring turns to warming meals such as pasta bake, fish pie and stew
With the clocks going back this weekend, the nights will be drawing in.
So if you have a thicker duvet, now is the time to bring it out. Some supermarkets sell winter duvets for under £20 - look for 10.5 tog or higher.

But there's something to be said for a craftily placed blanket, too. When it gets cold, Rebecca, 44, from Hertfordshire, sleeps with a blanket underneath her mattress, which she says stops draughts. "This was passed to me by my nan, she swore by it," she says. Others swear by placing a blanket above the mattress but under the bedsheet.

You can heat your bed before getting in with a hot water bottle, but make sure you check the expiry date. A guide by NHS Scotland, external says to let the water from the kettle cool for a few minutes before filling, only fill it two-thirds full, squeeze air out of the top before putting the stopper on, and don't hold it directly against your skin.

Using an electric blanket - to heat your bed before you get in or to wrap around yourself on the sofa - is "one of the cheapest ways" to stay warm, says Emily Seymour, energy editor at consumer organisation Which?. Testing by Which?, external shows it typically costs between 2p and 8p an hour to run an electric blanket at its highest setting. The London Fire Brigade, external says to unplug your blanket before you get into bed unless it has a thermostat control, not to use a hot water bottle at the same time, and replace it every 10 years.
Keep doors closed to trap heat in the room you're in. You can place curtains or blankets over your doors for extra insulation.
Embrace the daylight. "If it's sunny outside, open the curtains so the sun heats the room, then shut them when the sun sets to keep the heat in," says Rebecca.
Sunlight can help keep rooms comfortable for longer before you need to switch the heating on

"If you're using a hot appliance, let the heat into the room," says Lianne Macfarlane, 40, from Cheshire. She recommends leaving your oven door open after using it to help warm your kitchen, though this isn't advised if you have small children who could injure themselves.
As well as curtains, other soft furnishings like rugs can help keep a room warm, says Seymour.
Elin Davis fires up her log burner when it gets cold

If you have a fireplace, lighting a fire to warm the room you're in can be cheaper than turning on the central heating for your whole house. Elin Davis, 30, from South Wales, says her log burner is more economical than turning her heating on - though she added that "logs can cost quite a bit these days".
Gaps around doors can cause heat to escape, so place draught excluders around your door frames. You don't need to buy them - you can use towels or stuff socks into a pair of tights.

When it's a windy day, Seymour recommends looking for other draughts in your house and either finding ways to seal these spots yourself or calling in a professional to help. These include using foam strips, sealant and specialist chimney draught excluders if you don't use your fireplace. Things such as extractor fans and purpose-built ventilation shouldn't be blocked, she adds.

If your windows are single-glazed, then Sophie Burr of charity National Energy Action suggests looking at secondary glazing or investing in thermal curtains to help keep the heat in. Or for a cheaper option, some people suggest placing bubble wrap on your windows.
Even though it may be tempting, don't keep your windows closed all the time. Seymour notes that it's important to allow some ventilation in your house to prevent damp.
If you're after cheap insulation, especially if your window panes are single-glazed, then placing bubble wrap on them might help
"I wouldn't recommend not having your heating on at all," says Seymour, pointing to both the health issues this can cause as well as how pipes can freeze over.

But there are ways you can use heating wisely. These include checking whether your energy supplier offers cheaper prices at off-peak times, bleeding your radiators so that they're more efficient, and turning your heating up in small increments until you reach the right temperature. If you have furniture in front of your radiator, then try moving it to avoid blocking the heat.

You can also buy dedicated radiator foil or make your own with kitchen foil to reflect the heat back into the room rather than losing it through the walls, says Burr. She points out that about 35% of heat that comes from radiators is lost through walls.

Cora Harrison, 34, from Wakefield, says that she only turns the radiators on in the rooms her family is using and keeps the heating on at a low level when they're on holiday to avoid mould or pipes bursting. Some radiators have a snowflake symbol on the valve that activates the frost protection setting, meaning that if the room gets very cold, the radiator warms slightly to stop the pipes from bursting.
Another way to potentially reduce energy bills is to lower the flow temperature of your combi boiler. If you book a boiler service, an engineer can do this for you.
You can also find free warm spaces such as libraries and community centres in your area by looking online or contacting the council. Some spaces also provide free hot drinks.

Household energy prices are set to soar in January, with a typical bill expected to jump by £276 a year, according to a forecast last month from consultancy Cornwall Insight. The 16% predicted increase would mark the biggest rise for four years.
Rising bills are "particularly concerning for people with kids, people with health conditions and the elderly," says Emily Jeremy, project manager at Manchester South Central Foodbank.
An estimated 9.4% of households in England lived in fuel poverty in 2025, according to the latest government figures, external.

Rodney Winchester, 65, from Thetford, who spoke to BBC News through the charity Christians Against Poverty, says he's "extremely worried" about rising energy prices. Because of health conditions, he says he has to keep the heating on throughout winter but is concerned he won't be able to afford it.
"It's so scary," Rodney says, adding that he's been cutting back on food spending and keeps getting ill in the cold weather.

If you are struggling with prices, the debt charity StepChange recommends checking whether you qualify for any additional support, like the Warm Home Discount and Winter Fuel Payment. It also advises contacting your energy supplier, which may be able to agree an affordable repayment plan or discuss support schemes.

items.title: Thunderstorms, heavy rain and flash flooding predicted for much of Australia
paragraphs: Severe thunderstorms and heavy rain will sweep across most Australian states this weekend, adding to the deluge in an already drenched Queensland.

Flash flooding in south-east Queensland this week prompted hundreds of SES callouts and the closure of multiple schools. On Saturday morning, the Bureau of Meteorology had nine flood warnings in place for south Queensland.
The BoM is now warning of severe thunderstorms, heavy rain and flash flooding across South Australia, Victoria, NSW, Tasmania.

Senior meteorologist at the Bureau of Meteorology, David Crock, said severe thunderstorms and heavy rain were forecast across multiple locations in central and eastern Queensland on Saturday, including Rockhampton, Gladstone, Bundaberg, the Sunshine Coast hinterlands and Roma.

Severe storms could also sweep through parts of Victoria, including Melbourne’s eastern suburbs and central and eastern South Australia. Heavy rain is expected to develop in Tasmania overnight into Sunday morning.
“There’s plenty of rain across the south-east, as well as plenty of showers and storms and rain across much of Queensland as well, after what’s already been a really wet week,” Crock said.
The cold front will move across NSW on Sunday, bringing severe thunderstorms to the west of the state as well as north-eastern Victoria, Sydney and Brisbane.
“Tomorrow is a threat for thunderstorms right across eastern Australia, with severe thunderstorms likely through a wide part of inland eastern Australia,” he said.
This week, multiple areas in Queensland were hit by more than twice their average October rainfall across a few days.
“It was an incredibly wet week in Queensland. Much more typical of summer or January or February than this time of year,” Crock said.
The Sunshine Coast hinterlands and Caboolture were hit by flash flooding and recorded a seven-day rainfall total of 300-400mm of rain, with some areas reaching 450mm.

“It’s been notable how persistent this weather pattern has been, how much moisture has pumped in … then how those rainfall totals have accumulated across seven to 10 days through Queensland and northern New South Wales,” Crock said.
On Thursday, torrential rain in south-east Queensland caused flash flooding, water rescues and hundreds of calls for help while several schools were forced to close on Friday.
Thursday’s heavy rain stretched from Caboolture down to the Border Ranges, with some places copping well over 200mm falls.
The Queensland fire department carried out more than 16 swift-water rescues, including using a raft to retrieve an elderly man clinging to the roof of his vehicle at Caboolture.

items.title: Strictly's new presenters - after frosty reviews have they warmed up?
paragraphs: Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe have adapted Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman's "keep dancing" move for three

Strictly Come Dancing's new hosting trio received a very mixed reception when the latest series began a month ago. Ratings have dipped and the jury's still out, but critics say they are slowly getting into the groove.
Changing the hosting team on the BBC's flagship Saturday night entertainment show was never likely to be a waltz in the park.
And going from two presenters to three, and giving them slightly different roles, upset the show's rhythm even more.
Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman were always going to be a hard act to follow.

Into their sparkly shoes have stepped the safe and smooth Emma Willis; the flamboyant former professional dancer Johannes Radebe; and cheeky comedian Josh Widdicombe, a wildcard who was not hitherto associated with either the dance world or prime-time TV.
Willis and Widdicombe have been paired on the live shows, where he is tasked with injecting humour into the moments before and after each dance - with mixed results, say critics.
Radebe, meanwhile, has taken over from Winkleman upstairs on the mezzanine, bringing his warmth and dance expertise to the celebrity interviews following each routine.
The new hosts joined the judges on the dance floor when the series began
After they made their debuts in September, the Times' Carol Midgley billed them as, external "TV's most awkward ménage à trois".
The Daily Telegraph's Chris Bennion declared, external that Strictly's "new 'throuple' is an utter disaster", adding: "It's a mess, a muddle, a confusing pudding".
Widdicombe has come in for particular flack. He "felt like an awkward spare part" and looked like "the work experience boy", wrote Sasha Morris of the Daily Express, external.
And the Independent's Isobel Lewis said, external Widdicombe "is a problem the show needs to solve".
She believes things have now improved, although the show hasn't completely solved the problem.
"He's basically acting too much like a comedian to be a presenter," the freelance culture journalist tells BBC News.

"I think he's getting more comfortable with it. When it's him and Emma doing the bits when they intro each act, and they're obviously reading off an autocue, they feel way more confident there, and it feels more like it works."
Widdicombe has been at the centre of comic sketches with the other hosts and judges
The problem grows when Widdicombe does what comes naturally as a good comedian, Lewis says, and tries to be spontaneous.
"They've got, like, 20 seconds with each judge. It's such a tight amount of time, and that's what lends it to feeling sloppy and like he's constantly jumping in.

"Unfortunately it reads a bit like trying to steal attention and have the last laugh. I actually don't think that is what he's trying to do as a selfish act. I just think that is his comedic impulse."
She says it's unfair to put the criticism on Widdicombe, and says as time has gone on he feels less awkward, with comments online suggesting some fans are "warming to him".
"But at the beginning there's always that knee-jerk reaction of, 'I don't like this'," Lewis says.
Emma Willis has hosted shows including Big Brother and The Voice
Radio Times TV and podcast editor Caroline Frost agrees that the trio have gradually settled in.
"I think it's fair to say there were some bumps in the road in the first couple of episodes," she says, "but they do appear to be very slowly relaxing into their new roles."
When it comes to Willis and Widdicombe's double act, Frost would like to see more spontaneity, not less.
"They've been relying quite visibly on scripts and gags, and I would like to see them relax into themselves," she adds.

"It's completely understandable that they would be very scripted, very alert to the clock and to all of the other many demands of running a live show of that scale - but the really talented people can do that on the fly.

"Josh is very likeable, and we know he's a very funny man," she notes. "He doesn't need the shackles of the script that he's currently handcuffed to, and I would love to see him take off those cuffs and become more spontaneous."
One episode featured Widdicombe and Willis in a Mary Poppins-inspired sketch

Frost suggests sending Widdicombe upstairs to conduct the post-dance interviews instead of Radebe, who at times struggles to control his exuberant former fellow dancers. "It's a bit like when you get an internal promotion at work," she reflects.
The producers should make the most of Radebe's strengths and make him "a sort of talent pundit", she suggests.
"Have him in the rehearsal rooms, telling us what's going on. He would be a lovely middleman between what we're seeing on the dance floor and what is going on technically."
Ahead of the series, there had been reports that Radebe would be used as a "roving reporter".
Widdicombe previously suggested the trio's roles would be fluid, telling The Rest Is Entertainment it was "going to be like total football... We're going to be moving everywhere".
Radebe has already gained a reputation for his flamboyant fashion
But while some segments are flexible - especially in the Sunday result show - their main roles appear fixed.
Some fans have been won over by Radebe since he took over Winkleman's old domain.
"JoJo has been really brilliant up in... I guess the Claudatorium, but I'm not sure what we call it now," says Flo Sayers, co-host of the Strictly on the Sofa podcast.

"He is the link to previous Strictly, and I think he has taken to that role really well. I like that he's a bit different from Claudia. He's less the comedian and more the supportive friend for the contestants when they've got off the dance floor and they're probably feeling a little bit vulnerable.
"And his fashion has been amazing, so I'm excited to see what he wears every week."
Sayers isn't sure whether the new line-up has contributed to lower ratings - about six million people are tuning in every week this year, down by about a million.
But overall, she believes that the trio are getting used to the demands of the series.
The presenting trio watched on as Dame Sarah Storey and dance partner Julian Caillon were eliminated last weekend
Dr Karen Wood, associate professor at the Centre for Dance Research at Coventry University, agrees and says the trio "are now really starting to feel a bit more settled".
"I think JoJo has transitioned beautifully from professional dancer to host, and obviously he comes with all his fabulousness," she says.

"He's able to talk about the technical details as well as be very supportive to the professional dancers and the celebrities. And his outfits are just marvellous. So I think he suits that role very well.
"Likewise, Emma is holding her own when she's with Josh and when she's not. She's an experienced presenter. You can you can tell.
"And Josh is bringing the humour. I know it's come with some criticism. But last week was the first week that I felt, oh, these two are actually funny."
She concludes: "It's really feeling like they're finding their stride and their rhythm with it. And I think that's going to develop more and more - very much as the celebrities do."
Just as the show's celebrity contestants improve week by week, the same may be true of the hosts - except viewers can't vote them off if they don't like them.
The next episode of Strictly Come Dancing airs on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Saturday.

items.title: Are California voters about to impose world's first 'tax on billionaires'?
paragraphs: Few places on the planet have as many ultra-wealthy residents as California, a US state known for glamour, coastal mega-mansions and being home to many rich and famous.

Now voters are about to decide if the mega-rich among them - names that include media mogul Oprah Winfrey, Meta head Mark Zuckerberg, Skims cofounder and reality television star Kim Kardashian and filmmaker George Lucas - should hand over billions of dollars to pay for improvements to healthcare.
Proposition 40 is aimed at levying a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of all of California's billionaires.

There are a little more than 200 such individuals in the state - but that hasn't stopped the measure from dividing leaders and causing some of its ultra-wealthy residents to flee. One billionaire businessman says he's brought jobs to California, but the proposition made him feel "a little bit like I wasn't wanted".
But the vote is also offering regular everyday residents a voice on an issue that has riled politics for decades.

"I believe this is the first billionaire tax - meaning a wealth tax that is targeting a very extreme percentile of the wealth distribution," says Francesco Trebbi, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He noted the measure's historic nature and how it could help even out California's wealth gap.

The state has the largest economy in the country - and boasts the fourth largest global economy, bigger than India and the whole of the UK. And it is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the globe. But it also has the largest share of homeless people in the nation and one of the highest wealth gaps.

Those who back the measure have argued it helps ensure that the ultra-wealthy are contributing their fair share and will help backfill gaps in the state's budget. The move aims to raise $100bn (£75bn) to make up for federal funding cuts to the state's health-care system.

Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which helped lead the charge for the initiative, says the measure is a "short-term solution" for massive federal funding cuts coming to California as a result of President Donald Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill.
"If we do nothing, we're going to see a collapse of our healthcare system, while we figure out a longer-term solution to fund our healthcare," she told the BBC.

While the ballot measure has many supporters - including some billionaires like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang - it has faced fierce opposition from a variety of figures, from billionaires to the state's liberal governor.
Google co-founder Sergey Brin has given more than $100 million to a political nonprofit funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax, the Los Angeles Times reports, external.

California Governor Gavin Newsom, whose tenure is coming to an end, is perhaps the most notable political leader opposing it. He has voiced concerns that the measure could cause the wealthy to leave the state and drive out their crucial income tax revenue.

A September poll, external from the Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times found the proposition has not clearly won over a majority of voters, with 45% of likely voters in favour of the tax, 42% opposed and 13% undecided.
The statewide ballot measure would need to be approved by a majority of residents.

California is not the first place to toy with the idea of taxing the rich. Also on the West Coast, voters in US state of Washington are considering whether to accept or reject a "millionaires tax" - a 9.9% tax on income over $1m a year.

While wealth taxes were once a fairly common form of taxation in Europe, they have rapidly fallen out of favour and now only exist in three European countries – Spain, Norway and Switzerland, says Dr Kristian Niemietz, head of political economy at the Institute of Economic Affairs.

Niemietz believes wealth taxes are "more trouble than they are worth" because they cause administrative issues, suppress investment, lead to capital flight and, in the end, do not raise much revenue, she said.

In the case of Norway, a local news organisation found that an increase in the wealth tax led to more super wealthy people leaving the country in 2022, external than in the preceding 13 years combined. A study on Switzerland, external found that a 0.1 percentage point increase in a wealth tax reduced taxable wealth by 3.5%.
Google co-founder Sergey Brin has reportedly given more than $100 million to a political nonprofit funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax

The California measure, if approved, would apply retroactively to those with a net worth of at least $1bn who resided in California as of 1 January 2026. At least six of the state's 200 plus billionaires have reportedly left California ahead of that deadline to avoid the tax.
They include Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, venture capitalist Peter Thiel, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Hankey Group founder Don Hankey.
Hankey, a Los Angeles billionaire who has lived in California all his life, told Forbes he left for the state of Nevada as a result of the proposed wealth tax.

"I think we've created a lot of jobs in California. We have a few thousand people working for us and we have a profit sharing plan. And I have to leave the state," he added, saying the measure made him feel like he wasn't "wanted" in the state.

Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg told the company's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California over the proposed tax. To prevent him from leaving the state - where the company is headquartered - Meta agreed to a new stock deal that gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn, even more shares in the company to make up for the billions he would lose if the measure passes in November. Estimates say he could owe as much as $12.5bn.

DoorDash cofounder Andy Fang, who has an estimated net worth of $1.6bn, has called the measure "stupid" and wrote on X that "proposals like this make it irresponsible for me not to plan leaving the state".

Meanwhile, businessman Tom Steyer, who ran an unsuccessful bid for California governor earlier this year, is one of the few billionaires who has said, external he would vote in favour of the tax. Steyer said that although he believes the way the measure is written is "problematic", it is necessary to protect vulnerable Californians.
Huang, too, has expressed support of paying the levy.

"I don't mind paying taxes. The more you make, the more taxes you pay. I'm okay with that," the Nvidia chief executive said in an interview with the BBC's news partner in the US, CBS. "I am the ultimate American Dream."
Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, a vocal champion against income inequality, has campaigned in support of Prop 40.
While at a Los Angeles rally, Sanders said billionaires "believe, like the monarchs of the 19th century, that they have a God-given right to rule".
"They have all the wealth; they got all the power, and who the hell do you think you are challenging them? Well, I think on Nov 3 they're going to learn a very powerful lesson".

Income inequality in the US is at some of its highest levels, external in over three decades, with the top 1% of households owning nearly 32% of all US wealth in the third quarter of 2025. It is also near historic highs in California.

Economic inequality is a concern among most Californians, with 72% believing that the gap between the rich and poor is widening and a similar share holding that state government should do more to reduce the gap, according to a statewide survey, external from the Public Policy Institute of California.
Trebbi says it is an "anti-elite, anti-system sentiment that is behind a policy" like Prop 40.
"This is really not about Prop 40," he says. It's about trying to "re-balance the scale a little bit".
US Senator Bernie Sanders speaks at the "Ballots Over Billionaires" rally on 5 October in Los Angeles.

items.title: Ruins of Limoges city hall a symbol of France divided by national protests
paragraphs: For weeks, hundreds of thousands of people, mostly young, have engaged in protests that have only increased in size and scope. What started off as a demonstration over the poor state of high schools has expanded to a general frustration, even anger, over how challenging and expensive life has become.

In the backdrop is a daunting fiscal deficit, one of the biggest in Europe, and political candidates from across the spectrum claiming to have the answers ahead of presidential elections in six months' time.
In the middle is a centrist government, which is short on solutions, a majority in the National Assembly and time. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu visited Limoges on Friday evening.

Officials have banned demonstrations in various cities and promised to boost police numbers over the weekend to avoid a repeat of the rioting. That includes in Limoges, where overnight curfews have been announced, along with a limit on gatherings to 10 people in the centre.

Proud as the French are of their politics being rooted in street demonstrations, many in Limoges felt the town hall's destruction went far beyond the parameters of reasonable protest. But not everyone.
Whether the destruction of Limoges town hall changes the course and tone of an increasingly polarised political debate depends on who you ask.
"Of course it was really sad, it's a symbol of the republic, but what is more important: a town hall or people living in poverty?" asks Alexander, 24.

It is student night at the Lord John pub, and Alexander is one of several wearing a faluche, a colourful, traditional French student beret. Many chatting under the mist from their vapes took part in the demonstrations last weekend.
I ask Alexander whether the widespread looting and fires seen last weekend, with €500,000 (£420,000) of reported damage in Limoges, helped his argument?
"For some people it's a catastrophe and some things are not acceptable," he admits.
Jade, a 19-year-old, medical student, has a similar opinion: "I think burning the town hall is sad, but it's not the saddest part of the protests."
She complains of having to live on €300 per month.
"I feel we are not respected as young adults."

Their views on the town hall's fate are not replicated in Limoges' imposing market halls, where neat, narrow timbers sitting upon studded steel girders have been painted a duck-egg blue, using the same engineering approach as the Eiffel Tower.
This has been a "week of chaos" that 63-year-old Jean Roger Faucher would like to forget.
In a region renowned for producing beef, his family has run his fishmonger stool here for more than a century.
"It left us stunned," he says. "I got married in the town hall, so it had an unimaginable effect on us."
Asked whether he had sympathy for the protesters, Faucher said it was more complicated than that.
"On one side you have people with grievances you can understand, but from the moment there is vandalism and the lives of local residents are put at risk, then we can't accept it," he adds.
Among those tending to their iced displays of fresh produce or quietly sipping a steaming coffee, there is a desire for the temperature of the demonstrations to decrease.
"Of course, life is expensive!' says Pascale Vuylsteke, 59. "Life isn't all a calm river, it's complicated, but we grit our teeth and we work," she tells me leaning over shelves of butchered pork.
Pascale says she works 100 hours a week and struggles to understand why so many others have taken to the streets so easily.

Limoges has found itself at the heart of social action before. In the 19th Century, around the time the town hall was built, the development of its industries, notably in porcelain, led to it becoming a major centre for the French labour movement.

In 2026, the town sits centre-stage once more in a political rupture, although there is a broad hope that the loss of a prominent piece of its history will steer the demonstrations away from destruction and back to debate.
With France's political polarisation set to continue and further protests planned, it is a scenario far from assured.

items.title: The artist dropping her debut album after a billion streams
paragraphs: Releasing your first album is a big step for any artist, but for Jazzy it's one that's followed some huge strides.
The Irish singer and DJ has been streamed more than a billion times and worked with industry heavyweights including Calvin Harris.
If that's not enough, on Saturday she has her biggest gig yet when she'll be playing tracks like No Bad Vibes and Someday in front of a home crowd in Dublin.
For Jazzy, writing an album has always been in the back of her mind and now, finally, it's time to hit send.
She's previously released dozens of singles, building up a monthly listenership over 10 million strong, but Peace and Patience is her first full-length work.
"It's been quite a few years of creating some smaller projects," she tells BBC Newsbeat.
"That's given me enough experience now to feel like it was the right moment."
The 30-year-old, real name Yasmine Byrne, has been putting out music for more than five years and collabed with the likes of Sonny Fodera, Rossi. and KILIMANJARO on some of her biggest tracks.
Dance music has boomed in recent years, with Spotify previously telling Newsbeat that since 2020 the amount under-25s listen to the genre has grown by more than 73% globally.
It also dominated festival line-ups over the summer - including Radio 1's Big Weekend which dedicated all its stages to dance music on the opening night.
But artists in the genre have often moved away from albums, opting instead to release EPs and singles.
Jazzy has noticed the change, saying it feels "a lot different now, with people kind of siding with virality rather than quality of music".
"When I was making the album, I wasn't thinking about going viral or anything like that. I just wanted to make something that was true to me and sounded like a Jazzy album.
"I like to let things happen quite organically and I try to just let the music speak to me."
Jazzy is rooted in the Dublin club scene, starting her career as part of a group called Powerful Creative Minds in the city.
But as more and more clubs close, the DJ says there are fewer opportunities for artists to cut their teeth offline.
"When I first started going out, there was a lot more going on," she says.
"There was a lot more nightclubs to go to and it's very different when we look at it now, which is sad.
"There's definitely a home for dance music on the internet of course but club culture is very important and I think that's something that we need to keep going for sure."

Latest figures from the Night Time Industries Association, external suggest about 12 venues are closing across the UK every month, with almost 30% of the night time economy lost since the coronavirus pandemic.
"I hope to God that it doesn't disappear, the club scene altogether," says Jazzy, who describes a similar issue in Ireland.
"We all need to try and put a hand in to keep it going."
Jazzy's taking her new album on tour across the UK from next month, but first she has her biggest gig yet: Dublin's 3Arena in front of a home crowd.
Even after a Coachella set and supporting Calvin Harris, she describes this as the "biggest milestone of my career to date".
While she says fans can mostly expect her brand of uplifting records on the album, she says it's also more personal than her usual work.

She highlights one track in particular, Invisible, as a change from her more upbeat releases. It deals with a bad experience she had in the music industry, describing it as "like my first ever diss track".
"I hope [fans] learn a little bit more about me, because that was one of my goals with the album - to open up a little bit about experiences in life as well.
"So there's a little message from me in each song."

items.title: Celebrity Traitors left on a knife edge after a trip to the field of screams
paragraphs: Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode eight of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.
Original Celebrity Traitor Maya Jama, latest recruit King Kenny and now even the reluctant James Acaster - hurrah! - have developed a real appetite for murder this week.

And going into Friday's episode we knew that their collective cruel intention was to see that one of three faithfuls, Miranda Hart, Romesh Ranganathan or Sebastian "Bash" Croft, did not make it to breakfast.
When it became clear that the murdered Miranda had danced her last dance in the castle - leaving only 10 of the initial 21 players - the pressure began to mount and speculation was rife.
The self-declared Miss Marple wannabe had been stitched up, of course. "Miranda is a good detective," noted James A in a flashback to the turret talk from the night before.
"I don't know who I'm becoming," responded Maya - who has taken to treachery like a duck to water - "but I feel it in my loins, and Miranda is the only one that makes sense."
Miranda, who had been in her element sleuthing away on the show, did not take the news of her untimely death at all well, throwing her murder note to the ground. "No! Absolutely not," she cried.

"I'm so cross with myself, I was wholly focusing on my Joanne issue," she added, with reference to her theory about Joanne McNally being a traitor. One that even Miranda herself had - unwisely - "debunked" at the roundtable.

Ending on a more positive note, the comedian, who has had health issues in recent years, reflected: "Ultimately, in my little personal story, this has been quite extraordinary that I've been able to get back and do the thing that I love professionally and do the things that I love personally.
"Like wandering around a Scottish island and being in nature and laughing and connecting. There were times that I didn't think that would be possible again".
With Miss Marple now out of the picture, James A told viewers that two of the remaining traitor hunters, James Blunt and Michael Sheen are like "Holmes and Watson".
"Luckily they're completely looking in all the wrong places," he added.
Leigh-Anne, having lost her new Big Mix dance partner from episode six, said she was now praying that the heat on her would now cool down.

While Miranda was being murdered on Thursday night, out in the real world another Little Mix star Jade Thirlwell told BBC News - at the Mercury prize ceremony - that her groupmate was a real life "faithful through and through".
Those kind words would be worth little if the now nicely positioned traitors kept going at this rate, however.
"This is actually embarrassing," declared comedian Romesh at breakfast.
"We are getting battered," a sneaky Maya agreed. "This is just getting harder and harder by the second."
Breaking character in the safety of the diary room, the Gentleman actress and presenter admitted: "I'm not gonna lie, I feel terrible about Miranda, I really do and she will be sorely missed.
"But with great honour comes great pressure, and here I am, "OG Traits", still flying it up."
Joanne had earlier joked that Maya would not be killed or banished as "she's too hot. The hot ones always survive."
After breakfast, James B, who has been pretty consistently wrong with his theories throughout the series, continued his fine form, saying of Maya and Kenny: "I think they are the two most innocent."
He joked (it was a joke, right?): "Watching me in this castle must be like watching Sherlock at work."
With less heat on her than Christmas Day in Blackpool, Maya started planting a seed that roundtable "chief investigator" Michael Sheen might be up to something.
"How has that guy not been killed?" asked Romesh.
"It's like not getting rid of [Hercule] Poirot," he added, as the literary detective references kept coming.
Michael and Sharon - fast becoming a dark horse with her theory about Ross Kemp having been killed with perfume - said she was determined to catch a traitor and would "not be taking any prisoners".
On to Friday's mission, as the dwindling group arrived in a "field of screams", as presenter Claudia Winkleman aptly put it, full of scary-looking scarecrows.
"This is like the Wickerman," said Joanne. "A solo scarecrow is sinister enough. A gaggle of scarecrows is terrifying."
The task involved them attempting to retrieve bags of gold from inside the straw men with a pitchfork, in a bid to add thousands of pounds to the charity prize pot.
Joanne's knot-tying badge she claimed to have been awarded in her youth didn't seem to help her much, though, as she struggled initially to grab any gold.
"I have a newfound respect for the farming community," she declared.

But it wasn't only gold on offer, it transpired. An as-yet unrevealed game-changing power would be bestowed upon one player, but only after they had to blow up the proxy pumpkin scarecrow heads of all but three of the most trustworthy contestants.
Things got a bit awkward when poor Sharon "got so mad at the boys" - James B, Michael and Kenny - over which heads should roll.
In the most remarkably stupid moment of the series since Richard E Grant told everyone he was a traitor, the group chose to preserve the heads belonging to Maya, James A and Kenny.

"I had to hold in my laughter," said Maya, privately afterwards. "Of all people, you saved us. I just thought, 'oh my gosh, have we completed this game already? We are trusting. We are unsuspecting. We are killing you all'."
With the others en route back to the castle, Winkleman quipped to the traitors: "This is like an outdoor turret."
The special power was revealed to be a double dagger, enabling one of "the trustworthy trio", as James A is now calling them, to have two votes at the night's roundtable.
King Kenny became King Arthur being crowned keeper of the special blade.
"I think it's in the right hands," declared James B back at the castle, now colder than ever in terms of catching a traitor.
"I feel like whoever it is, they are five sets ahead of us," noted a befuddled Leigh-Anne. "We don't have a clue!"
Romesh then had to remind Joanne that her policy of not voting off Michael because he's "great company" is not really how the game should work.
With the double dagger in play and time running out for the faithful, Michael declared that he had to catch a traitor tonight.
Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday
The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in Uncloaked
As discussions began, double trouble Kenny warned: "Be nice to me everyone!"
Bash, who had flown under the radar until this point, drew some heat along with Leigh-Anne and Sharon at another roundtable led my Don Michael.
"If you're a faithful, why are you still here?" Bash asked the Welshman, who noted he had a shield last time out.

Romesh agreed: "I definitely would have killed you by now if I was a traitor. And I mean that as a massive compliment, because I think, for the morale of the group, you not being here would decimate us."
In an attempt to deflect attention away from himself, Michael stressed how Sharon had been acting like a "totally different person" of late.
Kenny bought it, sticking his double dagger into the Barbie actress. And James B voted the same way due to her "suspicious" actions earlier on.
Scotswoman Sharon received four votes, along with Irish comic Joanne, meaning that - after desperate final pleas from the pair - it went to second round.
"Do whatever youse want, it's a game," offered a seemingly defeated Sharon.
"I wish I didn't take this dagger," said Kenny, ahead of his decisive second thrust of the double blade. "But I'm gonna vote for..."
The producers then left things, quite literally, on a knife edge.
Ten contestant remain (for now): seven faithfuls (soon to be six) and three traitors, putting the cloaked interlopers in a great position going into the final two episodes.
With the hurly-burly done for another week, we will wait with baited breath until Hallowe'en's double header to see how the battle will be lost and won.

items.title: Father who killed Oregon school shooter describes anguish over children he couldn't save
paragraphs: A father who shot dead a gunman at his two daughters' school in the US state of Oregon has described "hearing children pleading for their lives" and his anguish over those he could not save.
Three students and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student at Silver Rail Elementary School earlier this month. The attacker was then killed by parent Kaylub Giamanco.

"I want to apologise for not saving their babies," Giamanco, who has been hailed as a hero, said of his thoughts for the parents of the children killed in an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB) that aired on Friday.
"The gratitude for saving people's children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn't save."
Giamanco, 36, said he wanted to meet the victims' families and "cry with them and hold them".
He credited a teacher who fought the attacker with giving him the chance to intervene without losing his own life.
"I would love to give her a hug because that's a real true hero," he said.

The students who were killed were all boys, aged five, eight and 11. They were among six people in total who were shot in a classroom at the school, police said. Alongside the teacher who was also killed, another child and a teacher were wounded.
Giamanco told OPB the day of the attack began with breakfast and packed lunches. He and his wife spent extra time getting their daughters ready because it was school picture day.
The carpenter had taken lunch to work but decided to go home to eat with his wife instead. That decision brought him past the school as the attack began.
He initially wondered whether someone carrying a long gun was playing a prank. Then he saw him fire at a pickup truck and head towards the school.
Giamanco retrieved a handgun from his vehicle and called emergency services.
"I said, 'I'm sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die,'" he told the broadcaster.
He followed the attacker, who shot through the school's locked glass doors. Hearing children pleading for their lives and more gunfire, Giamanco crawled towards the building.
"I told myself this is probably the last thing that I'm ever going to do," he said.
Giamanco crawled through a shattered window and reached the classroom, where a teacher was struggling with the gunman. He opened the door and fired.
Giamanco told OPB he fired again when the attacker reached for his weapon. He then placed his own gun on the ground and raised his hands as an officer appeared.
He described feeling like the "last line of defence" between the children and the gunman and said he "was supposed to be there" that day.
Afterwards, he called his wife to say he would not be home for lunch and that she needed to get to the school immediately. He then called his mother to tell her what had happened.
"Mum, I just had to take the life of what I think is might be a child because he ran into my daughter's school with a gun," he said.
Police identified the gunman as Griffin J John II - a former pupil who had attended special education classes at the school. His motive remains under investigation.

Police said the teacher who confronted the attacker had thrown her phone at him, tackled him and fought to take his shotgun. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said she "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".
The youngest victim was Rhoam Summer, 5. His father said the family was "broken and lost".
Megan Lambert, 25, the teacher who was killed, was working in what her family described as her "dream job".
"She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs," they said.
The other two boys have not been publicly named at their families' request.
The injured teacher has been named as Becky Drury, 54. She said in a statement shared with US media that the gunman shot her as she tried to shut her classroom door.

items.title: Russia steps up election influence efforts in final stretch of midterms
paragraphs: A pedestrian looks at his smartphone on an embankment with the Kremlin in the background in central Moscow on Oct. 8, 2026. Researchers who track online influence operations say Kremlin-backed groups are renewing tactics they've used to sow distrust and discord in previous elections in the U.S. and around the world. Igor Ivanko/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

Russian operatives are pumping out fabricated claims about Democratic candidates, AI-manipulated videos of celebrities and fake posts impersonating real news outlets in an effort to influence American voters in the final run-up to Election Day.

Researchers who track online influence operations and lawmakers who've been briefed by the intelligence community say Kremlin-backed groups are renewing familiar tactics they've used to sow distrust and discord in previous elections in the U.S. and around the world.

"It's a carnival out there," Rep. Jim Himes of Connecticut, the ranking member on the House intelligence committee, told reporters this week. "They're throwing everything out there to generate a sense of chaos and anarchy."
The goal is to exacerbate divisions, erode confidence in democracy and, crucially, undermine U.S. support for Ukraine.

"At the end of the day, the main issue for Russia is and has to be Ukraine," said Darren Linvill, co-director of Clemson University's Media Forensics Hub, who has tracked foreign propaganda campaigns for years.

Linvill says the Russian playbook is consistent. A false claim or divisive narrative is seeded on social media or on a fake website posing as a news organization or think tank. It's spread by state media, automated fake accounts or, increasingly, paid influencers, in the hopes that it gets seen and repeated by real people.

"In the same way that marketing companies will pay an influencer to disseminate, you know, 'Nike's a great shoe,' the Russians do it with false information and made-up lies," he said. "They use influencers that know their audience, that are part of that audience, and they know how to give that audience a message that they want to hear," Linvill said.
A Russian operation put that playbook to work this week to spread a baseless accusation against a Democratic U.S. Senate candidate.

Linvill and several other research groups attributed them to Russian operators the research community has dubbed Storm-1516. It's known for staging fake videos with actors and laundering their claims through influencer accounts with large followings.

Two fraudulent videos targeting the Senate candidate were posted on Tuesday on X by an account created last month that had few followers. The account's X profile said it was based in the U.S. but the social media platform publicly flagged it as possibly using a proxy such as a virtual private network, which could disguise its location.

The videos were likely created using artificial intelligence, according to Graphika, a research company that analyzes online communities. Linvill said a hallmark of Storm-1516 videos is the use of real actors whose faces are swapped using AI to look like someone else.

The post was immediately shared by a network of 15 accounts Linvill flagged as bots. About 12 hours later, one of the videos was shared in new posts by three X accounts with large followings, which researchers said have previously amplified other narratives attributed to Storm-1516. One of them has solicited paid partnerships on X. Soon other X accounts began resharing the large accounts' posts in replies to politicians and journalists.

One of the two fake videos racked up roughly 857,000 views within 24 hours, according to an analysis by Alethea, a threat intelligence company. By late on Wednesday, the account that first posted the videos and one of the large accounts that reshared the claim had been suspended by X, and the two other large accounts that amplified it had taken down their posts.

In the run-up to the 2024 presidential election, Storm-1516 posted fraudulent videos making similar unfounded accusations against Democratic vice presidential nominee Tim Walz and purporting to show ballots for President Trump being torn up.

Linvill says the operation tries to glom on to narratives that are already circulating among Americans. "It is hard to persuade anybody of anything, ever," he said. "But what you can do is reinforce beliefs."
This election cycle, Russian operations have also spread messages about Democrats turning away from supporting Israel and fabricated news reports accusing Democratic candidates of corruption.

"I increasingly have come to think of Russia as essentially a dark money PAC," said Lisa Kaplan, who founded Alethea. "You know they're going to be running advertisements. You want to understand what's out there. You want to understand if they're actually effective in moving people in one direction or another."
Intelligence officials have long said Russia has favored Trump and targeted Democrats in its efforts to erode support for Ukraine in the U.S.

On Wednesday, Himes and Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., vice chairman of the Senate intelligence committee, told reporters they'd seen a recent classified intelligence report on foreign election meddling showing Russia opposes candidates of either party who have backed Ukraine.
Himes stressed that while Russia and other foreign countries have sought to influence voters, there has been no indication that they have been able to interfere with the actual mechanics of voting.
"Nothing out there suggests that there is either the capability or the intent to do interference, whereas there is a pretty robust influence environment," Himes said.

The same Russian operations now active in the U.S. midterms have also targeted elections this year in France, Germany and elsewhere. They've used AI-generated audio and impersonated politicians, celebrities and media outlets, Graphika said in a new report on Friday.

"They have run this playbook in half a dozen other countries in the past six months throughout Europe. We're just the next in line," Linvill said. "They attack with these same themes. Anything that's going to make a candidate seem degenerate, seem corrupt, seem incapable."
Kaplan of Alethea says this focus on polarizing issues in the final stretch of the election is less about shaping voter's views and more about inflaming anger or fear to affect turnout.
"In these final posts in the lead up to the election, it's really more about evoking that emotion," she said.

Researchers tracking Storm-1516 and other groups say they expect more false claims and fake videos to come, and for these operations to focus on voting and ballot processing in the period immediately surrounding election day.
NPR's Eric McDaniel contributed to this report.

items.title: Xbox’s first chief operating officer is out after just a few months
paragraphs: Xbox’s first chief operating officer (COO) is leaving after the new role was created just a few months ago. Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft today, according to an internal Xbox memo seen by The Verge. Chiang has been at Microsoft for 21 years, serving as the head of Minecraft before being promoted to Xbox chief operating officer in July.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced Chiang’s departure in a surprisingly short memo today. “Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft today. I’m grateful for her years of service and wish her well,” said Sharma. As Chiang is departing today, her immediate responsibilities are being split up between other Xbox leaders for now, and Sharma notes that “We’ll share more on COO leadership as plans are finalized.”
