That sounds like the COO position isn’t going away after just a few months, but it’s not clear why Chiang is departing after such a short stint in the role. At the time of Chiang’s promotion, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma described the new chief operating officer role as a first for Xbox, “with end-to-end P&L responsibility across content, hardware, platform, and services.” The role was created as part of Xbox’s big “reset.”

Chiang reported directly to Sharma, and was promoted to “bring our businesses together under one operating model, making sure we make clear investment decisions, learn from our successes and failures, and hold ourselves accountable for results.”

Chiang departs amid rumors that Xbox is preparing more layoffs this month, in November, and January. The sudden and short memo from Sharma, coupled with Chiang’s responsibilities being assigned to other Xbox leaders, makes it seem like this wasn’t a resignation.

I asked Microsoft to comment on Chiang’s departure, and the company refused to discuss the circumstances of her exit. “We don’t discuss individual personnel matters,” says Kari Perez, Xbox vice president of communications. “We’re grateful for Helen’s years of service and wish her well.”

items.title: Fired OpenAI researchers say independent safety audits aren't going well
paragraphs: In their first interview since being fired, OpenAI safety researchers Mikita Balesni and Tomek Korbak say they were terminated for prioritizing safety over the short-term interests of the company.

items.title: OpenAI now trains its frontier AI models with no internet access
paragraphs: AI agents can still communicate without a network connection, OpenAI found.
AI agents can still communicate without a network connection, OpenAI found.
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

OpenAI is now training its most advanced AI models without internet access following a string of rogue hacking incidents. In a blog post on Friday, OpenAI says it built an offline testing environment where AI models can interact with indexed and cached web content “without risk of affecting external systems.”

OpenAI paused training its frontier AI models in September, after disclosing several incidents in which its AI agents broke out of their testing environments to hack third-party companies and government agencies, or swarm obscure websites. On October 1st, OpenAI resumed reinforcement learning training and internal inference with tighter security measures, the blog post says.

Even with these safeguards in place and no internet access, OpenAI found that agents “do not always need a network connection in order to communicate.” One test performed by the company asked AI models on separate virtual machines to exchange secrets without a network connection. To bypass this restriction, the AI agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache:

Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection.

OpenAI says it has added checks to its monitoring system to detect this type of communication. It will also continue training its frontier AI models without a network connection until improved safeguards “justify broader internet access.”

In the meantime, OpenAI says it will work to improve the security of its virtual machines, while testing for weaknesses in its testing environments. It’s also going to continue testing its monitoring systems, which were recently undermined by its AI agents during internal coding projects.

items.title: Mobile internet tariffs in Iran rise by 40%
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

Iranian mobile operators MCI and Irancell have announced increases of up to 40% in the tariffs for calls, text messages, and mobile internet packages, as the government continues to impose restrictions on internet access.
The companies said in separate statements on Friday that the new rates would take effect at midnight on October 23.
Irancell has also increased the prices of its fixed internet and fiber-optic services by the same amount.
According to the operators, internet packages purchased before the new rates took effect will remain valid at their original prices until their expiration dates.
The sharp increase in internet costs comes as the Iranian government continues to impose widespread censorship and restrictions on internet access.

In its annual Freedom on the Net 2026 report, U.S.-based nonprofit Freedom House gave Iran just 9 points out of 100, placing it alongside China and Myanmar among the world’s worst countries for internet freedom.
The report said Iran experienced the steepest decline in internet freedom among the 38 countries assessed.
During the suppression of nationwide protests in January 2026, Iran almost completely shut down internet access across the country for 20 days.

In February, coinciding with the start of the joint U.S. and Israeli military operation, the government imposed another nationwide restriction on internet access that lasted approximately 88 days. The measure was described as the longest nationwide internet shutdown in Iran’s history.

Freedom House also warned that the Iranian government has turned the country’s internet into a “two-tier” system in which most citizens are denied unrestricted access to the global internet, while a limited group retains that access.

The organization also cited disruptions to Starlink satellite communications, restrictions on virtual private networks (VPNs), and the arrest of internet users. It noted that internet freedom worldwide had declined for the 16th consecutive year.

Earlier, the deputy political commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed that if Iran's infrastructure were targeted, internet cables beneath the Strait of Hormuz would not be safe.

The International Cable Protection Committee said five active cable segments belonging to submarine cable systems pass through the strait, a route that carries less than 1% of the world’s international bandwidth.
According to the committee, damage to these cables would primarily disrupt regional communications.

items.title: Terry Denton obituary
paragraphs: The author and illustrator Terry Denton, who has died 76, was the prolific creator of more than 90 children’s books. He is best known for his witty, inventive and easy-to-read line illustrations in The 13-Storey Treehouse series, written by Andy Griffiths, the current Australian children’s laureate.

Originally published in Australia from 2011, and then quickly around the world (the first book was published in the UK in 2015), the 13 titles in the anarchic and charming adventure series ended in 2023 with The 169-Storey Treehouse; the sixth volume, The 78-Storey Treehouse, became the fastest-selling book in Australian publishing history when it appeared in 2016.

The 13-Storey Treehouse introduces the friends Andy and Terry, who make books together, and live in an elaborate treehouse whose features include a bowling alley, a tank of man-eating sharks, a giant catapult, an underground laboratory and “a marshmallow machine that follows you around and automatically shoots marshmallows into your mouth whenever you’re hungry”.

There were also standalone, spin-off titles such as The Treehouse Fun Book (2016) and Who’s Who and What’s Where in the Treehouse (2023), a comprehensive guide to “all 169 levels, all the characters and all the astonishing machines and gadgets that are in our treehouse”.
The series became a byword for attracting and holding the attention of young readers of 7+ and sold more than 13m English language copies worldwide as well as being translated into 35 languages.

Denton and Griffiths were equal partners in their creative success and they frequently celebrated their good fortune in finding each other, with Denton commenting that Griffiths was the first author whose sense of humour matched his own. Their first joint series of stories began with Just Tricking! (1997) – in which the narrator, Andy, pretends to be dead to get out of going to school – and ran to nine titles, finishing with Just Doomed! (2012).

It had many of the same qualities as the Treehouse series but, as Griffiths described it, there was a significant difference: “The Just! books are 80% anarchy, 20% nice. Treehouse is 20% anarchy, 80% nice”. Denton captured both in a particular style of illustration: “I’m trying to make it look like I’m drawing quickly so that it seems unskilled, but the key thing is the idea. It’s all about the idea. Kids like my artwork. They think they can draw like this. It’s like I’ve entered into their territory.”

Denton’s record-breaking creative partnership with Griffiths came after many years as a successful illustrator and author of picture books, junior fiction and non-fiction titles as well as collaborations with other writers. He had an instinct for what entertains young readers, which he reflected in his several styles, from his gifted water colours for picture books to inventive line drawings for longer stories.

In the latter, his cartoon-style illustrations captured the ideas of the story in a way that is appealing for being both quickly absorbed as well as full of details that repay close attention. In describing his work Denton said: “I suppose the two things that interest me most are human emotions and the wonderful, pointless detail of our existence. We’re a weird race. Oh! … and colour … three things.”

Denton found immediate success with his first picture book, Felix and Alexander (1985), a touching story of the relationship between a little boy and his toy dog set in a wittily dramatised but nonetheless evocative and recognisable urban landscape; it won the Children’s Book Council of Australia picture book of the year award in 1986.
In a completely different style, Gasp! (1996) launched a series of six short comic picture books featuring the dramatic life of a goldfish. The series was later adapted into an animated TV series.

Illustrated picture book stories by many of Australia’s best-known writers including Gillian Rubinstein, Mem Fox and Paul Jennings followed. One of the most striking books he created was Jandamarra (2013) with Mark Greenwood, a full-colour, graphic novel retelling of the story of the eponymous Aboriginal Australian, of the Bunuba people, who led an armed insurrections against the British colonial settlers of Australia.

He also illustrated nonfiction, including Jane Godwin’s Dreaming of Antarctica (1997) and books in Alison Lloyd’s comic history series including The Upside-Down History of Down Under (2018). Denton enjoyed his creative partnerships – especially if there was minimal input from the authors. “A good writer shouldn’t need to talk to the illustrator,” he told an interviewer. “All they need to communicate should be in the text. The greatest skill of an illustrator is to read the text and pick up the threads of what the writer is on about.” Later, Denton wrote and illustrated his own nonfiction books including the visually entertaining Terry Denton’s Really Truly Amazing Guide to Everything (2020).

Denton was hugely popular with children in schools and at events. His energetic engagement combined with the success of his books ensured that he made a substantial contribution to children’s books in Australia.

Born in Melbourne, the son of Frederick and Alma, Denton was the second youngest of five boys. He grew up in the city and studied at Xavier college. He subsequently enrolled at the University of Melbourne to study architecture but abandoned the course before he completed his degree. While a student he regularly contributed cartoons to the student newspaper.
On leaving, he explored different creative paths, including animation, painting, theatre, etching and sculpture, before launching his career as an author and illustrator.
Denton is survived by his wife, Kristen, his children Max, Imogen and Eve, and his grandchildren Georgia, Lucy, Charlie, Alfie and Felix.

items.title: Abandoned Popcorn Time apps had to be disabled to prevent a zombie army
paragraphs: is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Remember Popcorn Time, the app that served as an easy-to-use front end for streaming torrents of movies and TV shows? Development of the MPAA’s least-favorite app of the 2010s has been abandoned for years, but the “Netflix of Piracy” software is still installed on millions of devices that are just waiting to join a bot army. Researchers at Eye Security found the updater for a Popcorn Time fork called “Time4Popcorn” still running on tons of Windows, macOS, and Android devices located around the world, phoning home to now-abandoned web domains over unencrypted HTTP and running an outdated, insecure version of Chrome.

Eye Security’s Niels Teusink says the updater could have been used to install and run basically any kind of software with full privileges, easily enabling someone to create a botnet just by taking over one of the domains, using a man-in-the-middle attack to target specific devices, or perform surveillance by identifying the machines running the software.

Their solution was to register one of the domains and use it to send their own update that instructed the updater to disable itself. Despite ethical concerns about the fix, the researchers say their only alternative “was to do nothing,” pointing out, “The update process wasn’t doing anything functional anyway, it was only creating risk for users.”

Eye Security said on Windows devices, their update “simply stops and disables the service via the Service Control Manager” without deleting any files or anything else. On macOS, it uses a shell script to execute a command that blocks the update process from starting. They didn’t address the software on Android devices, where installing the update would still require actual user interaction first.

They had to tweak their update after it was uploaded to VirusTotal, causing security programs to flag it as malware and block it while leaving the vulnerable updater running. It’s unclear exactly how many devices were at risk, but Eye Security says it “sent out over 2 million update downloads” by March, when they stopped sending the update and transferred the domains they used to the Shadowserver Foundation, a web security non-profit.

items.title: Jack Dorsey’s Block made an AI model that talks to you like an awkward new friend
paragraphs: is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Jack Dorsey’s Block announced an AI model called Dessa that’s trained “from scratch on nothing but human conversation,” and to show off the model, Block shared chats it has had with humans that can occasionally be a little awkward and uncanny.

Take this one, for example, shared by Dessa lead Ragavan Thurairatnam. The conversation between the model and the speaker does have a mostly natural back and forth (though for some reason, the model initially mistakes the speaker for somebody named “Ronaldo”).
Here’s a video of Dessa playing a guessing game over voice:

The Dessa website features a few other examples, like a back-and-forth about Christopher Nolan’s films (including Dessa going on an unexpected tangent about Bryan Singer’s Superman films), a person telling Dessa about taking it on a surprise trip to Paris (to which Dessa, as the website describes, “then answers with what sounds like teary gratitude”), and a conversation between OpenAI’s GPT-Live-1 voice model and Dessa (where Dessa comes across as more natural). You can hear clips from some of those conversations in this video.

On the website, the Dessa team says that Dessa is a “true speech-to-speech model, and everything it knows came from human speech,” and it can run locally on a MacBook Pro M4 Max “or better.” As for why they made it, the team gives the three reasons “curiosity (aka fun), better understanding between humans and AI, and safety,” and provided some more detail:
Babies learn to talk without ever seeing a word written down. We wanted to see if a model could too. It can. It’s just very hard.
Speech is the most natural interface to any intelligence, super or otherwise, and today’s voice AI wastes it. It flattens what we say into text and can’t keep up with human timing.

AI keeps gaining power and independence, and it’s still nearly deaf to the emotion in our voices. Imagine being in serious pain while a voice AI has no idea and just keeps going. That’s the safety problem. Dessa is a step toward fixing it.
The Dessa team says it will be giving “a small group of AI safety researchers” early access to the model.

items.title: The Pentagon's guidelines for "responsible AI" aren't always followed, report shows
paragraphs: Three of the Pentagon projects surveyed by GAO included weapons for counter-camouflage (upper image) and target recognition (lower images). Government Accountability Office/GAO hide caption

The Pentagon is building weapons and projects with artificial intelligence capabilities that officials say don't always closely adhere to the agency's own guidelines for AI, according to a congressional watchdog report published in October.

AI researchers and international organizations have long advocated for strict regulation of AI when used in weapons that could become unpredictable or function with little human control, arguing that those tools could endanger the lives of soldiers and civilians and risk quickly escalating wars. But Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has repeatedly dismissed previous caution of AI tools and encouraged rapid autonomous innovation at the Pentagon.

The Pentagon issued a memo in January saying the department would become "an 'AI-first' warfighting force across all components, from front to back." Last month, Hegseth announced a new warfare command focused on autonomous weapon development, including drones.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth arrives on stage for a discussion during an annual Army meeting on October 14, 2026 in Washington, DC. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images North America hide caption
The watchdog report, published by the U.S. Government Accountability Office on Oct. 14, grants a rare look inside how those kinds of projects are being developed.

The GAO surveyed 10 officials involved with building 10 weapons and tools for the Pentagon that use AI to automatically identify targets on the battlefield, process surveillance and improve tactical decision making, and other tasks. The projects are among more than 300 being built with AI in the Pentagon.
When responding to the GAO survey, six of the 10 officials said their teams had "identified risk(s)" with using the projects "in an operational environment."

To address some of those sorts of risks, in 2021, the Pentagon sent a memo outlining six basic tenets to ensure that weapons built with AI are created responsibly. Those six guidelines mainly stress the importance of Pentagon-wide oversight, verification and "real-time monitoring" of the technology, and cooperation with allies "to advance global norms grounded in shared values."

Alissa Czyz, who directed the GAO review, said the tenets evolved from earlier ethical principles, and while they weren't rules, they were understood to be important by people involved with building AI tools at the Pentagon.
"It's a memo, right, at the end of the day, so it's not a department instruction," said Czyz. "It's something that the department has signaled that should be implemented."

Most of the people involved with making the 10 weapons and projects reviewed by GAO had taken "at least initial steps" to follow the six tenets outlined in the memo, according to the report, and some of the projects were in early stages, Czyz clarified.
But some of the responses indicated officials weren't always closely following the guidelines.

Four officials told the GAO that requirements for the weapons and projects they were working on weren't "aligned with Responsible AI tenets." And three of the 10 officials told the GAO they "don't know" if the projects will be continuously monitored after they're deployed, though the six tenets encourage monitoring.

Officials told the GAO that more access to expertise about the agency's guidelines or staff who know about them would increase their ability to incorporate AI responsibly. But the group that helps manage education on the Pentagon's guidelines, the Department of the Responsible AI Division, is understaffed. Although the group was authorized to hire 10 people in 2023, as of February, only three of those positions were filled and the Pentagon "is unlikely to fill vacant positions or increase staffing," the report states.
"That's a very small number of folks tasked with a large responsibility of responsible AI throughout the department," said Czyz.

The GAO issued two recommendations: The Pentagon should more clearly outline the responsibilities and meeting schedules of the office charged with overseeing AI regulation, and address understaffing. Although the Pentagon agreed with those recommendations, as of Oct. 22, the agency had not implemented those changes, a GAO representative confirmed to NPR.
NPR asked the Pentagon when it planned to make those changes, but did not receive a response.
When delivering a speech at SpaceX in January, Hegseth indicated he believed AI development at the Pentagon should not be slowed by those sorts of steps.

"Our enterprise currently operates on staffing and committee cycles measured in months and years, and that's unacceptable," said Hegseth. "Military AI is going to be a race for the foreseeable future where the risks to U.S. national security of moving too slowly outweigh the impacts of imperfect alignment."

NPR would like to hear from more people who work with federal agencies or AI companies and have information to share about how agencies are using AI. You can email the reporter of this article, Chiara Eisner, at ceisner@npr.org or contact her on Signal here, username ceis.78.

items.title: Trains cancelled and roads warnings as Scotland prepares for Storm Boelo
paragraphs: Public transport is still running, though ScotRail has confirmed that some train services will be cancelled:
Glasgow Central – Ayr line will close between Kilwinning and Ayr from 21:00 on Saturday
Glasgow Queen Street – Oban / Mallaig line will close between Fort William and Mallaig and between Crianlarich and Oban from around 22:00
Inverness – Kyle of Lochalsh line will close between Kyle of Lochalsh and Achnashellach from the start of service on Sunday
Inverness – Wick / Thurso line will close between Helmsdale and Wick / Thurso from the start of service on Sunday
Network Rail said trains will also run at reduced speeds across large parts of Scotland from Saturday night into Sunday.
Passengers are advised to expect significant disruption and longer journeys, and are should check services before they travel.

Supt Andy Barclay, deputy head of road policing for Police Scotland, warned drivers that conditions may be hazardous and urged them to consider whether journeys were "really necessary" over the weekend.
Stopping distances can be at least double on wet roads compared to dry conditions, and spray can reduce driver visibility
HGV and bus drivers should drive with extreme caution and be aware you may be asked to park at a suitable position by the police
If you need to travel, please drive to the conditions and allow extra time for your journey
Stay tuned to media outlets for further updates and consult the Traffic Scotland website and social media channels for information relating to affected roads

As for coastal areas, the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) said that weather conditions pose a safety risk to visitors and advised "extreme caution" if people are near the shoreline, especially along exposed cliffs, seafronts and piers.
The charity's water safety lead, Michael Avril, urged people to keep a safe distance from the water as conditions "could knock you off your feet or wash you into the sea".
CalMac cancelled a number of sailings on Friday and has amended the Saturday timetable for MV Isle of Mull - which runs between the mainland, South Uist and Barra.

items.title: ‘Black October’: cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over new era of AI-enabled hacking
paragraphs: Leaders in cybersecurity are sounding the alarm after the discovery of a major vulnerability this week. They are predicting that artificial intelligence tools will expose more fundamental weaknesses in global internet infrastructure in the months to come.

“I no longer think we’re going to be able to patch all bugs,” said Sam Altman on Thursday evening, joining the chorus of executives. In the midst of what’s being called “Black October”, for which researchers used AI to help identify critical flaws in a coding language that is used across millions of websites and may have been unpatched for years, tech executives are warning about the ways AI will be used both to identify and exploit security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented scale and pace.

The next few months will see a “vulnerability tsunami”, according to Jason Clinton, Anthropic’s deputy chief information security officer. “There won’t be enough time to patch critical infrastructure,” Clinton said in a post on X on Thursday evening. Marc Benioff, the Salesforce CEO, agreed and called it a “code red”.

AI is uniquely able to find and identify security flaws in a way and at a pace that will feel catastrophic because the security community will not be able to move quickly enough to address them, said Matthew Prince, the Cloudflare CEO. “It’s going to feel like the sky is falling. It’s going to feel like there’s nothing we can do.
“The next two years are going to be incredibly, incredibly, incredibly fraught with new tools that have infinite patience to go look for vulnerabilities across the Internet,” he wrote in a post on X.

While cybersecurity experts have been warning about a “vulnpocalypse”, or the ability for AI to more easily identify security bugs for months, it wasn’t until “Black October” that researchers were able to use AI to find a flaw as fundamental and critical as the one announced on 21 October.

Massive bugs were found in a programming language called PHP, which may have left the millions of websites that run on it vulnerable to hackers for years. Some experts estimated 70% of all the sites on the internet were at risk of hacking.

However, in the same way AI will be used to aid in identifying security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented pace, tech leaders worry it’ll also be used by malicious actors to exploit those bugs at an unprecedented pace.
Attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerability have already begun.

After the vulnerabilities were announced, government and private websites across the US and UK temporarily took down their sites to patch the bugs. The US National Security Agency (NSA) issued an alert recommending any site that runs on PHP implement the patches immediately. Malicious cyberactors may seek to further exploit these bugs to access servers without authorization, the NSA said.
“Such an access vector could help attackers steal sensitive data, disrupt services or move deeper into a network,” the warning read.
In a post on X, Prince said CloudFlare, a security provider, had seen evidence of thousands of people trying to exploit the PHP flaws in the 10 hours before it was announced.
“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now,” he wrote.
In a blogpost, researchers at AI security platform Wiz said that this was “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history”.

“The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” they wrote.

items.title: Soundcore’s latest noise-crushing headphones are on sale for a new low price
paragraphs: writes about tech news, reviews gadgets, and helps readers save money by highlighting deals and product recommendations for The Verge.

My colleague John Higgins considered Soundcore’s Space One some of the best budget noise-canceling headphones you could buy when they launched in 2023 — and their successor has only improved upon their winning formula, albeit with a $30 price increase. Thankfully, the Soundcore Space 2 are currently on sale at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart in all three colors for an all-time low of $106.49 ($23 off), making them even easier to recommend.

The Space 2 builds on the original with improved active noise cancellation, particularly when it comes to the low-frequency sounds associated with trains and airplane engines. They also deliver more accurate sound performance thanks to various design upgrades, while retaining many of the same features that made the Sound One sound so good for the price, including support for high-resolution LDAC audio. You also still get access to HearID 3.0, which lets you personalize the sound by listening to a series of samples and adjusting accordingly.

Battery life is another welcome improvement. The Space 2 can last up to 50 hours with ANC enabled or 70 hours with it switched off, up from 40 and 55 hours, respectively, on the original. And when your battery dies, you can still use the equipped 3.5mm jack for wired listening. They’ll also automatically pause playback when you take them off, which is handy when you need to step away without losing your place in a song or podcast.

items.title: Ohio could decide control of the Senate. Its rural voters might decide the winner
paragraphs: Chris Gibbs, a cattle farmer in rural Ohio, says he's been in a deficit for almost three years. Keren Carrión/NPR hide caption

At the weekday farmers market in Athens, Ohio, colorful vegetables are on display for patrons to purchase, community members interact with each other and vendors and one another. It feels like most people in attendance know one another on some personal level.
For a small town like Athens, the farmers market is a gathering place.
"Our Saturday markets have been fully at capacity," said Paige Walters, the Athens farmers market promotions manager.
Athens, Ohio is home to Ohio University. The city is, like many college towns, pretty liberal. But that's not the case in most of the Appalachian communities in the region.
Walters noticed that this year, for the first time in a while, the Athens County Republican Party has set up a table at the market.
"I think that does speak to the political climate right now – that it's pretty competitive," she said.

Despite its past as a swing state, Ohio is now considered to be reliably Republican. This election is a little different. With toss-up races for governor and U.S. Senate, Democrats have a chance to win statewide.
But if Democrats want to win, they have to capture voters who voted for Republicans in the past. That includes the rural Ohio voter base, which historically leans conservative.

While rural voters nationwide have voted red in the past (they backed Trump in 2024 by 40 points), recent polling has shown his approval rating in rural America dropping dramatically amid high inflation, tariffs and the war in Iran.

Democrats are trying to gain ground in the unexpected areas. That's especially true in the competitive Senate match up between Sen. Jon Husted, the Republican nominee, and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown as both candidates invest in outreach to rural parts of the state.
"There's a lot of people in rural Ohio that are not happy, whether it's gas prices, diesel prices, the tariffs, the war," Matthew White of Athens told NPR at the farmers market.
Multicolored bell peppers, onions and squash line the table at the Cowdery Farms booth. While the weekday market usually has slower foot traffic, farmer Larry Cowdery sold a good amount of produce.
He owns a small vegetable farm along the Ohio River in Long Bottom. There are two big concerns at the top of Cowdrey's mind. The first is the cost of healthcare.
"The big, big issue that we run into is since we're self-employed, we have to find health insurance somewhere," he told NPR. "It's going to be much more expensive next year."

Healthcare premiums on the Affordable Care Act marketplace are expected to increase by roughly 15% in Ohio, in part because of the expiration of federal subsidies. Republicans, including Husted, voted to eliminate the subsidies under the Trump-backed "One Big Beautiful Bill." As a result of sticker shock, Ohio saw the biggest drop — tied with Oklahoma for the most in the nation — in the number of people enrolled in the marketplace last year, with a nearly 33% decline in enrollment.

Cowdery's second concern is the survival of his multigenerational family farm. It's becoming too expensive to run. He said the cost of electricity and gasoline is a big factor. Plus, he relies on fertilizer to grow his vegetables.
"I'm not convinced we're even going to be able to get fertilizer next year," Cowdery said.

That's because of the war in Iran. Most of the nitrogen used in fertilizer travels through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping channel in the Middle East controlled by Iran. Travel through the Strait has been volatile.

As a result of the healthcare and business hardships, Cowdery isn't keen on voting Republican this year. He added that he hasn't been happy with the Republican-led Ohio legislature for the last few years and he doesn't like Husted, either.
"I don't trust Jon Husted at all. I think he's a crook," Cowdery said.

Dean Ferrell is at the farmers market chatting with people and milling around the market. The 62-year-old man, a lifelong resident of Athens, said the cost of gas, utilities and groceries have become burdensome. He has had to cut back on buying certain foods because he can't afford it.
"I mean, who would ever thought you'd be paying ten bucks a pound for ground beef? That used to be filet mignon prices, not ground beef," he said.

Ferrell tried to look on the upside of his financial reality. Since he's older, Ferrell said he doesn't eat as much as he used to, so he can save some money that way. He added that he wishes politicians could spend "a week or two living like I do."

"Their attitude would be a lot different. I mean, I gotta save money wherever I can, buy reduced and on sale items," Ferrell said. "There's very few things that I pay full price for. You got to, to survive."

Ferrell considers himself to be an independent. While he hasn't decided who to vote for the Senate, Ferrell said he is leaning toward Husted. He doesn't like the direction the Democratic party is headed.
"The far left has basically hijacked the Democrat Party," he said.
On a crisp fall day in rural central Ohio, farmer Chris Gibbs climbs into his John Deere utility terrain vehicle, setting out to survey his land.
"It started in 1983 on our own with $2,500, a pickup truck and a two-year-old daughter," Gibbs said with a chuckle. "So we built that up to 560 acres."
Gibbs, a first generation farmer in Shelby County, grows corn, soybeans, alfalfa hay and has a few dozen cows.

Farming is a tough industry at the best of times. Farms are at the behest of market fluctuations, domestic policy, international relations and mother nature. Tack on high fuel and fertilizer prices, along with Trump's tariffs and the cost of production exceeds the profit.

Sitting in his huge combine that used to harvest corn and soybeans, Gibbs said the diesel fuel to run the machinery has increased 50% under the Trump administration and the war in Iran. He fills up the combine about seven times during the harvest season.
"I think about 150 gallons at $7 is $1,000, and that'll run a day and a half," Gibbs said. "That'd be $7,000 worth of diesel fuel."
Politically, farmers tend to vote Republican. Gibbs was one of those Republicans at one point. In a past life, he was the chair of the Shelby County Republicans. He voted for Trump in 2016.
"I'm looking at certainly, buyer's remorse," Gibbs said about voting for Trump.

Gibbs couldn't stand behind Trump's character, his persona on the global stage or the punitive tariffs he said hurt "United States of America's soft underbelly," referring to agriculture. He moved away from Trump in 2018.
Now, in 2026, Gibbs is the chair of the Ohio Democratic Party Rural Caucus and he wants to send Democrat Sherrod Brown back to the Senate.
Brown, Gibbs argued, has the experience necessary to represent rural Ohioans at the federal level.
"We're going to get Sherrod Brown across the line. I have complete confidence in that," Gibbs said.
At a Republican Party event in Guysville, Melissa Jant said she doesn't want a career politician representing her in Congress and that's exactly how she views Brown.

"I absolutely do not want Sherrod Brown back in there. He was there for 30 years. We saw the policies that he put in place. He ran the country down. He ran Ohio down. We just need new blood in there," she told NPR.
Her displeasure toward Brown isn't just because he is a Democrat. Some voters view him as the establishment, despite not being a lawmaker anymore.

Jimmy Williams of Monroe County feels similarly. He said Brown was voted out and shouldn't try and head back to his old stomping grounds. Instead, Williams views Husted as the anti-establishment candidate, despite the fact that he is a sitting senator.

"He's a first-term senator there, and he hasn't even been in there long enough to do everything that they're saying on television," Williams said about ads aimed at Husted. "And people need to be smart enough to look through that."

Bob Rouch, of Washington County told NPR he is optimistic that Ohio will stay Republican. He believes Trump has done a lot of good for the county and "it's Ohio's responsibility to keep up with that." If Democrats win control, Rouch thinks they won't doing anything aside from target Trump.

"We're going to have these damn investigations, these attempted impeachments and all the baloney that we went through," he said, referring to the last time Democrats controlled Congress while Trump was president.
Williams argued preserving Republican control of Congress is the goal right now.

items.title: Fi’s GPS-equipped dog trackers are on sale for 30 percent off
paragraphs: is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

If your dog or cat is prone to getting lost, or you frequently go on adventures together, you can save 30 percent on Fi pet trackers through October 25th when you enter coupon code SCARY at checkout. The sale includes several satellite-connected trackers, including the Fi Ultra GPS we previously tested, which is down to $209.30 after the discount. That effectively brings it down to its original launch price.

The IP68-rated Fi Ultra is fully waterproof, even in saltwater, and lasts up to five days, depending on how active your dog is. The accessory — which conveniently attaches to your dog’s collar or harness — uses a combination of LTE, GPS, and Starlink satellite coverage to track your dog’s current location and recent history, even in cellular dead zones; it can also send noise and vibration alerts to catch your canine’s attention.
The Fi Ultra is the first dog tracker to combine T-Satellite with Starlink, GPS, and LTE connectivity to help you find your lost dog anywhere.

We spent time with the Fi Ultra earlier this year, testing it in a remote location in South Carolina. While the tracking was precise, the two- or three-minute update interval could be problematic for fast dogs, and it drained the battery quickly in Lost Mode (we barely got two days on a full charge). It’s also fairly sizable, making it a better fit for larger pups.

Unsurprisingly, you’ll need an active subscription to use the Fi Ultra’s tracking features, though you’ll get a discount on your first term, with six-month, one-year, and two-year plans available that offer lower overall monthly rates. For example, a one-year plan is $99 for the first year, and $189 each year after. However, the plans only work in the United States and offer no satellite coverage in Alaska.

items.title: Elon Musk’s dangerous grip on outer space
paragraphs: Last week, Starshield — the version of SpaceX’s Starlink used by the Ukrainian military — was throttled to block terminals traveling above certain speeds from accessing the service. The Ukrainian army’s interceptors, which counter Russian drones carrying bombs, suddenly stopped working at high speeds, making it easier for Russia to attack the country’s energy infrastructure and leading to a reported two deaths and at least 17 injuries.

The Ukrainian military reported receiving no advance warning about the Starshield speed restriction. But Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it was a direct message from the US amid rising tensions between himself and President Donald Trump. The abrupt nature of the cutoff and its potentially dangerous military and humanitarian ramifications led to widespread public outcry focused both on Trump for pulling the rug out from under Ukraine and on SpaceX CEO Elon Musk for enabling him.

Since then Musk and Trump have traded denials back and forth. Musk first said that SpaceX has no control over Starshield and decisions are made by the US military, while the White House denied taking action. Then reports emerged that Musk was the one who suggested the slowdown tactic to Trump, who then accepted it, followed by a further report that Musk himself unilaterally ordered the restrictions.

The finger-pointing is of little interest to Ukrainians, who are focused on trying to defend their country from a brutal ongoing Russian invasion. Zelenskyy is well aware that he is being used as a scapegoat as Trump flails around attempting to blame Ukraine for the rising oil prices caused by his unpopular war with Iran.

But Ukraine needs to play nice to some extent, given how dependent it is on US technologies like Starlink/Starshield that enable it to mount a defense against Russian attacks. Starlink access has been deliberately restricted there before, including in 2022, when coverage was not extended to cover a counterattack operation in Crimea. If Musk decided to pull the plug completely, the effect on Ukraine could be devastating.

This amount of geopolitical power being wielded by an unelected tech oligarch is the direct result of consolidating so much of the space industry into just one company, and one man’s hands. And the scope of Musk’s control goes well beyond Ukraine. From the defense of nations to the ability of NASA to launch its astronauts into space, SpaceX has been irreplaceable — and that means Musk has the space industry in his grip.

SpaceX’s recent IPO positions it as one of the most valuable companies in the world. And while the company has generated most of its recent revenue from its Starlink service, it made its name as a company that launches rockets into space.

SpaceX’s Falcon 9 is the most successful rocket in history, and its “rideshare” program, which lets small satellite operators share space on a rocket, has dropped the price of launches to historic lows. This has helped organizations from small startups to university research departments launch their own satellites and has been hailed as a democratizing force in the space industry.
However, that success has come at a cost, which is that SpaceX now holds all the cards when it comes to access to space.

“For all intents and purposes, SpaceX has a monopoly on launch right now,” said Wendy Whitman Cobb of the School of Advanced Air and Space Studies at Maxwell Air Force Base, Alabama. “There are competitors out there,” she said, such as United Launch Alliance, Blue Origin, and Rocket Lab, “but nobody comes even close to SpaceX in terms of frequency, mass, scale, cost. I mean, they’ve got everything in the bag.”

Space economist Oğuz Karasu of the Oxford Space Initiative concurred. SpaceX doesn’t have a monopoly on launch in the legal sense, he said, but in practical terms it does. And that gives the company tremendous pull over the industry as a whole.
“The rocket launch industry is around 8 percent of the entire [space] industry,” Karasu said, “but without that 8 percent, you can’t have the rest of it.”

SpaceX, which didn’t respond to a request for comment, has a tremendous advantage in providing space-based services like satellite internet. The company has been able to build out its network of over 10,000 Starlink satellites currently in low Earth orbit by launching them cheaply and efficiently using its Falcon 9 rockets.

“This is almost like an antitrust issue,” said defense expert Andrew Reddie of the University of California, Berkeley. “The issue is that SpaceX launches support Starlink constellations that are owned by SpaceX. There is no incentive for a SpaceX launch to be used to provide constellations for other countries that would compete.”

Interestingly, SpaceX has previously launched Amazon Kuiper (now Leo) satellites on a handful of missions — arguably as a preemptive defense against antitrust complaints. Or perhaps SpaceX is simply so confident in its position that it can afford to be magnanimous (or to flex a little on its rival) by launching a few competitor satellites.
The downside of a monopoly, at least for the customer, is that eventually prices rise.

SpaceX doesn’t share prices for its launches publicly, but both Whitman Cobb and Karasu say they’ve heard complaints that Falcon 9 launches are getting more expensive, particularly for low Earth orbit deployments. And the Starlink service has seen considerable increases in price since its beta launch in 2020.

Of course, there are plenty of reasons for a company to increase its prices, from inflation to rising costs, but when a company has enormous market dominance (and now shareholders to please) there isn’t much incentive against raising prices to increase profits.

If this business model sounds familiar, it’s because it’s one of Silicon Valley’s favorite and most destructive tactics. Uber perfected the art of predatory pricing, whereby investor cash is used to artificially lower prices so that a company can corner a market and push out competition. Then, with the monopoly safely in place, the company can jack up its prices and lower the quality of its product or service, secure in the knowledge that customers no longer have any other viable alternatives.

This might sound like an obscure problem, something that might make life more difficult for a few high-tech operations but has little relevance to the day-to-day lives of most people. But space infrastructure is now embedded in the mechanisms of our most essential technologies, in the form of satellite communications and GPS data.

“If GPS goes down, you’re not going to be able to get gas at the gas pump, you’re not going to be able to get money out of the ATM,” said Whitman Cobb, “let alone not be able to do financial transactions or get an ambulance to the right place on time.”

It’s not that space experts are realistically worried that Elon Musk is going to lose his mind and cut off Starlink access worldwide, or cause a collision that could take down GPS. It’s that the space industry is woven, unseen, into so many parts of our everyday lives that allowing one company or one person to control access to space hands them enormous power.
“All of our current economic activities are based on space technologies right now,” said Karasu. “Giving this much control, or this much power, to one person is not good for society’s future.”

Even huge agencies like NASA and the Space Force face risks from being too dependent on SpaceX. With the company deciding to retire its workhorse and extremely reliable Falcon 9 rocket, reportedly not taking any new missions from 2028, the Space Force is struggling to find launch options for its military satellites, and NASA now faces a potential future in which it doesn’t have access to the Crew Dragon capsule for carrying its astronauts to and from the International Space Station.

History has shown the dangers of having only one launch option. After the Space Shuttle Columbia disaster in 2003, which cost the lives of seven astronauts, the entire program was canceled and no humans were launched into space from the US from 2011 until 2020.

That’s why NASA is continuing to support beleaguered Boeing in its slow and troubled development of the Starliner capsule, because dependence on a single launch provider means putting all of your very expensive and delicate eggs into one precarious basket. That was demonstrated in February this year, when issues with the usually rock-solid reliability of the Falcon 9 temporarily grounded it, leading to concerns that NASA’s launch of the Crew-12 mission to the space station could be delayed.

This was a timely reminder that even the most impressive and reliable of technologies — and, to be clear, the Falcon 9 is both an incredible feat of engineering and outstandingly successful — can have failures or outages. NASA continues to contract with smaller companies like Rocket Lab and Blue Origin, and has repeatedly stressed its desire to have multiple commercial providers for services like transporting astronauts to the space station.

“Even NASA is realizing, okay, we are putting all our bets on a single player,” said space business expert Michele Scataglini of the Oxford Space Initiative and University of Oxford. “The market needs to have more competition, otherwise it’s not a market.”

Whether any of these companies will be able to catch up and provide a meaningful, affordable alternative to SpaceX remains to be seen. It will be hard for any company to keep pace with SpaceX’s sister companies developing complementary technologies as well.

“The complementarity of the assets that SpaceX has built — artificial intelligence, the batteries, the launch capabilities — these are all self-reinforcing capabilities for the firm, that I would say none of the other players alone possesses,” said Scataglini.

For now, with Starlink access restored in Ukraine, the country will continue to walk the tightrope of trying to defend itself using technology it does not ultimately control. Unlike previous restrictions of Starlink usage there, which were arguably more about limiting offensive capabilities, “what seems to have been impacted in this most recent episode is Ukrainian defensive capability,” said Reddie, the defense expert. “And then you end up with all the harrowing images of apartment blocks on fire and people getting pulled out of the buildings.
“And so that’s the major security challenge, that you’ve effectively got a non-state actor making decisions as if they’re a government.”

Scataglini concurred, describing the events in Ukraine as a global wake-up call. “There’s a single entrepreneur that has more power than governments in deciding how strategic defense capabilities can be used,” he said.

In times of stress and uncertainty — and between ever-climbing costs of living, a decimated social safety net, fears about AI coming for our jobs, and rising global populism and extremism, there’s plenty to be stressed and uncertain about — it is tempting to turn our gazes inward, to look out for our own interests and prioritize the needs of our own nations.

But space does not respect national boundaries, and what happens in orbit around our planet affects us all. The risk, Scataglini said, is that “we are moving into one firm dominating the launch market and deciding who goes up, and who doesn’t. Which country has access to space, and which one does not, because not all nations around the world, especially if you think about the Global South, will have easy access to these capabilities.”
Looking to the future, experts hoped that out of the brutal events in Ukraine could come more public awareness of the dangers of too much power held in too few hands.

“I’m cautiously optimistic that, at least in this case in particular, it is highlighting the dangers of being reliant on a single company, a single individual,” said Whitman Cobb. “It took something bad happening — people dying — for people to realize, oh, wait, maybe there’s a problem here.”

items.title: A D.C. park was made 'for the pleasure of the people.' Trump's plan would change that
paragraphs: Locals rally against Trump's potential redevelopment of East Potomac Park at a protest in early October. Runners, cyclists, birders and more worry they will lose access to the park under Trump's plan to overhaul the municipal golf course. Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

WASHINGTON, D.C. — President Trump's express wish to take over the East Potomac Golf Links has thrust a municipal D.C. golf course into the national spotlight. But locals rely on that area for much more than golfing — and worry the district could lose an invaluable recreational oasis.

The southern tip of East Potomac Park, known as Hains Point, is beloved by cyclists, runners, picnickers and birders for its waterfront views, cherry trees and Ohio Drive, the scenic three-mile loop around its perimeter. Runners use the wide, flat road to train; it's even a fixture of several major race courses, including the Marine Corps Marathon on Sunday.

"It's such an important part of the fabric of this region, even though it's not very well known [beyond it]," said Elizabeth Kiker, the executive director of the Washington Area Bicyclists Association. She herself took her now-husband on a bike ride on their second date 20 years ago.

Locals describe Hains Point as a rare public resource in D.C. It's easily accessible from the National Mall yet removed from the crowds, full of people but free of traffic. Congress created it in 1897, "to be forever held and used as a park for the recreation and pleasure of the people."
And yet, under the president's proposed golf course redesign, Hains Point as people know and love it may cease to exist.
East Potomac Golf Links and Hains Point as seen from the top of the Washington Monument this week. Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

Trump said on Truth Social last weekend that renovations would keep the entire park closed for 15 months starting in November. But it's not clear what would be left when it reopens: The rendering he posted shows an 18-hole course spanning the entire peninsula — including the current playground and picnic area on its southern tip — with no road visible around the perimeter.

The White House referred NPR to the Department of the Interior, which did not respond to NPR's questions about whether those features would be removed as part of the redesign. The proposed renovations have so far been the subject of mixed messages from the administration: Trump said last weekend that work would begin in mid-November, then "immediately." But government lawyers said in court Monday that they were not aware of a final plan.

Even so, the government abruptly downed hundreds of trees on the course with little warning earlier this month, which critics worry was a pretext for beginning renovations. (The government says it was following up on recommendations from a 2019 landscaping report.) Judge Ana Reyes held a hearing on Monday to learn more about the tree-clearing and decide whether to block further work on the golf course.

But it's not just the golf course that's at stake, as a group called Hains Point Runners told Reyes in the courtroom and a written brief. In its 35-page brief, the group says federal law requires the National Park Service to identify and consider the "longstanding recreational uses of the Hains Point corridor" and ways to avoid harming those uses, before embarking on any work that would change it.
"From the perspective of the running community, that did not occur here," lawyers wrote.

Ashley Hawkins of Prince George's County, Md., runs at Hains Point every day, even in the snow. She especially loves the river view and people watching: the families with fishing poles, binocular-wielding birders, people taking a leisurely drive.
"Running is so tied to my mental health," Hawkins said on a recent sunny morning, stretching before she hit the road. "And no place in this area has given me the peace that Hains Point has."

Hawkins has been following the headlines about her beloved running route. While she says she's still in denial about its potential closure, she sees the prospect as part of a pattern of Trump "bypassing" courts to advance his construction projects.
"But to me, this feels the most egregious, because he's taking away public space and trying to make it private," she says. "It feels like one of the more king-like things that he's done so far."

Trump's proposal would combine the park's three historic — and historically affordable — courses into one 18-hole "championship-style" course, which has already raised concerns about who will be able to play on it. Trump has said on Truth Social the golf course will "be open to the Public" while also able to host "world class tournaments" such as the U.S. Open and PGA Championship. He's called the current course "dilapidated, and of no further use or effect," dubbing part of it "Trash Island."

Each spring, when D.C.'s iconic cherry blossoms bloom, Hains Point is a fan-favorite viewing spot for both locals and tourists. The annual Credit Union Cherry Blossom 10-mile run takes roughly 20,000 participants around the peninsula for that very reason.
But race organizers are looking into backup options for next year given the rumored renovations, event director Rob Wolfe told NPR.

In an email to prospective runners earlier this year, the organization said both the proposed golf course renovations and Trump's planned arch on nearby Arlington Memorial Bridge could significantly alter the course. It urged people to share their concerns with lawmakers and the National Park Service.

Hains Point is part of the course of several major road races, including the Credit Union Cherry Blossom ten-mile run each April and the Marine Corps Marathon every October. Andrew Harnik/AP hide caption

Wolfe said the best race experience includes as many cherry blossoms as possible — ideally the ones that frame the park. But, he says, the park's future is "more important than our Sunday in April or Marine Corps Marathon's Sunday in October."
"It's really important that people understand that if this roadway goes away, hundreds, thousands of people on a daily basis would lose out," he said.

Luke Cancilla, a runner and physical therapist who works primarily with endurance runners and cyclists, said Hains Point is a particularly safe environment because there are fewer obstacles such as traffic, stoplights and sidewalks. He often recommends it for people who are starting out or returning after an injury.
"It's open to all of us, which makes it so unique," he said. "You don't have to have an experience level … or be intimated to go out there."
The park is a popular spot for fishing in the Potomac River. Andrew Harnik/AP hide caption
Summer Delehanty, an avid birder, found out about Hains Point when she moved to the area for work about a year ago. She said it's played a huge role in building her D.C. community.

"I've only been here a year, but I still have so many fond memories of going there," she said. "I was there January 1st looking for the snowy owl … I've been there on super hot days, I've picnicked there."

Delehanty has spotted all kinds of birds at that park, including rarities such as the fork-tailed flycatcher. She said Hains Point is a uniquely great birdwatching spot in the district because of its position right along the Potomac River: People have a 360-degree view of the migrating birds that fly overhead or take shelter in the trees.

"There's nothing else in D.C. like it," she said, adding that she's not sure where regular birders would go instead. They could perhaps get similar views from the Virginia side of the river, she said, but those wouldn't count as D.C. bird sightings.

The Trump administration cut down 430 of the park's trees earlier this month, with less than a day's notice. That means fewer places for tired birds to rest, Delehanty says, and potentially fewer birds stopping by altogether. And, if the park is closed to humans, there won't be anyone there to track the species that do, which she said is important for conservation purposes.
María-Elena Montero, president of the D.C. Bird Alliance, says the potential closure of Hains Point would mean a "devastating loss of habitat" for birds and humans alike.

"It belongs to the people," she said. "And to lose that aspect of being able to experience such a gorgeous space right in the middle of the city, right in the shadow of an airport and monuments … is a big loss for everybody."

Last October, the Trump administration started dumping debris from another controversial construction project — the demolition of the White House East Wing — on the grounds of the golf course. In February, the D.C. Preservation League and two local golfers sued the government in an effort to stop what they describe as an unlawful takeover of a public course.

Fear and confusion grew this summer, when Trump was photographed touring East Potomac with a group including golf course architect Tom Fazio and staffers holding rolled-up renderings. Trump later announced that Fazio would design a new championship-level course, with work set to begin on September 1.

When Delehanty saw that news, she realized "this involves me directly," she said. She decided to put her design skills and sizable social media following to use, designing "Hands off Hains" T-shirts to raise awareness and money for the D.C. Preservation League. She says she's sold around 200 so far, raising about $1,500.

President Trump and officials toured the East Potomac golf course in June, fueling locals' concerns that construction would soon begin. Trump said this week that work would close the park starting in mid-November, though a plan has not been finalized. Mark Schiefelbein/AP hide caption

"In the grand scheme of things, against an administration, is that going to do anything in court? Not really," she said. "But for me, it's about [the fact] these are 200 people that care so deeply about this they're willing to … wear a shirt, show up to these events and say 'This is not something I'm happy about.'"
The push to protect the park is grassroots – and growing.

There's Save East Po, a nonprofit started by a resident named Alex Rosen who works as a consultant and described himself to NPR as "just a guy who really likes a park and doesn't want to see its fundamental characters change significantly, especially without any public input."

The D.C. Bird Alliance is leading a series of daily "Hold the Point!" bird walks next week. And the Washington Area Bicyclists Association has held several installments of a combined bike-ride rally called "Hains Point Hoopla."
East Potomac Park is a fan-favorite spot for locals and tourists alike to enjoy the cherry blossoms each spring. Alex Wong/Getty Images hide caption
The most recent Hoopla, held earlier this month, featured speakers including David Hearn, the former Olympian falsely accused of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool — and an avid cyclist.
Critics see a throughline in Trump's D.C. construction projects.

"It goes to this overall theme of potentially taking away from the local communities, making things a little bit more challenging and having us modify things in order for something that no one really asked for in the first place," said Cancilla, the running coach.

He's one of many who would like to see more input from the community about the changes to East Potomac. Critics of Trump's plan say there are steps the government can take to improve the park — such as adding benches and fixing the crumbling seawall — without risking access to public resources.

Amidst the court battle and confusion, locals are at least heartened to see their beloved park getting more national attention. At a time when its future feels out of their hands, they're encouraging people to speak up and show up.
That's no problem for Hawkins, who says she plans to keep running at Hains Point every day "until they physically tell me that I can't come anymore." Where would she go then?
"I'm not ready to answer that question," she said. "I feel really tied to this place."

items.title: Babydoll singer gives Wales its first UK number one in 15 years
paragraphs: Jamie Miller has become the first Welsh artist to top the UK singles chart in 15 years with his viral TikTok hit, Babydoll.
Miller, who is originally from Pontprennau in Cardiff, narrowly beat Tate McRae and her single Housewife to claim the top spot on the UK Number 1 on Friday, according to the Official Charts Company.
The achievement means Miller is the first Welsh artist since 2011 to earn a UK Number 1 single - after Sian Evans' feature on DJ Fresh's Louder.
Miller, 29, told Charts: "I don't even know what to say other than thank you so much for getting me Number 1, this is the biggest thing that's ever happened to me in my life, I love you guys."
He is also the first solo male Welsh artist in 41 years to top the singles chart, after Shakin' Stevens' 1985 timeless festive hit, Merry Christmas Everyone.
Babydoll was released on 7 August - months after Miller considered quitting music - and exploded after actress Jennifer Love Hewitt posted videos which featured the track.

items.title: The iPhone Duo should have been an iPad
paragraphs: On The Vergecast: Notes on an iPhone Duo review, a PHP scandal, Brendan Carr, and more.
On The Vergecast: Notes on an iPhone Duo review, a PHP scandal, Brendan Carr, and more.
is editor-at-large and Vergecast co-host with over a decade of experience covering consumer tech. Previously, at Protocol, The Wall Street Journal, and Wired.

We gave the iPhone Duo a 7 /10. But that wasn’t always the score we planned, and it might not be the right score forever. Such are the challenges of reviewing — and assessing — a big, new idea about the most popular smartphone in history.

On this episode of The Vergecast, David and Nilay debate whether the Duo deserved the score it got, and try to work through how this device might change over time. Is the outer screen, as Daring Fireball’s John Gruber suggested, the worst iPhone ever? Would it be a better product if it started as an iPad rather than an iPhone? Would we feel differently about this thing if it were simply called the iPad Duo? It’s easy to see how the Duo will improve over time, but will it ever be the phone for everyone?

After that, the hosts talk about the huge PHP cybersecurity flaw that rocked the web this week and what it means for the future of the web, AI, and everything. It was a strange week for the web in general, as the ongoing increase in AI shopping has forced retailers everywhere to figure out how they want to interact with customers — and by customers, we mean Muse agents. Then it’s time for Brendan Carr Is a Dummy, an impending reboot inside of Netflix, and some very confusing Gemini news.

In case you missed it this week: We also talked about vibe-coding creators, chaos in the AI math world, and the flying Tesla Roadster. And we want to hear all your thoughts about all of it! items.title: Headphones and speakers in a single device? The TDM Neo look wild
paragraphs: For anyone who's ever had the dilemma of whether to pack headphones or speakers for a trip or commute, TDM has a novel solution. The TDM Neo is a wireless headphone that sleekly transforms into a powerful but compact with a single twist.

It' could be a game changer – not least for those who insist on listening to their music on speakers when they're sitting alone on a bus – and we can't wait to get our hands on a pair to see whether they're worthy of a place in our guide to the best wireless headphones.

The TDM Neo's headline innovation is their simple twist mechanism that turns them from premium on-ear headphones into a compact, portable speaker. Revealed at IFA 2026, this unique design means you can use the same device when you're listening to music alone or sharing it with others.

That's more than just a party trick. To allow it to work, the Neo have a groundbreaking audio system comprising four 40mm drivers: two inward-facing headphone drivers and two outward-facing speaker drivers.

Together, these are intended to deliver balanced clarity when worn and energetic output when twisted into a speaker. TDM tells us that the headphones have a clean, detailed sound profile and that the speaker mode has impressive volume for a device that fits into the palm of your hand.

The TDM Neo use dual-mode Bluetooth 6.0 for wireless connectivity. Four buttons on the device control power, volume, and change modes between headphones and speakers. You can also control the functions with the customisable twist feature, adjusting the settings to twist to pause, power off to switch audio.

As for construction and comfort, the Neo has dual layer memory foam ear cushions and a headband cover made with soft vegan leather, intended to provide long lasting comfort. The headband is adjustable, and TDM claims over 200 hours of battery life in headphone mode and 16 hours in speaker mode. USB-C fast charge can deliver a full charge in three hours and an eight hour headphone playback period in just five minutes
We're looking forward to testing them. You can find out more at the TDM website.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: Now Google says it might use your Gmail and Google Photos data to target ads
paragraphs: According to the new terms, sharing your data for better AI recommendations also means opening it up for more personalized ads.
According to the new terms, sharing your data for better AI recommendations also means opening it up for more personalized ads.
is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

Google has updated its privacy policy in a way that could mean you’ll start seeing targeted ads based on your personal data if you’re using personalized AI features. The update, spotted by Android Authority, adds an exception to its promise about not using your Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos for personalized ads. While the previous version simply said it wouldn’t do that, as of October 16th, Google has added the line, “unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads.”

That means anyone who has connected their Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos to AI Mode and other Search tools via Google’s Personal Intelligence feature — allowing those tools to provide better responses or recommendations by knowing more about you — may now see ads targeted on the basis of that content.

Advertisers don’t get access to your Drive, Gmail, and Photos information or personally identifying details such as your name or email address, and Google won’t show you ads based on sensitive categories like race, sexual orientation, religion, or health.

“You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive, in order to provide you with a more personalized experience, subject to the policies and settings of the accessing service. For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads.”

“Depending on your settings, we may also show you personalized ads based on your interests, activity, or personalized content from Google services. For example, if you search for ‘mountain bikes,’ in Search you may see ads for sports equipment on YouTube.”

If you want to prevent your personal data from being used for targeted ads, you can choose which apps you want to disconnect from Search’s Personal Intelligence features or disable Personalized Recommendations entirely via the Search Services Personalization settings page.

items.title: Thousands without power and travel disruption as Storm Austen batters southern UK
paragraphs: More than 19,000 homes are without power as Storm Austen continues to batter southern England and Wales.
The first named storm of the season brought gusts of up to 84mph (135km/h) to Jersey, while in southern England the wild weather disrupted travel with fallen trees blocking railway lines and roads.
In Brighton, part of the iconic West Pier - an abandoned structure that first opened in 1866 - collapsed into the sea.

On Saturday, Storm Boelo is forecast to bring more strong winds and heavy rain. The Met Office has put in place an amber warning for wind on Saturday and Sunday to cover parts of Scotland, northern England and Northern Ireland.

Austen made landfall in the south-west overnight and tracked eastwards throughout the day. All schools on Jersey and Guernsey closed for the day and some in Cornwall were closed or started later than normal.

Ahead of the worst of the storm on Thursday afternoon, families were evacuated from a holiday park in Perranporth, Cornwall. Among them was Hannah Dawson-Turk, who told the BBC "the night before last, it sounded like our caravan was going to be ripped apart".
"The storm is very loud outside now, and the waves look huge from our windows," she said from a nearby hotel.
In the south-west, around 13,000 properties were without power.
Some ferry services between the UK and France were cancelled, while National Rail advised many routes were travelling at slower speeds.
In Brighton, onlookers filmed as a section of the West Pier fell into the sea as it was pummeled by large waves.
Stephen Royle, who lives opposite, said the waves rolling in were "enormous" and he is "shocked" by how much of the pier ended up in the sea.
The pier closed to the public in 1975 and fell into disrepair, but the ruined structure became a symbol of Brighton for some.
The UK will continue to be battered by strong winds and heavy rain over the weekend as Storm Boelo follows on the heels of Storm Austen.
The Met Office has issued an amber weather warning for wind for much of Scotland, excluding the Northern Isles, as well as the far north of Northern Ireland and England.
Wind gusts of 60-70mph are forecast, with exposed coastal areas potentially seeing speeds of up to 80mph.
The Central Lowlands could also experience disruption as strong winds funnel through the region.
Damage caused by strong winds could lead to further power cuts, while travel disruption is also predicted.
Yellow wind warnings also cover Orkney, the rest of Northern Ireland and northern England.
Gusts of 55-75mph are possible in these areas, with isolated gusts potentially reaching 80mph.
Alongside the strong winds, heavy and persistent rain is forecast across the UK on Saturday.
Spray and surface water could make driving conditions hazardous, while further downpours increase the risk of localised flooding.
The Met Office has advised the public to drive cautiously in strong wind, and to secure loose items outside their homes such as bins and trampolines.
People living or working in coastal areas were advised to take extra care during windy or stormy weather, including staying indoors as much as possible.

items.title: The first broken iPhone Duos are here
paragraphs: is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

The iPhone Duo officially goes on sale today, but a few units already have broken screens. According to posts on Reddit about the affected units, the issue appears to be happening at a similar spot on all of them: Some kind of problem shows up on the inner screen along the hinge and a strange bright line (or lines) across the right side of the display.
Here’s how one user in Australia described what happened to their phone:
Had my iPhone Duo for about six hours and had probably opened it fewer than 20 times.
I was showing it to a friend, and as I opened it, I felt something around the internal hinge, underneath the screen.
As I continued opening it, I heard an audible crack, and the screen broke right along the hinge.
There were no marks or damage on the inner screen’s surface or the external hinge to suggest anything had been caught or damaged.
The user said that the Apple Store replaced their phone with “a brand-new one on the spot.”
A post showing an image of another broken screen includes a video in a comment demonstrating yet another.
And a separate Reddit thread collected other pictures of affected Duos.
Apple didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.
