Meanwhile, a "cheese roll" - bread and cheese - instead became slabs of cheese rolled into a sushi roll.
While some on social media said they found the images "hilarious", another was less interested in the AI-generated dishes, saying: "Well, that lot just helped my diet".
Meanwhile, one person on Instagram, external questioned why customers would ever want to see AI images of a restaurant's food even if they were closer to the real thing.
"I want to see what the dish actually looks like as it helps me decide who to order from or what to order," they said.
"These 'perfect' AI versions just lead to disappointment if that's what you think your meal will look like."

items.title: Johnston Marklee unveils designs for Bass Museum expansion
paragraphs: California architecture studio Johnston Marklee has unveiled designs to expand the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach, USA, including elevated galleries and courtyard spaces.
The project will extend the Museum of Art (the Bass) into the 22,000-square-foot area at the southwest corner of the museum’s campus with indoor and outdoor space.

Renderings show two rectangular pavilion structures that sit on a thin concrete plane, elevated off the ground to meet “resiliency guidelines”, likely in reference to Miami-Dade County’s stated floodwater risks due to sea-level rise. Courtyards will pass underneath the structure.

This elevated structure also keeps the corner of the property open and increases public access, according to Johnston Marklee founding partner Sharon Johnston, who called the project “transformative”.

“Through careful analysis of light and shadow, space and volume, and the surrounding park and urban context, we are planning a transformative project that will increase public access to the museum’s programs and artworks,” said Johnston.
Formally, the expansion will feature sheer white walls for the upper structures, with more texture on the walls at ground level, underneath the elevated structures.
At the centre of the project, a backlit oculus will illuminate the passage under the structure at night.
The passages will also lead to landscape garden areas, with the blank face of one of the pavilions providing a screen for screenings.
This space will connect to the trees that are part of Collins Park, which extends from the east face of the museum.
Facade perforations will be placed at the top of the rectangular pavilions and on the walls separating the covered courtyards from the street.
The expansion builds upon the original art deco building designed by Russell Pancoast as a library in the 1930s before the Bass opened in 1964 and the Arata Isozaki expansion.

Primary exhibition space will be held in the rectangular pavilion structures, with renderings showing white-wall galleries, rectangular windows and a skylight placed on top of the one nearest to the Isozaki building.
“We are thrilled to reimagine the southwest corner of Collins Park for The Bass,” said Johnston Marklee founding partner Mark Lee.
“This project continues the storied architectural heritage of the museum, preserving Russell Pancoast’s 1942 Art Deco design while honoring Arata Isozaki’s vision of a porous campus.”
Other recent projects by Johnston Marklee include a green-metal skyscraper in Phoenix and a minimalist pavilion for Danish furniture brand Vipp in Upstate New York.

items.title: This Pac-Man snow blower makes me want a robot I don't need
paragraphs: I rarely shovel snow, and when I do get the odd bit of it here in the UK, it's hardly enough to justify buying a snow blower, let alone spending $6,399 on a robot to do it for me. But Yarbo has just put one of my favourite retro games, Pac-Man, on one of its autonomous snow-clearing machines and, well, I want one. I can't really explain why, other than that watching a giant yellow arcade character trundle around the driveway eating snow is more appealing than watching a normal snow blower do its thing, or plodding around myself with a shovel.

The Yarbo x Pac-Man machine is a limited-edition version of the company's Y40 Core and Snow Blower Gen 2, bringing the familiar arcade look to a machine that can navigate a designated area and clear snow without you having to stand outside in the cold. It uses tracked movement, RTK-GPS positioning, and intelligent path planning, plus a two-stage snow-throwing system designed to tackle everything from light cover to deep, wet snow. It can also recharge and pick up where it left off, something I can't say for myself after five minutes with a shovel.

Serious machinery sits beneath the nostalgia, but the Pac-Man bit makes me stop and look. Yarbo could have sold this as another expensive bit of outdoor tech, with all the usual talk of automation and saving time, but instead it's given the thing a character most of us recognise from an arcade cabinet, an old console or that period when games were something you played in the pub while waiting for your food. It's the sort of instantly recognisable design that makes Pac-Man one of gaming's most memorable logos.

The full system costs $6,399 and is available through Yarbo's website and Amazon. It's not coming to the UK, at least for now. Buy an eligible system between 22 October and 2 November, and you'll also get a plough blade thrown in, a rather practical extra for a machine dressed up as a video game character.

Pac-Man celebrated its 45th anniversary last year, and here in the UK we could run around a real maze in a very British bit of in-real-life lunacy. The character has spent decades escaping the maze and has turned up in just about everything, from unexpected design Easter eggs to the odd Pac-Man Google Doodle that can swallow an entire morning. A robotic snow blower is still a fairly unexpected destination, though, and I'm curious how many people will look at this and start imagining one in their own garden.

That's the funny thing about nostalgia branding. Brands are increasingly using nostalgia to hook us, and I can see why it works here. I don't need this machine, I don't have the weather for it, and I can't imagine ever making a sensible argument for spending that much money on one. But make it look like Pac-Man, and suddenly I'm picturing it scooting around the driveway, chomping through snow while I watch from the warmth indoors. Now give me a Kirby robot that hoovers up cut grass, and let's really see where this tech game's branding can go.
Take a look at limited edition Yarbo x Pac-Man.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

items.title: The massive Creality Halloween sale slashes 3D printer prices by up to 42%, with options for beginners and pros
paragraphs: Halloween is coming, and that's not only good news for kids in search of candy and everyone who wants to unleash their inner goth. It's also a fantastic time to get into 3D printing or upgrade your setup to a more professional machine thanks to the massive Creality Halloween Sale.

If you're new to 3D printing, Creality's compact Sparkx i7 Color Combo reduced by 13% to $349 is a great place to start thanks to its easy setup and affordable price. For pros looking to step up to larger print sizes or batch production, the K2 Plus Combo, which we rate as the best large-format machine in our guide to the best 3D printers, is reduced by $300 from $1,099 to $799.
There's also up to 25% off filament when you buy in bulk. There's still time to make the most of the deal until the end of the month, but hurry if you want to print your own Halloween decorations.
Subscribe to the Creative Bloq newsletter for details of expert-curated offers, bringing the tools you need to create – and products perfect for the design-obsessed.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: A grieving female elephant carrying a stillborn baby: Federico Veronesi’s best photograph
paragraphs: My love of African animals, in particular elephants, dates back to when I was three or four years old, growing up in Milan in a house full of old nature books. When I was six, my parents took me on my first safari in Kenya – I cried on the plane home, feeling I was being torn away from the savanna I’d dreamed of, somewhere I really loved. But for the past 20 years, that’s where I’ve lived, guiding photographers on the Maasai Mara National Reserve and elsewhere in Africa.

I’ve spent time photographing other animals, especially big cats, but elephants are still my favourite subject. They have this extraordinary presence, dominating the landscape and making it come alive. I love to follow them in different habitats. They are extremely adaptable – in Kenya they’re associated with the savanna and acacia woodland, and they can also live in extremely arid areas, such as the deserts of Namibia, where this photograph was taken.

I was there last September, guiding a group of photographers. We had been following a group of elephants walking along a dry riverbed as night fell. Even though there is no water in these rivers, they retain some vegetation and act as a lifeline for the elephants, who follow them from the hills in the west towards the Atlantic Ocean.

Because it’s a sandy river, it was quite easy to follow their tracks until we found them again the next day. But among the tracks was something quite unusual, like a dragging mark. Sometimes bull elephants, when they’re full of testosterone, will do crazy things to demonstrate their power and intimidate their opponents – I’d seen one lift a log before, and thought perhaps that’s what was being dragged.

We drove on until we found them, and that’s when I realised one of the females was carrying a baby. When people see this picture, they sometimes think it’s of a young elephant hugging its mother, but in fact the calf is dead and the leg you can’t see is wedged between the adult’s tusk and trunk. As I took this photograph, another elephant was approaching and the female swung her head so the baby was lifted up and out of its way. I have other photographs that make the reading of the scene more straightforward, but this one leaves the interpretation open and adds a layer of mystery.

We followed the herd for several hours, and the female carried the calf for the entire time, only putting it down so she could feed before picking it up and continuing on her way. She was still carrying it when we last saw her – eventually the elephants started climbing into some rocky hills where we couldn’t follow.

I’ve since read that 17 out of the 19 calves born in that area during the past four years have not made it. There’s clearly a problem, but researchers aren’t yet clear why this is happening. What has come to light, however, is that the elephant carrying the calf was not its mother, as I had assumed. Her mammary glands were not swollen as they would have been if she’d recently given birth, and the researchers were able to identify her as a female who had a miscarriage a couple of years before, and had since been seen picking up the stillborn calves of other mothers. In a sense, that makes the image even more deep and profound, as it implies that she perhaps hasn’t moved past that trauma.

Most of my elephant photographs are in black and white. Sometimes I use colour – in Tsavo, Kenya, elephants are often covered in red earth, which makes for a striking contrast against green vegetation, and in Etosha, Namibia, there’s a place where they visit a waterhole full of white clay and end up looking like ghosts. But black and white highlights the texture of elephants’ skin, and also, as here, removes distracting elements and exposes emotion in a more straightforward way.

This is a painful image to look at, but at the same time it reveals so much of the psychology of elephants, their interior complexity, personality and feelings. Here we see a creature that feels just as much as we do, that experiences the same grief at losing a baby, the same sense of not wanting to let it go. My hope is that photographs like this help people realise how important it is to coexist peacefully and respectfully with animals that look different to us on the outside, but inside are very similar.
This image is the adult grand title winner of Wildlife Photographer of the Year. The exhibition is at the Natural History Museum, London, until 11 July 2027.

Born: Milan, Italy, 1975. Moved to Kenya in 2002 High point: Probably this award, and the three books I published Top tip: Explore ways to convey emotions to the viewer through your photographs, carefully choosing light, atmosphere, shooting angle, framing, backgrounds, and so on

items.title: Sir Donald Insall obituary
paragraphs: Donald Insall, doyen of conservation architects, who has died aged 100, was very clear about the distinction between preserving buildings and conserving them. “Preservation,” he pronounced, “is what you do for marmalade.” Though Insall could see the value of preservation, he was an adroit conservationist rather than a stodgy marmalade maker, always seeing how historic buildings could be revived and put to new uses.

Marshalling teams of architects, craftsmen and builders, he brought Windsor Castle back from the brink following the devastating “annus horribilis” fire of 1992. The exacting rescue scheme encompassed a range of strategies, from complete restoration to renewal in spirit. “As well as keeping things as they were, or putting them back as one thinks they were – which is chancy and not the main aim – we had to find new solutions to parts that had been irreparably destroyed,” Insall told Country Life in 2018.

Other high-profile projects included the renovation of Kelmscott Manor, the Oxfordshire country home of the writer, designer and socialist William Morris, following its acquisition by the Society of Antiquaries in 1961, and the restoration of Kedleston Hall in Derbyshire, Robert Adam’s Palladian masterpiece, now in the care of the National Trust. “Kedleston was our first big job,” Insall recalled. “I used to take a scooter on the train, hop off at Derby and go to the hall, where I was met by the butler and the dogs. Once or twice, Lord Scarsdale, the owner, came on the back of the scooter for a ride around the estate.”

Insall was also involved in the lengthy rebuilding of Wotton House in Buckinghamshire, which had previously been remodelled by John Soane following a fire in 1820. Derelict and teetering on the brink of destruction, it was bought in 1957 by the enterprising Elaine Brunner, daughter of King George V’s valet, who had first arrived there, chauffeured by an antique dealer friend, to scavenge columns to adorn her swimming pool and then embarked on a decades-long programme of restoration.

Commissioned by custodians of the country’s most significant historic buildings, from town halls to royal palaces, Insall changed the scope and ambition of conservation practice, shaping pioneering approaches to heritage management at a time when historic buildings were widely seen as impediments to progress rather than assets to be cherished. In deftly addressing issues of heritage, sustainability and contemporary use, his approach has a renewed resonance and relevance. When Insall once worked for the College of Arms, he was granted a personal coat of arms. Aptly, he chose the motto “Bring Forth the Best”.

The son of Phyllis (nee Hill) and William Insall, he was born in Bristol into a family of long established manufacturers of traditional luggage, such as trunks, cricket bags and portmanteaux. He attended Bristol grammar school, and his interest in architecture was piqued when his father commissioned and built a new family home at Henleaze, in the north of the city. During the blitz, Insall witnessed the wartime destruction of Bristol’s ancient churches and historic buildings, and in 1942 started architectural studies at the Royal West of England Academy School of Architecture. He saw wartime service from 1944 in the Coldstream Guards, completing his education after being demobbed in 1948.

Insall studied civic design in London at the Royal Academy Schools and later at the RA’s School of Planning. In 1951 he was a Lethaby scholar with the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings, the organisation founded by William Morris in 1877 in response to the activities of Victorian architects, whose misconceived enthusiasm for restoration often caused calamitous damage. As a Lethaby scholar, Insall worked with and learned from an array of traditional craftsmen, including thatchers and lime plasterers, going on to spend 18 months measuring and surveying Winchester college for the medieval historian John Harvey.

It proved a formative education in which he got to know and understand historic buildings from different periods. He claimed to have no favourites. “I love them all,” he said, relishing how social change was reflected in architecture. “It’s all part of a lively continuity.” What also mattered to him was not just the quality of individual buildings, but their wider contextual relationships with streets, towns and cities. The role of conservation architects was, Insall believed, to help make “every place to be truly more itself”.

Insall initially joined Phillimore and Jenkins, a London-based practice specialising in the restoration of country houses in the greatly altered postwar milieu. In 1958, together with a fellow Lethaby scholar, Peter Locke, he founded Donald Insall Associates, working from the kitchen table in his flat in Belgravia. His father and then his wife, Libby (nee Moss), a lawyer, whom he married in 1964, did the accounts. From these tentative beginnings, the practice is now over 100 strong, operating out of eight offices across England and Wales.

With modernism then in the ascendancy, it was a bleak time for historic buildings. Country houses that did not find a saviour were all too often demolished, as were urban swathes of Victorian and Georgian terraces. While conservation fired Insall’s imagination, taking an interest in old houses was regarded as perplexingly antiquarian, as he recounted to Country Life. “Nice to meet you, but when will your father be coming?” asked the builder on one early job.

Insall’s 1968 study of Chester was a landmark for urban conservation and town planning. Undertaken as a part of a government pilot project surveying four historic towns (the others were Bath, Chichester and York), it recognised for the first time the importance of groups of structures with historic or architectural value. Insall and his team “crawled in overalls” over some 400 buildings, evaluating their merits and advocating that the best ones should be retained.

This led to his appointment as conservation consultant for Chester, and, ultimately, to the establishment of municipal conservation officers in local councils across the country. It also helped formulate many of the principles that underpin today’s conservation management plans and historic building appraisals.

Over time, Insall became a driving force in the workings of the Ancient Monuments Board and the Historic Buildings Council for England. There he befriended the architectural historian John Summerson, and the historians and conservation activists Nikolaus Pevsner and John Betjeman. These liaisons seeded the formation of English Heritage in 1984, of which Insall was a founding commissioner.

Conservation techniques are continually evolving and Insall kept abreast of developments. In the decade-long restoration of Westminster Hall completed in 2020, for instance, nanolime (nano-sized particles of calcium hydroxide dissolved in alcohol) was used to consolidate weathered limestone, and latex poultices employed to remove staining. Insall was also a thoughtful writer, summarising his philosophy, principles and practice in Living Buildings (2008), reprinted a decade later with a foreword by the then Prince of Wales.

For the last three years, Insall projects have won the Europa Nostra award, Europe’s highest accolade for heritage conservation: for the restoration of Westminster Hall (2024), the saving from dereliction of the 18th-century Camellia House at Wentworth Woodhouse, in South Yorkshire (2025) and the revitalisation of Rochdale’s imposing neo-Gothic Town Hall (2026).

Whether resplendent in elegant tweed suits on Instagram, commuting to the office on a BMW 750 motorbike, or vertiginously face to face with Nelson at the top of his column, Insall cultivated a suavely swashbuckling persona, laced with charm and humour. Though he retired as practice chairman in 1998, he continued to work as a consultant until his death.

“Buildings are so very much like people,” he observed. “They all have their own characters, their own strengths and weaknesses, their own message, their own background in terms of the influences that have made them. People change throughout their lives – so does a building.”
Insall was knighted in 2010. He is survived by Libby and their three children, Robert, Christopher and Hilary.

items.title: Severely ill ICE detainees face imminent deportation to unknown African states, advocates say
paragraphs: Relatives of gravely ill detainees at two Florida immigration jails say authorities are about to deport their loved ones to unknown countries in Africa despite worsening medical conditions.

Flights are scheduled as early as Wednesday, according to the families and the immigration advocacy group the Workers Circle, which has been monitoring conditions and speaking with detainees inside two Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facilities in south Florida.
The group said multiple sick detainees with varying conditions had been targeted for imminent deportation, and learned about the operation only in the last few days.

“I received a call from several detainees letting me know that men were being pulled in to interviews with deportation agents, where they were being informed that because of their medical conditions, Mexico would not be accepting their entry, and they will be sent to Africa,” Arianne Betancourt, the group’s immigrant rights organizer, said at a Tuesday night press conference.
“We know that once they are deported and sent to these third countries, they are not receiving medical care in detention. They have difficulties getting medicine.”

The affected detainees are at the Krome North processing center in Miami, which was found to be experiencing severe overcrowding by a government inspector’s report last month, and the Broward transitional center in Pompano Beach. Both facilities are privately run on behalf of ICE.

Anisley Cortés, the wife of Noslén Sendra, a 41-year-old Cuban national, said her husband had been incarcerated since last November, first at the now closed “Alligator Alcatraz” immigration jail, and at Krome since April. She said he has uncontrolled diabetes and acute pancreatitis that resulted in a weeks-long hospital stay earlier this year.

“He lost over 50 pounds. They wouldn’t give him his medication, and they would not give him enough food. It was a nightmare of a time for all of us,” she said. “He is very sick and needs the right healthcare.

“Cuba will not accept him as a deportee, and we now have proof that Mexico will not accept him as a deportee because he is so sick. And so they told him that because he could not be accepted at either of those two countries, ‘Oh well, we’re going to have to send you to Africa.’

“They told him that Mexico would not accept him because he has too many medications that he requires, and so they said, ‘Well, we have to deport you anyway.’ We’re left with the uncertainty of not knowing how he is, or if we’ll see him again.”
Shalyn Fluharty, an immigration rights attorney, said information from the detainees indicated deportation flights were imminent.

“We understand that just this week, within a couple of days, likely Thursday and Friday, there will be two flights going to Africa, in particular to the Central African Republic, and we also believe Burundi,” she said.
Fluharty said previously deported immigrants were shackled at their hands, ankles and waists during lengthy flights, and some who complained were placed in full body wraps with no ability to move.
“This is what we anticipate will be happening this week for these individuals, based upon what we’ve seen in the past,” she said.

“Travel can last sometimes up to 24 hours. What if you’re somebody who has a heart condition? Who has a high risk of stroke? Who is experiencing diabetes and requires regular access to food or insulin? These conditions take your already vulnerable medical state and make them, unfortunately, often life-threatening.”

Responding to a request for comment, a spokesperson for the homeland security department demanded to know the affected detainees’ personal information. The department did not respond further when provided with Sendra’s details.
Betancourt said families risked retaliation for their relatives by coming forward. “This is not a single one-off story,” she said.

“The inspector general’s report confirmed that there is a lack of medical care inside of the Krome detention facility. Families have been demanding oversight, and every day they are experiencing real fear to speak up and advocate for their loved ones.”

During two unannounced visits to Krome in May, government inspectors found multiple violations of noncompliance with detention standards, including severe overcrowding. Holding 1,102 detainees in a facility with a maximum capacity of 882, the report said, “jeopardizes the safe and orderly operations within the facility”.

Other listed violations included an inadequate number of operational toilets, sinks and showers, and previous complaints included female detainees made to use toilets in full view of men, and arriving detainees held for more than 24 hours in a bus in the parking lot because of a lack of space.

Advocates say Donald Trump’s sweeping second-term immigration crackdown has caused overcrowding in detention centers nationwide that the DHS has attempted to alleviate by ramping up deportation flights to so-called third countries.
The controversial practice, approved by the US supreme court last month, has seen hundreds of detainees deported to at least a dozen African countries where they have no ties.

A Human Rights Watch report earlier this month found countless examples of abusive treatment during and after the flights, and detainees subjected to persecution, arbitrary incarceration and torture following their arrival.

items.title: Why has a crumbling bottle plant been rebuilt in Paris? The stunning show suggesting the future is Ghana-shaped
paragraphs: Ibrahim Mahama has dug through the ruins of post-colonial Ghana, sorted through the ashes of its ancient history, picked through the industrial detritus, the corporate waste, the piles of rubbish, and found something pretty unique: hope.

Sit on one of the Asante stools in his circular Parliament of Ghosts and you can almost feel a new future being worked out right in front of you. It’s the first installation in this huge exhibition at the Fondation Cartier in Paris, and it sums Mahama up pretty neatly. He’s looking at the collapse of the Ghanaian government in 1966, the way the hope of the post-colonial project was crushed in a military coup, and he’s looking at ancient Ghanaian history, at the empires that fell centuries ago and the way colonialism tore them to shreds. But he’s not lamenting any of them. He’s not mourning. Instead, he’s reclaiming them, asking how things can be rebuilt, how we can move forwards by learning from the past.

And he does it over and over. In 2024 he bought an old bottle factory – a symbol of industry and its collapse. He’s rebuilt it here, in the centre of Paris. Its steel roof beams, rusted and crumbling, reach up to the ceiling, its walls are lined with thousands of green bottles in Coca-Cola, Schweppes, Kool and Club Minerals crates. It’s a whole history of manufacturing, of commerce in West Africa post-independence. Not left to rot, but rebuilt and reconfigured into something new.
Nearby, he’s taken some of those bottles and piled them around a collection of local pottery. The industrial meets the artisanal, two lost arts creating a new one.

But this huge show isn’t really about Mahama, it’s about the people around him. Most of the work here is by nine other artists and collectives. Mahama runs three art centres near Tamale in Ghana, giving time, space and opportunities to local artists. Their work is given priority here, alongside art by his mentors and collaborators. He’s taken this massive exhibition opportunity and used it as a chance to celebrate his community. It’s almost as if he’s trying to make the rest of us feel bad.

Way up on the top floor, a long scroll of jute and bark by Dorothy Akpene Amenuke undulates across the floor. If it looks like Mahama’s work, it should: she was his art teacher back in 2013. Knowledge, and the past, gets reconfigured and reshaped once again.

Nearby, the wall of a farmhouse has been built by artist and architect Courage Dzidula Kpodo out of red earth clay, a material lost as modernism brought in concrete. Now, historic methods become a kind of resistance, a symbol of tradition’s ability to endure.

Those core ideas get repeated through pretty much every presentation here. Influential 97-year-old photographer James Barnor captures the communities around Mahama in large format, grainy Polaroids. Gideon Appah’s hazy, dream-like paintings imagine fictional Ghanaian youths staring out to sea, congregating on beaches in utopian, idealised visions of the country’s past. Some of the works are absolutely stunning, like Peter Doig and Noah Davis transported to Accra.

The best work, appropriately enough, isn’t by one artist but a collective. On the top floor, a bunch of lumpy, surreal sculptures of birds, bodies and men wrestling bulls is by the Congolese Plantation Workers Art League (CATPC). Each one is made of chocolate, sculpted in the DRC but poured into moulds in Amsterdam. Everything they make from selling the art goes towards buying back land confiscated in the early 20th century by the Lever Brothers, who we now know as Unilever. The work is a whole conversation about global trade taking place in sculptural form, an act of resistance and reclamation through chocolate.

This exhibition is essentially an ambitious, ultra-idealistic group show of West African art. It is art exhibition as political utopianism. Which is great, even if not everything in it is good. And the real draw is Mahama, with his archival approach to monumental installation art, and it’s a shame to not get a load more of it.

Mahama has sacrificed himself for the greater good, basically. But this collaborative approach is the point: he’s saying collective action, community, togetherness, that’s how we’ll build a future. It might sound a bit cloying and earnest, but then you see the results, you see the art and the ideas, you see the community and the hope and the idealism and you eventually say: “Get me a one-way ticket to Accra. I’m in.”

items.title: Cyber chiefs tell websites to make critical safety update or go offline
paragraphs: Organisations which rely on the PHP programming language are being told they should install a significant software update today - or consider taking their websites offline.
Two critical vulnerabilities with PHP, which is widely used across the internet, have been identified.
The PHP Foundation, which supports it, is issuing updates which address them on Wednesday afternoon.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia have urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes as soon as they become available.
The Netherlands' cyber-security agency says it is taking its own website offline due to the vulnerabilities identified.
The country's National Institute for Public Health and the Environment, an agency of the Dutch government, has taken down its website.
Similarly the website of the Tweede Kamer, the lower house of the nation's parliament, has become inaccessible.
"Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a note, external.
Japan's national cyber-security office and EU cyber-security officials have issued a similar warning, external.

"PHP is everywhere. It ​quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful ⁠lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cyber-security company Huntress said.
Cyber-security expert Don Smith, from the Sophos Counter Threat Unit, told the BBC this would "likely be a priority target" for hackers.
The immediate challenge was not simply installing a patch to fix the issue, but finding and managing every instance where PHP was running, he said.

"The use of PHP is pervasive, it can sit beneath public websites, content management systems, hosting platforms and third-party products, sometimes without even being obvious to the organisation using it.
He said it was crucial that organisations looked out for signs that an attacker "might have already have gained a foothold".
The European Union Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) said the risk scores given to the vulnerabilities "indicate the potential for unauthenticated remote code execution".
Such a cyber-attack could potentially allow hackers to install malware and take down websites.
Dane Knecht, chief technology officer at internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, said he was, external "seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up".

The NCSC said once organisations have installed the update, they should "continuously monitor for security updates from third-party software vendors, including for appliances and services that may bundle PHP".
It is not yet clear which versions of the programming language are affected, but CERT-EU said it could affect all versions of it dating back to PHP 5 onwards - which launched in 2004.
PHP was created for web development. It is used on servers to implement what you see when you visit websites.
Not all websites use it, but it nonetheless powers a large portion of the internet.

items.title: Someone turned Draco Malfoy into a girl with AI, and now I need to know what happens next
paragraphs: Meet Miss Malfoy (that’s what I’m calling her), the internet’s gender-flipped take on Draco Malfoy, the platinum-blond Slytherin who spent seven books making Harry’s life hell. Fan artists have been drawing her for years. Now the idea has jumped to AI animation, complete with cinematic scenes, dialogue and a slow-burn romance. Creator Foyege’s In Another Universe series reimagines the Potter story with Draconia and Harry at its heart, and it's oddly compelling.

It’s weird to watch, no question. And I had to ask the team’s more in-the-know Gen Z members if it’s ‘okay’ and not some weird, lewd corner of the internet I’d rather not give oxygen to (I’m uncomfortable with the more common ‘Milfoid’ term surrounding some of this; it feels a bit Incel-y). I was told 'all of the internet is weird, so here we are. But there are some interesting design insights and AI uses here, not least how Foyege’s shorts, in particular, get Hogwarts right; the character design is instantly familiar, but there’s also that slightly uncanny thing about seeing a generated face move and talk.

People are watching, and many have become actively engaged and want to know what happens next. Fans have spent years drawing, writing about, and arguing over Draco. He’s arrogant, privileged and spiteful, then gradually turns out to be far more complicated than the school bully we first meet. By flipping his gender and changing his relationship with Harry, the character gets a whole new playground to work in (and yes, I'm sure there are parts of this fan fiction I'd rather not find), and fans are already on X debating why it does and doesn't work.

But ultimately, videos like those by Foyege represent a new, professionalised aspect of fan fiction. This works because nobody needs the backstory explained. Blond hair, green and silver, a face that’s permanently unimpressed: job done. With fan fiction, the creator can skip the introductions, go straight to the interesting stuff, and pull familiar ideas in new directions. And the enemies-to-lovers trope? It works because familiar insults become flirting, hostility hides affection, and two people who’d rather 'Depulso' each other than share a room end up at the centre of a love story.

What AI adds is performance, and that’s both an odd thing to write and a very 2026 reality. A writer can describe a moment and an artist can draw it, but a voiced, animated scene brings timing and expression. Even a short clip can feel like a scene from a parallel-universe film, and Foyege’s movies drew me in with clever edits, camera movement, subtle details, and even a K-Pop-like power ballad to tie it all together, hitting every emotional hook and hanging dramatic ending Netflix has spent a decade mastering.

I’m not about to declare that the future of cinema has arrived with AI because a slick shot tells us nothing about whether the story works, how much human direction went into it, or how many hours were spent fixing glitches by hammering prompts into a keyboard. Hitting ‘generate’ doesn’t make you a filmmaker, and even those behind the emerging tech, like Autodesk's VP of M&E Strategy, Maurice Patel, have told me "it's terrible at directed content". Quality animation remains the preserve of studios like Laika, which excel at real human-made art, and Wildwood shows that in every frame.

But writing it all off because AI was involved feels lazy, too. Someone still has to decide what the story is, which moments earn screen time and how the characters should act. Someone has to work out what makes this Draco still Draco, what’s changed, and why anyone would come back for episode two. That’s where the creativity lives.

And yes, the thorny questions remain: copyright, training data, and using characters from a world other people built. Loving Harry Potter doesn’t make every use of it ethically straightforward, and one popular fan video doesn’t mean everyone has made peace with AI-generated work.

Even so, some audiences clearly will engage with AI-assisted storytelling if it gives them something they actually want to watch. What I like most is that there isn’t one definitive 'Miss Malfoy'. The 'Malfoid' thing is a shared idea, and every artist and creator puts their own spin on it. People draw their own Draconia, write their own stories, or try their hand at animation, and one fan’s version becomes the jumping-off point for the next.

That’s closer to a participatory fandom than a standard film release, and AI speeds some of that up by opening production to more people; while the reality is that one in a hundred ideas are good, there’s something engaging about watching all the failures until one video or idea lands. But someone with an idea can now take it further than they could before. Generative AI brings its own questions and trade-offs, and its origins in scraping artists' work casts a dark cloud it will never escape, but it also offers a new way to experiment.

This weird fan-fiction 'Miss Malfoy' trend doesn’t mean AI has cracked creativity, and it’s certainly no argument for replacing the artists who built the worlds we love, as a human wrote Harry Potter, and more humans developed it into films and games. It shows that people bring their own ideas and attachments to whatever tools they pick up. AI can make a character who looks the part, but can it make us care what happens to her? That’s still up to a human.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

items.title: Astronaut surprise video leaves pupils starstruck
paragraphs: Primary school children have been left amazed after receiving a personal video message from British astronaut Tim Peake.
Pupils at Thornbury Primary School in Plymouth, Devon, were sent the message after teacher Emily Trevarthen's father met Peake while working on a cruise ship over the summer.
Trevarthen explained that her father and the astronaut got chatting and her father mentioned she was a teacher. "We didn't expect to get what we got really," she said.

Peake told pupils, external: "I hear you've been studying all about space, a subject very close to my heart, something I love, so I'm very pleased that you enjoy it too. Stay curious. Keep looking up at the stars."
Trevarthen said that some children had previously assumed all astronauts were American, but learning about a British astronaut had helped them see that such ambitions were possible.

items.title: Dezeen launches "richer and more versatile" new website
paragraphs: Dezeen has updated its website for the first time in 10 years. Dezeen’s co-CEOs Benedict Hobson and Wai Shin Li explain the changes.
You might have noticed that things look a little different around here. Yes, after many years, we have redesigned our website!
It has been 10 years, in fact – the last major revamp of Dezeen was in 2016. And as with our previous redesign, evolution, not revolution, has been the aim.

Dezeen was launched by Marcus Fairs from his spare room as a basic WordPress blog in 2006. When it started to take off, he brought designer and typographer Micha Weidmann on board to design a logo and layout for it, and this has been the foundation upon which Dezeen has been built ever since.
We really like it, and millions of readers around the world seem to like it too.
So our ambition for this redesign was to bring the site up to date while staying true to the core identity that has helped Dezeen become what it is today.
Underneath the bonnet, there’s been a complete overhaul
We have worked with creative technology studio Made by On to refresh the look and feel of the site and improve the user interface to make it more useful and enjoyable to use.
Underneath the bonnet, there’s been a complete overhaul.
Our previous site was built on ageing technology that had grown clunky over time. Things broke too often and, as regular readers will know, fixing them was a slow and often painful process.
So we tasked Made by On with rebuilding both the front- and back-ends of the site from the ground up to make Dezeen much more stable and responsive.
Reducing the carbon impact of the website was also a key priority, so Made by On focused on performance and efficiency throughout the build, doing a lot of work on image optimisation in particular.

We also used the opportunity of the rebuild to move our hosting to The Positive Internet Company, whose server infrastructure runs on 100-per-cent-renewable energy, and moved our search and recommendation engines, which were previously run by external services, onto our own infrastructure.
Dezeen has expanded far beyond a daily news publishing platform
The new website is faster, richer and, we hope, more enjoyable to use. It also better reflects what Dezeen is today.

Over the past two decades, Dezeen has expanded far beyond a daily news publishing platform to become a suite of services for the global architecture and design community: Dezeen Awards, Dezeen Events Guide and Dezeen Showroom, to name a few.
These were added in a fairly ad hoc way over time, so the overall experience could feel fragmented.
To bring everything together, we returned to Micha Weidmann, who refreshed our brand guidelines, introducing updated colour schemes and logos across all our sub-brands to create a coherent family.

Made By On then used these guidelines to create a cohesive web experience, carefully engineered to meet the latest web accessibility standards, ensuring Dezeen can be enjoyed comfortably by all our readers.
Every service across dezeen.com has undergone a major redesign to ensure it offers real value to our readers. Our jobs website dezeenjobs.com will be updated in the coming weeks.
Navigating the site should now be easier thanks to a fresh menu, search and filtering system
So, what has changed? (And what has not?)

Visually, we have retained the classic typographic treatments that go back to Micha’s first design nearly 20 years ago. However, we have introduced new styling formats to bring greater hierarchy and visual interest to the pages, as well as splashes of colour to better identify content relating to our different services.

We love how eclectic Dezeen is – every story starts at the top and works its way down the homepage, regardless of subject matter – and this will continue. At the same time, our content offering has expanded significantly over the years, and it was too easy for some of our best content to get lost.

So the core, reverse-chronological feed of news stories remains, as do our signature square images. However, we have introduced varied image sizes alongside new horizontal scrolling sections to break up the vertical feed and spotlight specific content types.

Navigating the site should now be much easier thanks to a fresh menu, search and filtering system, which is unified across all of our services. We have also decluttered the right sidebar and added parallax scrolling to create what we hope readers will find to be an intuitive, easily navigable and enjoyable experience.

Video and audio have also been improved: we can now integrate vertical video much more seamlessly, and our podcast Dezeen Weekly, which we launched earlier this year, has been given greater prominence.
We have also built significantly more flexible and visual article layouts.

We will continue publishing amazing buildings, interiors and products from around the world, and we can now include larger images, as well as photo galleries and slideshows, in our articles and across our services to ensure these projects really shine.
In an era increasingly dominated by AI, we believe human-created journalism is more important than ever

Since starting as a basic blog, our editorial range has expanded into long-form features, interviews and opinion pieces, and the new layouts will create a far richer environment for these stories too.
In an era increasingly dominated by AI-generated content and algorithmic feeds, we believe human-created journalism, curation and critical opinion are more important than ever.

While we are using smarter technology to power our new search, filtering and content-recommendation systems, the stories you read on Dezeen continue to be sourced, written and edited by our team. This takes a lot of time and effort, and with this redesign we want to ensure this content has the high-quality platform it deserves.

We know readers generally do not love advertisements, but Dezeen would not exist without them (and if you use an ad blocker, we’d like to use this as an opportunity to kindly ask you to turn it off for Dezeen so we can continue bringing you our content for free).

We have updated our ad formats to deliver better performance for our partners while respecting our readers’ experience. We have also introduced clearer and more consistent badging of partnership content.
Our aim has been to create an ad experience not dissimilar to a high-end glossy magazine: integrated thoughtfully with appropriate partners so that it enhances the page rather than detracts from it.
The aim has been to retain the spirit of Dezeen
Overall, the ambition has been to create a richer and more versatile site that retains the spirit of the Dezeen that you know and love.

Marcus’s vision when he started Dezeen almost 20 years ago was to set the global architecture and design agenda, and Dezeen has since grown to become one of the most influential architecture and design media brands in the world.
The new website will enable us to continue that mission for the years ahead. We hope you enjoy exploring it.
Benedict Hobson and Wai Shin Li are co-CEOs of Dezeen.

items.title: Dosorozco uses stone and blackened timber for textured home in Mexican forest
paragraphs: Architecture studio Dosorozco has used a palette of blackened timber, stonework and pale plaster at Casa Sima, a Mexican home designed to echo the textures and tones of its forest surroundings.
Named Casa Sima, the 150-square-metre dwelling sits on a sloping forest site in Sierra de Tapalpa in Jalisco, with panoramic views towards mountains in the distance.
Dosorozco’s decision to avoid excavation or tree removal informed the home’s elongated plan and the placement of its blocky volumes, which instead align with the contours of an existing clearing.
“Casa Sima started with something very simple, the place already had its own order before we arrived,” the studio’s creative director Guillermo R Orozco told Dezeen.
“One of the first decisions we made was that no existing trees would be removed. That sounds simple, but it affected almost every decision that came after,” he explained.
“Their position affects the geometry of the house, the views, the shadows, the terraces and even the points where the building can touch the ground.”
Casa Sima is accessed via a stepped walkway elevated above the forest floor, which leads from the base of its sloping site to the home’s rectilinear volumes perched at the top.
Marking the transition from the forest into the home is what Orozco calls an “elevated courtyard”, comprising a timber wall supported by a steel frame, positioned above this walkway.
This timber was finished with a local technique that uses oil and heat to weatherproof its surface, giving it a rough, blackened finish intended to blend with the surrounding trees.
“There is a brief moment there where you are not really outside anymore, but you are not inside either,” Orozco explained.
“You become aware of the ground below you, the structure around and above you, and the trees beyond it,” he continued.
“It is suspended above the terrain, framed by the structure and open to the forest, so it works almost like a vestibule without ever becoming a conventional room.”
The living spaces of Casa Sima are housed within two intersecting, rectilinear volumes, with the ground floor given over to a large living, dining and kitchen space flanked by two stone walls.

These stone walls are left visible, complemented by dark timber ceilings and fully-glazed walls that open onto two distinct terraces – one at ground level to the south and another elevated to the north.
A study and bathroom also occupy the ground floor, while above, the central cubic volume contains two bedrooms lined in timber and plaster. These both have access to rooftop terraces.
“The house is compact, but it doesn’t really feel compact when you are inside it,” said Orozco.
“The rotation between floors, the terraces, the diagonal views and the constant relationship with the exterior make the spaces feel much more open,” he added.

Other homes in Mexico recently featured on Dezeen include a lime-rendered home next to a wooded hillside in Cristóbal de las Casas by local studio Colar, and a holiday home in Valle de Bravo by Chain + Siman comprising a row of gabled forms.

items.title: Who is London’s Batman? Is it Niko Omilana?
paragraphs: A mysterious caped figure has been helping the people of London. Not dealing with the criminal hi-jinks of The Joker or Catwoman (thankfully), instead doing good deeds for others: paying for fuel at petrol stations, helping people across busy roads and even filling in potholes.
London's Batman has gone viral on TikTok for their work in the community - and many are trying to work out their secret identity

These may not be the type of do-gooder acts that sell comic books, but London's Batman, as they are known, has already got 297k followers on TikTok and their posts have had more 2m likes since they first appeared at the end of September.

Despite the capital’s hero doing their best to make people’s days a little brighter, one question keeps hounding them: who are they? Can they be like Bruce and keep their identity secret, or will they soon be unmasked?
Socials are awash with the theory that London's Batman is none other than Niko Omilana, known for posting prank videos on socials and as a contestant on the first series of The Celebrity Traitors.
Niko appears to be the most popular candidate for London Batman’s secret identity as he has a reputation for pranks which take a lot of organisation and can involve handing out goods to people.
In 2021, he opened a fake store in the city and gave away free smartphones to the public as his comment on what he saw as the high price of technology.
Niko posted a short video of himself on TikTok showing he was in the heart of New York, a move some people interpreted as him trying to prove he is not London’s Batman.

That hasn’t stopped others trying to prove otherwise. Comments on the post suggest it could have been pre-recorded as the theatre advertisements behind him don’t reflect the ones playing in the city at the moment, although this hasn’t been verified.
TikTok user officialroyce1 posted that Niko’s video was meaningless as he could have flown to New York and back in the same day to cover his tracks.
TikTok user @officialroyce1 claimed that Niko is London's Batman after disputing a video that he was in New York, saying it was possible for the YouTube star to have gone there and back in a day
At the moment, there are lots of theories but absolutely no evidence that Niko is dressing up as a superhero and helping out in the community.

A similar situation happened earlier this year when some posters on socials were convinced that the Liverpool rapper EsDeeKid was really the actor Timothee Chalamet in disguise. This was later disproved after the theory went viral.
When you see stories like this online it's always important to check your facts before repeating or reposting the information, to prevent false information from spreading.

Until London’s Batman pulls back their mask to reveal their secret identity, we can’t say for sure. But we can use the same kind of critical thinking which has saved Gotham City countless times. And how many of us wouldn’t want to be more like Batman?
This article was published in October 2026
Back to our homepage for more quizzes and explainers about fake news, viral trends and media skills.

items.title: Takero Shimazaki upgrades makeshift theatre into permanent "church-like" London venue
paragraphs: A crane tower becomes a soaring beacon at The Yard Theatre in London‘s Hackney Wick, which local studio Takero Shimazaki Architects has revamped and extended using reclaimed materials.

Originally established in 2011 in a converted warehouse and designed by Practice Architecture to last as a three-month project, Takero Shimazaki Architects‘ redesign transforms the theatre from a makeshift space to a permanent performance venue with a bar, backstage facilities and community space.

Aiming to maintain the character of the site, Takero Shimazaki Architects used reclaimed materials to overhaul the existing 110-seat theatre space and extend the venue into the adjacent studios and former brewery with brick walls.

“The core discussion had been about The Yard Theatre ‘growing up’ and for it to have a more permanent presence in the new architecture,” Takero Shimazaki Architects founder Takero Shimazaki told Dezeen.

“The building’s form emerged from the playful idea of creating a civic cultural space by referring to a church-like form made from industrial light-weight materials, as well as the facade brickwork,” he continued.

“The overall architectural form also created stacked boxes on top of the existing warehouse, breaking up the horizontal industrial language and creating a more monumental presence using readily available and sustainable materials.”
Takero Shimazaki Architects retained the brick walls of the former brewery, which now contains a new 224-capacity theatre space with curved amphitheatre seating.
The theatre’s pitched structural frame was made from laminated veneer lumber atop reclaimed tubular steel.
A crane tower was refashioned as a ventilation chimney that rises 23 metres tall, clad in translucent polycarbonate boards to form an eye-catching beacon from outside.
A bar and public foyer occupy the former theatre building, where Takero Shimazaki Architects added a new roof and retained as much of the walls, floors and windows as possible.
The theatre’s backstage facilities are located under the auditorium’s tiered seating, and lifts and stairs were added to connect the bar to the theatre’s upper-level seating.
Materials that were demolished in the construction of the transformation were reused, including exterior bricks used for the stage wall and external infills.

The extended exterior of The Yard Theatre was finished in fibre-cement sheeting, polycarbonate panels and colourful low-carbon named K-Briq, which are made from more than 95 per cent recycled materials.
Atop the roof of the boxy volumes stands a human-shaped sculpture designed by British sculptor Antony Gormley.
Other projects by Takero Shimazaki Architects include a Japan-influenced overhaul of a flat in the Barbican estate and a renovated 1960s house with black-painted brickwork outside of London.
