items.title: An AI chatbot files for bankruptcy. Is it a bad omen for the industry?
paragraphs: Character.AI, which lets users create custom chatbots for immersive roleplaying, has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy following a string of legal challenges and the loss of top talent.

items.title: Apple showcases upcycled found furniture and banana palm-paper lantern at Designers of Tomorrow show
paragraphs: Designers Parafernalia, Yoonjeong Lee, Salem S Charabi and Isabel Rower will celebrate “the art in the making” at technology brand Apple‘s Designers of Tomorrow exhibition at Design Miami.Paris.

The emerging designers, who have all designed furniture or lighting, were chosen by exhibition curator Rodman Primack, together with a jury that included Design Miami president Jennifer Roberts and designer Nifemi Marcus-Bello.
For its latest edition of the exhibition, which opens today, Apple wanted to showcase how its products are used by emerging designers in the process of creating their pieces.
“Designers of Tomorrow celebrates the process – the art in the making,” Apple said in a statement.
“Each of the designers use Apple products in a variety of ways within their creative processes, from early ideation to creation,” the company continued.
“Apple has long believed that the full potential of their products is only fully realised when put in the hands of the world’s most talented creatives.”

Among the works on show will be Egyptian-Danish designer Charabi‘s delicate lamp, made from date palm from Saqqara, limestone from the Galala Mountains and paper made from banana palms in the Nile Delta.
The theme of the exhibition this year was Design for Presence, which Charabi took into consideration by pondering “what is present?”
“A structure inspired by the date palm-cleaving methods of the qafassin, makers of boxes and trays used in the country’s souks and bakeries,” the designer said.

“A skin created by multiple layerings of banana stems, found in Beheira, in the Nile Delta of Egypt,” he continued. “A mass carved from limestone from the Galala Mountains, carrying the trace of its making through repetitive patterns.”
Seoul-based artist Lee, meanwhile, explored how objects can change their functions by using a pencil to nail paper to a surface, before taking the idea further by creating a lamp.
“For this project, I took that approach further, using wood to build a table that holds the pencil nail and paper, completing the piece as a three-dimensional lamp,” Lee explained.
“To make the table, I repeatedly stacked thin sheets of veneer to build a new, solid piece of wood – approximately 5,000 layers, perhaps more.”
Designer Rower used upcycled furniture for her piece, which she then decorated with ceramic beads.

“The chair was made using found furniture left on the curb near my studio in Brooklyn, reconstituted into a wooden armature onto which I built up layers of papier-mâché and a pulp composite containing wood glue, sawdust, and paper pulp made from shredded waste paper,” Rower said.
After spraying the surface of the chair with black paint, she glued 1,500 handmade ceramic beads to it.
The final designers taking part, Sebastián Zorrilla and Genki Matsumura of studio Parafernalia, created their design, MonoAmbiente 1, as a “landscape”.
“Its acid-etched stainless steel surfaces invite closer observation as light reveals and conceals details across them,” the designers said.
“As it unfolds, the landscape unfolds with it: rocks become stools and a table, turning a distant scene into a place for two to converse, play, or share a drink,” the designers continued.
Apple first launched Designers of Tomorrow at Design Miami.Paris last year, when it showed pieces including a table designed to look like butter.

Designers of Tomorrow takes place at Design Miami.Paris 2026 from 21 to 25 October 2026 at L’hôtel de Maisons, 51 Rue de l’Université, 75007 Paris, France. See Dezeen Events Guide for more design events and exhibitions around the world.

items.title: Glen-Gery clads Princeton University health centre in bricks made with reclaimed materials
paragraphs: Burgundy-coloured bricks incorporating reclaimed manufacturing waste wrap Princeton University’s Frist Health Centre in Princeton, New Jersey, as shown in this video carousel produced by Dezeen.
Called Ponderosa Western, the bricks are part of North American manufacturer Glen-Gery‘s Western Series and incorporate materials recovered from its own manufacturing process.
The extruded bricks, which were laid in a horizontal running bond pattern, feature sharp, precise edges and a surface texture that combines velour, grooved and sanded finishes.
The facade was designed to complement the century-old Gothic brickwork of the university’s historic Eno Hall, which was constructed in 1924.
The new building features metal sunshades to help reduce solar heat gain, alongside mineral wool insulation behind the brickwork to support the centre’s energy performance.
Courtyards, green roofs and diverse plant life surround the building, creating a landscape designed to provide a calming environment for students and faculty.
Exposed mass timber and visual connections to the outdoors continue throughout the interior of the building.
The project has been recognised by AIA New York State for its use of biophilic design and adaptive reuse.
Frist Health Centre at Princeton University is a 76,500-square-foot facility dedicated to holistic health and student wellbeing. It opened on the university’s campus in 2025.
Glen-Gery is a brick manufacturer that specialises in creating custom facades for cultural, residential and educational institutions across North America.
This process means that the artists themselves were unsure of what the pieces would look like until they were completely finished.

“The thickness of the shingle coat varies depending on the complexity of the shingled area,” Wegwerth and Dehn said. “As a result, the final silhouettes and tonal values only emerge gradually during the process.”
To find out more about Glen-Gery, visit its website.
This video was produced by Dezeen as part of a partnership with Glen-Gery. Find out more about Dezeen partnership content here.

items.title: Why is Elon Musk plotting a mega-merger of SpaceX and Tesla?
paragraphs: Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together.
Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes."

The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed.
With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5tn (£1.1tn) and SpaceX at $2tn (£1.5tn), a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever.
Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together.
"In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, the Chief Technology Advisor at The Futurum Group, a market research company.

The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said.
Musk, the CEO of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects.
Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations.
The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers.
Over the past year, Musk has moved to consolidate his businesses, with SpaceX acquiring xAI and X, formerly Twitter, before going public this year.
Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car?

But the merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, with half of Tesla's needed to back the deal, a threshold even Musk described as "quite a high hurdle". Musk, as CEO of both companies, cannot participate in shareholder discussions.
Even so, Musk, a key shareholder of Tesla, will likely get his way in the next few years, said investment analyst Dan Sheehan from Telos Wealth Advisors.
He believes shareholders will back the deal as the technology the companies develop complement each other, Sheehan said.
But the merger would mean that Tesla shareholders will likely hold a "smaller slice of a much larger and more complex business," he added.
"There's no real precedent for how a public company like Tesla gets priced in this," Sheehan said.
SpaceX shares rose 8% in after hours trading while shares of Tesla climbed by 1.5%.
Experts told the BBC that Tesla drivers are unlikely to see much drastic change in the near term, even if the two companies combine.
In fact, vehicles seem almost like "an afterthought", overshadowed by the potential to combine the Tesla and SpaceX's tech capabilities, Nicholson said.
Changes are already underway at Tesla. The carmaker said earlier this year that it would prioritise its best-selling Model Y and Model 3, shifting focus away from less popular models.
Tesla also started using a manufacturing plant in California to produce humanoid robots, known as Optimus.
Tesla's vehicle line-up includes the Cybertruck and Model 3
Pairing Tesla's self-driving technology and robotics with SpaceX's AI and satellite network could result in more capable vehicles, Sheehan said.
"The question is how much priority cars get inside a company increasingly driven by AI infrastructure," he added.
The recent Roadster showcase suggests SpaceX technology could be pulled into future Tesla products, which could attract more customers, said Tu Le, the founder of advisory firm Sino Auto Insights.
The Cybertruck-maker faces intense competition from Chinese carmakers like BYD, which overtook Tesla as the world's biggest EV maker in January.
The biggest winner is probably Musk - the world's richest man who also became the world's first trillionaire earlier this year.
The merger would give Musk greater voting control over the combined company than he currently has at Tesla, a factor the special committee assessing the deal would have to consider.
A single company makes it easier for Musk to run his AI strategy the way he wants, Sheehan said.
"The deal itself doesn't add to Musk's wealth, but it concentrates it further in one stock," he said.
However, the merger could attract scrutiny over Musk, already a polarising figure in the US, Nicholson said.
The move could also face more regulatory pressure if Democrats - many of whom have been critical of Musk - win more seats in the US midterm elections next month.
Shareholders have backed Musk's desires before. Last year, Tesla investors approved an unprecedented compensation package for Musk valued around $1tn.
"I honestly don't think Musk will be keeping track of what the merger will do for his wealth," Nicholson said.
The deal also brings Musk closer to what Nicholson says is "his mission in life": colonising Mars.

items.title: Nigeria confirms Ebola case as outbreak spreads into western Africa
paragraphs: Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the health ministry said.

The woman began showing symptoms on 7 October and was admitted to a hospital in Abuja four days later, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola. It is unclear when she arrived in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country.

The health minister, Muhammad Pate, said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. “We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said.

Uganda’s ministry of health said the patient had only transited through Uganda and that she is a Nigerian woman who had been on a business trip to Congo’s eastern region. The Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality.

“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed active Ebola cases”.

Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases, but it later declared itself free of the virus.
Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that “we are facing an extremely serious threat,” with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases.
“This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa,” he said.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola in Kenya and strengthening the country’s preparedness for a potential outbreak.

“These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers,” the agency said.
Nigeria established an Ebola taskforce in June after the outbreak in Congo in mid-May.

The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,500 people and killed more than 4,600 people.

The latest Ebola outbreak is the fastest-spreading on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, the 11,000 people killed in West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, WHO has said.

items.title: Ali G is back. But is the character past its sell-by date?
paragraphs: "This is the biggest gathering of cultural appropriators in history," Sacha Baron Cohen tells the camera in his parody of a street accent.

Behind him, hundreds of fans cram onto a London Underground escalator, all wearing Ali G's trademark yellow shell suit and skullcap. Baron Cohen shouts the character's catchphrases through a megaphone, with the crowd enthusiastically finishing each one.

Earlier this month, more than 300 fans attended an official Ali G lookalike competition, ferried around London on an open-top bus that stopped at landmarks including Big Ben, Leicester Square and Covent Garden.
The stunt was promotion for an upcoming sequel to 2002 film Ali G Indahouse - called Ali G: Who iz I? - which hits cinemas on Friday.

But not everyone is excited about the return of Baron Cohen's comedy character. Critics have long accused the actor of perpetuating racial stereotypes with Ali G, and criticism of the upcoming sequel has gained traction online, with social media posts from comedians, content creators and film fans attracting thousands of likes and comments.

Among them is singer and presenter Jordan Stephens, who has posted multiple TikToks criticising the franchise's return. And last month, discussing the film's trailer on the Jeremy Vine show, Labour MP Paulette Hamilton called the character racist. She said she believed Baron Cohen would not get away with portraying any other racial group "in the way he has done with the black community".
Baron Cohen has not directly addressed criticism of the character's return, and did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

However, he acknowledged an inevitable backlash when he first announced the sequel, writing on X: "In an age where a comedian's career can be ended by a single un-PC joke, I thought I'd play it safe and bring this guy back."

Recently, he shared a video, external posted to a newly created Instagram account, in which a grey-haired academic urged viewers to boycott the upcoming film. The character appeared to be Baron Cohen in prosthetic makeup.
Has Ali G passed his sell-by date? Or are racial stereotypes, and those who believe them, the true butt of the joke?
Alternatively, as some critics argue, is the whole thing simply not very funny?

The character of Ali G rose to fame through a series of deadpan TV interviews with figures including Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed and the Beckhams, from which catchphrases such as "Booyakasha" and "Is it because I is black?" entered popular culture.
But some critics say these catchphrases have since been appropriated by others in a real-life context to mock black people and dismiss their concerns.

Comedian Dane Baptiste, the first black British comic nominated for an Edinburgh Comedy Award, remembers hearing Ali G catchphrases everywhere during the character's noughties heyday. "A lot of the time, I would hear people using phrases like 'Is it because I is black?' or 'Booyakasha'," he recalls.

"Even taking the phrase 'Is it because I is black?'... that was used to the point of caricature, whereby, whenever black people experienced actual grievances relating to systemic and institutional racism, it was reduced to this catchphrase."
Baptiste believes the character, which he calls a "black caricature", is returning at a time when black creatives are being "starved of opportunities".
When Ali G first arrived on our screens, characters like him were far more common, says social psychologist Amy Kean. She argues they are no longer "culturally relevant".

"Ali G, Little Britain, Catherine Tate, all of those comedians and sketch shows, they made the voice the joke," says Kean, who has written on accentism, drawing from her experiences being teased for her Essex accent.
"I remember going to school in the 90s and people would take the piss out of anyone whose voice wasn't exactly the same as everyone else's."
Baron Cohen has in the past suggested that his character had a knack for pushing powerful interviewees into uncomfortable territory by playing with biases and expectations.

Speaking on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert in 2020, Baron Cohen reflected on interviewing Donald Trump for Da Ali G Show, and recalled how the programme's producer was a well-spoken Englishman who Trump had assumed would be conducting the interview.

"I remember Donald Trump looking at me, and I'm wearing a sweatsuit," Baron Cohen said. "His face dropped. He was immediately furious that he was going to have to speak to somebody from a lower-class borough rather than this rather astute Etonian producer."

Writing for Time magazine in 2020, Baron Cohen said: "By getting people to reveal what they really believe, I have at times exposed the ignorance, bigotry and conspiratorial delusions that often lurk just below the surface of our modern lives."

Yet, when discussing the upcoming sequel on CBS on Tuesday, Baron Cohen's "primary objective" appeared less ideological - to "get people to laugh really hard". Though he added that "smuggled in there is a bit of satire".

The actor is no stranger to putting himself in potentially dangerous situations for his comedy. In a previous film, he infiltrated a gun rally, disguised as a "right-wing singer", while secretly wearing a bulletproof vest.
Once members of the crowd realised they were being mocked, Baron Cohen was escorted into a getaway vehicle as an angry crowd "started pounding on the vehicle with their fists".

Judging by Baron Cohen's description of the upcoming film, there may be further potential for danger. He told CBS he wanted to examine "conspiracies and lies" and test whether "we, in a matter of hours, could turn intelligent people who believed in the theory of race replacement into murderers".
Colton Dunn, one of the film's black writers, questioned why Baron Cohen would put himself in danger, where interview subjects might react violently, if his intentions were racist.
"From my point of view, Ali G is not a racist character. Ali G is a tool to expose racists," Dunn told Deadline.
"That's why I signed on. I wouldn't sign on to work with somebody that I thought was racist, that's against everything that I've done," he added.
Almost 25 years on, Ali G still has loyal fans - especially in his "home town" of Staines, in Surrey.
Staines-upon-Thames resident Alex Balkan, who campaigned for a statue of Ali G in the town, says the character remains a source of local pride.
While acknowledging not everyone welcomes the proposal, he says Ali G put Staines on the map.
"Everyone knows about us because of Ali G, and many of us wear that as a badge of pride," he says. "It's a great conversation starter. It feels nice that people know about your town."

Asked about accusations of racial stereotyping, Balkan believes the character is designed to be seen as a white man attempting to put on a stereotypical gangster persona, rather than to poke fun at black culture itself.
One of the character's defenders is one of his most famous prank victims, politician Sir Jacob Rees-Mogg.
"It is clever, satirical humour which makes the country, and many of us look foolish, and that's no bad thing," Sir Jacob posted on his social media.

While some argue that audiences may have moved on from Ali G, supporters of the character contend that objections to his return reflect growing concerns about creative freedom in comedy. Balkan goes further, arguing that people today are more easily offended than they were two decades ago.
"This excessive zeal of political correctness, of left-wing po-facery, is crazy," Sir Jacob said. "It's a joke, it's comedy and it is poking fun at society as it is, as the best comedy often does."

It would be unwise to judge the film before audiences have seen it. But the controversy surrounding its release suggests that, more than two decades after Ali G first appeared, the debate over who exactly is being laughed at is far from settled.

items.title: Elon Musk says Tesla-SpaceX merger being considered
paragraphs: Elon Musk has said he likes the idea of a merger of Tesla and SpaceX, two of his most notable companies, and it is under active consideration.
"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts over the quarterly business results of SpaceX on Tuesday.
While Musk noted the certainty of such a merger should not be assumed, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies have been formed to examine the move.

"The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," Musk added. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained."
With Tesla valued roughly $1.5 trillion and SpaceX valued at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.

Over the last year, Musk has taken to bringing more of his various companies under fewer banners. Before it went public earlier this year, SpaceX acquired xAI and X, the platform formerly known as Twitter, both of which Musk owned.

The recent launch of Terafab, a combined effort to manufacture computer chips between Tesla and SpaceX, was another signal that Musk sees his companies as potentially more effective when working together.
Musk said on Tuesday a full merger between the two companies would make sense for the work each is doing around chips, artificial intelligence, software and more.
Musk, who became the world's first paper trillionaire after SpaceX stock market debut earlier this year, said he is not included in either of the special committees considering the mega-merger.
He described himself as a "conflicted party" as the chief executive of Tesla and of SpaceX.
Even commenting on the possibility of a merger between the two companies, Musk compared to being like "tap dancing through a minefield".
He added a merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders. At least 50% of Tesla's shareholders would need to approve the merger, which Musk described as "quite a high hurdle to achieve".
Shareholders have supported Musk's desires before. Last year, a majority of investors in Tesla approved a compensation package for Musk valued around $1 trillion.
While Tesla is known as an electric car company, Musk has lately been shifting resources there to work around robotics.
SpaceX quickly outstripped Tesla on the stock market in terms of value when it made its stock market debut.
The company, which builds space rockets and Starlink internet satellites, is now expanding into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, like Anthropic and Google.
That line of business is now the most profitable part of SpaceX, bringing in $7.5bn according to the latest quarterly results.

items.title: US relations with Central Asia a priority, says Secretary Rubio
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio says U.S. relations with Central Asian nations is a priority.

He made the statement after a meeting Monday with his counterparts from Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan at the C5+1 Forum in the historic Silk Road city of Samarkand in Uzbekistan.

“Let there be no doubt that the United States wants to be a partner of this region and wants to be a partner of this country. We already are, and we intend to build that and grow it,” said Rubio at the U.S.-Uzbekistan Business and Investment Council.
During the meeting with the Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, Rubio pledged government and private sector cooperation, with the announcement of 54 agreements and proposed projects.
"There were agreements achieved worth $12 billion, and for us, it’s a great achievement," President Mirziyoyev said Monday.
The C5+1 diplomatic forum aims to bring together the five Central Asian countries and the United States to discuss security, trade and other concerns.

Washington has given special attention to trying to secure greater access to Central Asia’s rare earth minerals, a priority underscored by Rubio’s visit to Samarkand with a delegation of more than 200 U.S. business leaders, the State Department said.

items.title: Ukraine showcases its defense tech at the AUSA Expo 2026
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Ukrainian article.

For the first time ever, the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington hosted the Ukrainian Defense Tech Pavilion. Organized by Fenicks Group, the pavilion brought together 17 Ukrainian companies to showcase their aerial and ground drones, and their communications systems.

Following Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine rapidly expanded its drone production and made technical innovations to adapt its Unmanned Aerial System (UAS) to the demands of modern warfare.

The president of North Carolina-based Fenicks Group, Enrique Herrera, said, “The Ukrainian technologies that the United States is really looking for, that we're trying to bring from Ukraine to the United States, is the counter-UAS systems, the unmanned ground systems ... the one-way attack systems.”

One of the pavilion participants, Tencore, a Ukrainian producer of ground drones, known for their evacuation missions at the frontline in Ukraine, signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Canadian defense firm Dominion Dynamics during the AUSA conference.

The partnership is part of a larger defense cooperation deal that will include the manufacture of thousands of battle-tested drones and uncrewed systems in the next two years, with one-third earmarked for Ukraine's defense, according to a statement from the two companies.
In his remarks at the AUSA, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth acknowledged that the U.S. has learned a lot from Ukraine, though he noted that Ukraine’s vulnerability is its reliance on Chinese parts.

"We've learned a lot from Ukraine, but you can't use everything that's in Ukraine because of all the Chinese components involved in it," Hegseth said. "So, you've got to be able to ensure that we take the best of that and the lessons learned."

The United States, Ukraine and the EU, are among the countries limiting reliance on Chinese components in defense production. President Donald Trump signed an order in July making it harder to for U.S. weapons producers to purchase supplies from China.

Michael C. Horowitz, senior fellow for technology and innovation program at the Council on Foreign Relations, told VOA that Ukraine still must rely on Chinese components to defend itself. “Very often what is available and cheap are the Chinese components. He remarked that ensuring independence from China is “absolutely existential from the point of view of cybersecurity.”

The Pentagon has noted Ukraine’s progress in limiting purchases of components from China. “Most of the drone companies that you would go to see in Ukraine have brought their supply chains onshore,” said Travis Metz, recently promoted to acting director of the Defense Innovation Unit, told the podcast School of War in September.

Several Ukrainian companies have participated in the Pentagon’s Drone Dominance competition, which is aimed at purchasing small lethal drones and creating a U.S. industrial capability to produce such drones at scale. A Ukrainian company was selected to build a facility in Ohio.

Still, Derek Berlin of the New York-based Palisade Bergschrund company says cooperation could be moving faster, but says “Ukraine is fighting an active conflict, and it's very hard to focus on international markets when you're fighting for your survival. Ukraine would be much better able to share its technologies internationally if we were able to bring peace about in a lasting way for Ukraine,” he told the VOA at the AUSA conference.

Berlin says other factors impeding Ukraine’s access to U.S. markets include Ukraine’s complex export system, especially for intellectual property, and a complicated U.S. procurement program. “The companies that have been working in this market for 50, 100 years — even for some of the defense companies — still need to hire teams of people to figure out how to productively do procurement in the United States.”

items.title: With direct delivery to Pyongyang limited, US litigants turn to North Korea’s UN mission
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

Since the international express carrier DHL announced the suspension of services to North Korea in August, the country's mission to the United Nations in New York has become a key route for serving U.S. court documents tied to lawsuits against Pyongyang.

The U.S. State Department has repeatedly used diplomatic channels to deliver complaints, summonses and court judgments to the North Korean mission, effectively making it a conduit for legal communications between American courts and the North Korean government.

The State Department recently confirmed that it received court documents in cases involving North Korea and transmitted them to North Korea’s mission to the United Nations in New York under procedures established by the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (FSIA).

In an email to VOA early this month, a State Department spokesperson speaking on background confirmed that the department received the Alkhalili litigation documents and provided records to the court "reflecting transmission to the DPRK" under its statutory responsibilities for serving foreign states.

In September, the federal court in the Eastern District of Virginia ordered North Korea and Iran to pay approximately $487 million in damages in the Alkhalili lawsuit, brought by 47 Americans, including victims and family members affected by seven attacks in Iraq, Syria, Kenya, and Israel. Following the ruling, the plaintiffs asked the State Department to effect service of the judgment on North Korea, a request the Department fulfilled.

Court records reviewed by VOA also show that the State Department has filed formal certifications confirming that judicial documents were delivered to the North Korean U.N. mission under cover of diplomatic notes in other major anti-terrorism lawsuits.

According to filings in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, summonses and complaints were served on the North Korean mission on June 24 in two separate cases: Estate of Yona Betzalel Brief, et al. v. Islamic Republic of Iran, et al., filed by victims and families of the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, and the estate of Lillian Ladae Clamens, et al. v. Islamic Republic of Iran, et al., brought by the surviving family of a U.S. soldier killed in a 2007 rocket attack on Camp Victory in Baghdad.

In both cases, John Ballard, managing director of the State Department’s Directorate of Overseas Citizens Services, certified on September 30 that the diplomatic notes were dated June 17, 2026, and delivered to the Permanent Mission of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea to the United Nations in New York on June 24, 2026. Jared N. Hess, an attorney adviser in the State Department’s Office of the Legal Adviser, formally transmitted the certifications to the clerk of the court on October 1, completing the record of service.

Earlier, in March, the State Department transmitted an amended court judgment and a notice of default judgment to the North Korean mission in a lawsuit brought by the family of Reverend Kim Dong-shik, a South Korean missionary who was abducted by North Korean agents in China in 2000. The court had awarded his family $366 million in damages.
Diplomatic notes used to deliver court documents

With routine diplomatic contacts between Washington and Pyongyang largely dormant, the diplomatic note—traditionally the highest and most formal vehicle for government-to-government communication—is increasingly utilized to transmit judicial paperwork.

Diplomatic notes typically convey official positions or address issues between governments. In these cases, however, the State Department has used them to fulfill its responsibilities under U.S. law to serve legal documents on foreign governments.
The formal mechanism persists not as part of diplomatic negotiations, but to satisfy the stringent requirements of U.S. judicial procedure.
In previous years, plaintiffs suing North Korea relied on DHL, which operated a liaison office in Pyongyang, to deliver court documents directly to the North Korean Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

However, DHL ended its non-diplomatic delivery service to North Korea around 2020, which was publicly exposed when former detainee Kenneth Bae sued the North Korean government and attempted to use DHL to serve the summons to North Korea's foreign ministry.

More recently, in court filings related to a $1.5 billion cryptocurrency cyber-theft lawsuit filed by Bybit, it was disclosed that DHL has suspended cargo services to North Korea indefinitely. With other major commercial couriers and the U.S. Postal Service offering no registered delivery options to North Korea, direct deliveries to Pyongyang have become virtually impossible.
As a result, attention has turned to the U.N. mission in New York, where receipts of service have occurred.

items.title: Israeli prime minister tells Mossad, IDF, military intelligence "to overthrow Islamic Republic"
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says his directive to his country's Mossad intelligence agency, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), and the country’s military intelligence agency is to “overthrow” the Islamic Republic of Iran.
In an interview with Israel’s Channel 14 television this week, Netanyahu discussed last summer’s military operations against Iran.
“First and foremost, we acted alone. I personally launched Operation Rising Lion because we had to eliminate the existential threat posed by nuclear bombs to the state of Israel," he said.
The United States joined Israel last year in targeting Iranian nuclear facilities. Both countries launched military operations against Iran on February 28.

The Israeli leader went on to describe the issue as “a matter of our very existence, because if this regime acquires nuclear bombs, we will no longer exist. If we do not overthrow this regime, it will destroy us,” he said. "And this is my directive today to the Mossad, the Israeli military, and military intelligence: overthrow this regime."

Separately, the U.S. news outlet Axios cited unnamed sources within the U.S. government who said U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth met with Netanyahu on Monday, during a previously unannounced visit to Israel.

The Department of War declined to comment when asked by VOA to confirm the visit by Hegseth. Hegseth had posted on X that he visited troops under the U.S. Central Command, or CENTCOM, without specifying a location. CENTCOM is based in Tampa, Florida, but has a forward headquarters in Qatar – the largest U.S. airbase in the Middle East.

The reported meeting between Hegseth and Netanyahu took place just eight days before Israel’s election, while Washington and Jerusalem are discussing the possibility of resuming large-scale military operations against Iran.

U.S. President Donald Trump has expressed support for Netanyahu, endorsing him for his re-election. During a phone call with President Trump, the Israeli prime minister said, "unfinished business concerning the Islamic Republic needed to be completed."

On Monday, Netanyahu posted a video of the conversation on his account on the social media platform X. Addressing President Trump, he said, “Donald, we have something we need to finish, and we will finish it together. We will finish it, and no one else will do it.”
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on X on Sunday, " Last time you wanted to "finish the job", Iran emerged even stronger.
President Trump has said he would not order new military strikes against Iran before the upcoming November 3 midterm elections in the U.S.

items.title: From Soybeans to Data Centers, China Debate Hits US Midterm Campaigns
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

With two weeks until the November 3 midterm elections, the U.S., and China’s relationship is on the ballot in some closely contested races nationwide — from soybean exports and factory jobs to the cost of powering data centers.

Candidates for the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate are debating how to counter Beijing while addressing a question closer to home: Who is benefiting from those policies, and who is paying a price.

In North Carolina’s competitive 1st Congressional District, Democratic Representative Don Davis as recently as September called on President Donald Trump to secure what he called a “a verifiable, structured timeline" for promised Chinese purchases of U.S. soybeans. Davis faces Republican challenger Laurie Buckhout.

There have been signs of progress. Last week, Chinese state-owned buyers had ordered a combined 1.2 million to 1.5 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans. But sustained purchases and actual deliveries will be key tests of any trade commitments.

In Iowa’s Senate race, agricultural trade is also a flashpoint. During an October 7 debate, Democratic candidate Josh Turek said tariffs on trading partners, including China, were hurting agricultural export markets. Republican Ashley Hinson defended efforts to hold Beijing accountable for its trade practices, while pledging to support manufacturing and reduce fertilizer costs.
The push to compete with China in super intelligence, commonly referred to as artificial intelligence, is colliding with concerns about electricity costs and local control.
In Pennsylvania’s 8th Congressional District, Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti, a Democrat challenging Republican incumbent Rob Bresnahan, has made data center development a campaign issue.
Cognetti’s campaign has criticized tax breaks for such centers and a lack of transparency, warning that residents could be left with higher costs.

Bresnahan has proposed legislation to protect communities that reject data center projects, limit developers’ ability to sue over those decisions, and require some federally subsidized projects to deliver tangible local benefits.

President Trump has made expanding U.S. AI infrastructure a national priority. At an October 3 rally in Ohio for Republican Senator Jon Husted, Trump defended data center development with a warning: “They’ll go to China.”

Husted’s Democratic challenger, Sherrod Brown, has criticized his Republican opponent's support for data centers and tax incentives, arguing that the facilities should pay the full cost of their electricity use.

Husted sponsored the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would require states to consider standards making data centers cover grid upgrades needed to meet their additional power demand. The House passed the measure, but it failed to advance in a Senate procedural vote in September. Democrats argued that it did not provide adequate protections.

The dispute is not simply whether to build data centers, but how to ensure the costs do not fall on households and small businesses. The issue is also featuring in Senate races in Georgia, Texas and Maine.
Tariffs present another tradeoff. Measures intended to protect U.S. producers can also raise costs for businesses that rely on imported components.

The Associated Press reported on factory layoffs that employers say have attributed to higher import costs, while also noting that tariffs are not the only cause of manufacturing job losses. The White House responded by saying a factory boom is underway.
Michigan’s Senate race highlights another distinction: opposing broad tariffs does not necessarily mean rejecting targeted trade restrictions on China.

Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed has criticized the Trump administration’s sweeping tariffs while leaving room for targeted measures tied to industrial policy. Republican Mike Rogers has defended some tariffs but called for an end to tariff disputes with Canada.
The debate underscores how trade policy toward China can also affect U.S. businesses and economic ties with other trading partners.

items.title: ‘Borscht Battle’ in Washington Raises Funds for Ukrainian Medics
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Russian article.

A chilly rooftop in downtown D.C. was turned into a culinary battleground last weekend as more than a dozen cooks made their best versions of Borscht, a traditional Ukrainian dish. Money raised from the fifth annual “Borscht Battle went to the Leleka Foundation which provides medical equipment for Ukrainian combat medics.

The competition featured a wide variety of recipes: traditional, vegetarian, vegan, and even borscht made with sprats, the small oily fish found in the Mediterranean and Black Sea. Each dish was identified only by a number, to make the voting as objective as possible, allowing guests to judge the soups solely on taste. This is the fifth year the event has been held in the U.S. capital. Organizer Gleb Latnik. says what began as a friendly debate over whose borscht is best has grown into a major charity fundraiser, bringing together members of the Ukrainian community and American guests.

“It all started when two friends argued about whose borscht was better. We decided to organize a battle, invite other participants, and hold a competition,” said Latnik. “The first year, we hosted it on my rooftop. After that, it became an annual event. The beneficiaries change each year, but the money always goes toward helping Ukraine.” This year, admission to the event was a donation to the Leleka Foundation. The organization supplies Ukrainian medics with medical backpacks and emergency equipment, including tourniquets, hemostatic gauze, airways, chest seals and splints. A separate fundraising effort was dedicated to purchasing thermal blankets, which help keep wounded Ukrainian soldiers warm during evacuation before they reach a medical facility.

Foundation representatives said assistance is provided in response to specific requests from the front lines in Ukraine's fight against Russia. Medics and unit commanders can contact the organization directly to report their needs.

“People can submit a request through our website. Medics or unit commanders fill out a form, and our staff in Ukraine receive the information and contact them directly to clarify exactly what is needed," said Ivan Vidyakin, co-founder of the Leleka Foundation. "We have focused specifically on medical backpacks for medics. If one medic is properly equipped, a single backpack can help that person save, for example, 10 lives on the battlefield."

For many guests, the competition was not just a charity event but also an opportunity to experience Ukrainian culture. Some came looking for a familiar taste from childhood, while others were trying borscht for the first time.

“My family is from Odesa. I’m the first person in our family to be born in the United States. My grandmother used to make borscht when I was growing up, so I’ve been eating it since childhood,” said Anthony, one of the visitors. His friend Rachel admitted she had never tried borscht before.

“I like beets, but I’m not a big fan of cold soups. Anthony told me about this event, so I decided to come and give it a try,” she said. Rachel’s favorite was the vegan borscht made with mushrooms and cabbage. "It's delicious. It’s completely different from what I expected,” she said.

The winner was determined by a vote among the guests. First place went to “Mariupol Borscht,” the one made with sprats. It also placed in the top three last year but won the top spot. Organizers say the event brought in over $5,000 dollars.

items.title: Katie Razzall: BBC closures make business sense, but far more savings are needed
paragraphs: The BBC's announcement that it will close three of its linear broadcast channels - BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra - makes sense financially.
BBC Three's most popular show on Monday night was a repeat of an old episode of Top Gear. Around 77,000 people tuned in.

BBC Scotland's TV channel was watched, according to this year's annual report, by a weekly average of 12% of the Scottish population. Scots simply aren't tuning in in the numbers to make it cost-effective.
(Interestingly, BBC Alba, which is aimed at Gaelic speakers and learners, reached 43% of Gaelic viewers in Scotland weekly - was it boosted by its rights to broadcast Italian football's Serie A?)
It's hard to argue - although no doubt some will - that there is a business case for keeping BBC Scotland's TV channel open.

The same goes for BBC Three, although the hokey cokey that has gone on with that channel - launched to fanfare in 2003, later made digital-only, then brought back to linear in 2022, now back online only again - has looked indecisive. Bizarre even.

But the bigger picture is that viewers and listeners are already migrating online - increasingly finding the BBC's programmes not via those linear TV and radio channels but on iPlayer, BBC Sounds, and, more recently, YouTube.
So that's the business case - and the BBC needs to save £500m over the next three years. That figure is concentrating minds.
But axing the three linear channels is a drop in the ocean financially. I understand it will save less than £10m in total per year.

Last year the BBC spent £42m creating content for BBC Scotland. It still plans to create many of those shows for iPlayer - and BBC Two in Scotland will be reconfigured to deliver Scotland-only programming.
The part of BBC Three that commissions programmes will actually get more money to spend on creating content aimed specifically at 16-34s (with a core focus on the 16-25s).
This was the network that commissioned Normal People, Fleabag, Killing Eve - programmes of quality and wide appeal.

There's also been a recent announcement of commissions dreamt up specifically for YouTube - to reach those 16-24s who the BBC (and other public service broadcasters) find so difficult to lure to their own platforms.

Many of Radio 4 Extra's programmes will also still be on BBC Sounds. If you listen to the Daily Service, first broadcast in 1928 and the longest-running programme of its kind anywhere in the world, you will still be able to find it.
So these aren't major cost savings. The BBC would likely argue, when it comes to audiences, who are at the heart of everything, it is pivoting to find them where they already are.
What's been announced today is more about the direction of travel. It's about the continuing evolution of the BBC, a streamlining as audience habits change.

That doesn't mean it isn't painful to all of us inside the BBC. Job cuts are always difficult. In News, 100 more roles are being axed. That's on top of the 200 already announced. And the news division is still nowhere near its target of £51m of cuts.
And with only two fifths of the £500m of total savings now announced, there is still a very long way to go.

As a BBC user, you are going to hear much more about cuts in the coming months. Some will think that is a good thing as the BBC reflects the belt-tightening going on in most homes and companies across the UK. Others fear that the BBC's important role in public life is being chipped away.

There is a bigger fight going on here. The BBC is negotiating with the government over its future - and how it will be paid for. It won't harm the negotiations if it can show the corporation is being streamlined and made more efficient.
As long as it can also demonstrate that audiences aren't being left behind.

items.title: The dangers of letting tech billionaires shape our world
paragraphs: Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you while sitting in front of Roy Lichtenstein’s monumental Drowning Girl, on view in New York City. Today in tech, we’re discussing the perils of Elon Musk’s one-man global infrastructure, AI-generated music, and a Guardian AI conference in Paris.

Elon Musk’s SpaceX is the single largest satellite operator in the world, larger than any government space bureau. The life-threatening consequences of that dominance and centralization of power are on full display. One man is in charge of global, vital infrastructure, which is thumbing the scales in the war on Ukraine.

SpaceX’s internet service was throttled in Ukraine amid a series of devastating attacks by Russia last week, leaving the country extremely vulnerable. The US government controls StarShield, the satellite internet service produced by SpaceXSI for the Pentagon, which is what Ukraine relies on. Objects moving faster than 100 mph (160.9 km/h) – drones, the centerpiece of Ukraine’s counteroffensive – lost connectivity. The sudden restrictions Tuesday evening led to the failure of several Ukrainian combat missions. Russian drones fly at nearly 200 mph (328.9 km/h), so Ukrainian interceptor drones can’t catch them without Starlink, and no alternative is as yet viable. In response, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky warned “people will die.”

The cutoff comes alongside Donald Trump’s mercurial souring on Ukraine. Pressured domestically by the high price of diesel and upcoming midterm elections, the US president has eased sanctions on Russia, and Zelensky has said US intelligence agencies on several occasions in recent days didn’t warn Ukraine of incoming missile attacks, as they usually do. Musk has denied his own involvement in StarShield’s malfunctioning, writing, “This is not under SpaceX control.”

Musk’s denial has been met with skepticism given his close ties with the administration. It is impossible to disentangle him and SpaceX from the Trump administration. He has realigned himself with the White House in recent months, patching up his explosive feud with the president from a year ago and appearing with Trump at major events. Musk has been appointed to a Pentagon commission on the future of war and has given hundreds of millions of dollars to conservative Republican candidates.

Musk has also personally ordered the restriction of Starlink service in Ukraine before. In 2022, SpaceX cut off Starlink – not StarShield – service during a Ukrainian counteroffensive in the regions of Kherson and Donetsk. He refused Ukraine’s request to extend connectivity to Crimea the same year.

One tech tycoon’s political leanings are determining the tides of war between two sovereign nations. Musk’s alliance with the White House implicates him in the pressure campaign against Ukraine to end the war with Russia, likely via surrender.

In recent weeks, notable musicians have confronted the growing presence of AI-generated music, saying they are open to it but wary, even boosters like the singer and producer Grimes, former paramour of Musk and mother to three of his 14 children.
Fans, by contrast, are voting with millions of streams against artifice in music. Songs and albums harkening back to analog instrumentation are dominating the Billboard charts, no futurism wanted.
Both A$AP Rocky, rapper and partner to Rihanna, and Grimes took the same position: I accept AI-generated music, but I don’t make it.

“I prefer to do things myself, practically,” A$AP Rocky told Billboard. “If somebody does a totally AI-generated song where all they did was prompt something, then I think that’s their thing. But who am I to say what’s standard and what’s not? I’m just doing me out here, and I’m doing my music practically – the right way.”

Grimes, one of my own favorite musicians, has begun promoting her first new album in six years, Psy Opera, which she described to The Paris Review as capturing the “emotion of being thrust into the future”. Stereogum described the album as “AI-inspired but not AI-generated”, citing Grimes’ own insistence that her team of 70 be credited rather than reduced to machines.

Grimes offered a free license of her own voice to AI enthusiasts to make what they would three years ago. That she declined to generate her own music indicates that, even to a futurist like her, AI-generated music is lacking, similar to Rocky’s stance.

I have also found myself listening to an AI-generated song, Bomboclat Wallahi, brought to my attention via frenetic, overstimulating videos on Instagram. Despite the song’s comical sonic maximalism, it lacks any staying power. Listening to it the day after I first heard it left no impression, similar to the way low-quality food leaves me hungry again just a few hours after eating. “Slop” is still the best word to describe AI-made content.

In contrast to artists’ nuanced stances, fans are making their position on tech-made music clear: They don’t want it. Billboard’s charts of the most popular albums and charts of the past week showcase a preference for music without obvious modification. Songs and albums that feature a simple voice-and-guitar arrangement are dominating. On the Top 200 album charts, most of the Top 10 albums foreground a singer over analog instrumentation – Olivia Rodrigo’s you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love, Ella Langley’s Dandelion, Olivia Dean’s The Art of Loving, Taylor Swift’s The Life of a Showgirl, Noah Kahan’s The Great Divide and Stick Season, and Morgan Wallen’s I’m the Problem. In the Hot 100 singles chart, the top four songs bear the same sonic signatures: Swift’s Patient Zero, Langley’s Choosin’ Texas, Stella Lefty’s Boston, Wallen’s Been by Now.

Incredibly, The Beatles’ Rubber Soul, released in 1965, also makes an appearance at No 4 on last week’s Billboard rankings. Some listeners want to return to a time when producing music with artificial intelligence wasn’t even an option.
My colleague Robert Booth reports from the Hacking Big Tech conference, a Guardian conference in Paris:

As the Paris Streets erupted with protest and violence on Saturday, a parallel radicalism was on display at the Hacking Big Tech conference organised by the French media organization Mediapart in conjunction with the Guardian. Amid the contributions from experts in military AI and how to fight against datacenters, a theme emerged about how people might respond to the tech wave: be more human.

The writer Naomi Klein told the audience that the technology companies intend AI to be used as an “everything app and also as a truth machine”. This, she said, was “very clearly a fascist idea, to centralise knowledge, to standardise what intelligence is”.

At a rare tech conference not addressed by representatives of tech companies, Klein painted a bleak AI-driven future in which there is “going to be more resource scarcity, there’s going to be more people who have no role in the economy and need to be contained and surveilled”.
A response was available, she said: “We decide that we want to be more human.”

Humor was another answer. German Salazar, a Chilean activist campaigning to save water in his native country in the face of a wave of AI datacenters, showed how his community had set up a human chatbot to encourage people to prompt less and save water. The idea was simple: a team, ranging from children to town elders, offered human responses to chatbot queries from anywhere in the world for a day. If you want an image of a dog doing yoga, one of them will paint it for you. Want to know what love is? A human will tell you it is “the wish of someone else to be happy”.
There were 2,300 requests for images, 135 for dating advice and one for the meaning of life.

items.title: Labor and the Coalition are poised to take a reckless gamble on AI. Haven’t they realised community support has collapsed? | Edward Santow and Sarah Sacher
paragraphs: Australia’s major political parties are edging towards rare consensus. Labor and the Coalition increasingly want to take a major bet on artificial intelligence. Yet, just as the parties are coming together, the Australian community is running the other way.
Last year, only 30% of Australians believed the benefits of AI outweighed the risks. In 2026, community trust in AI appears to be falling even further.

It was an unusual step for our parliament to form a joint select committee on AI. It signalled that the decisions being made now on datacentres and how we adopt AI could define our economy, environment and society for generations.

As a fresh round of hearings starts this week, the committee members must confront the gulf between the politics of AI and the stark reality on the ground. Some parts of the business sector are urging us to prioritise innovation and AI adoption, which is often another way of saying: “Do a better job of selling the upside of AI.”

Whether you’re an AI optimist or a sceptic, this is a terrible idea. Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and the other titans of Silicon Valley have a golden megaphone to spruik the benefits of their technology. Australians don’t want our elected representatives to do the same thing – especially when the technology is already bringing both opportunity and harm.

This doesn’t mean being blind to the benefits of AI. On the contrary, Australia is among the highest users per capita of Anthropic’s Claude and other generative AI applications. But we must also be clear-eyed about potential risks. And, crucially, we don’t see a compelling response to our concerns from government or the AI companies themselves.

Take the impact of AI on work. Our community is asking practical questions. How will AI impact our jobs, and the jobs of our children? What is the government doing to ensure the AI systems used in Australian workplaces are safe?

Our new report, Drawing the Line, lays out how AI is propelling the rise of harmful tech-enabled worker surveillance. Often workers are unaware of the extent to which they are being monitored – including through their work devices and phones, and via software such as Microsoft Teams.

Unlike some of the hypothetical (and frankly terrifying) risks that the joint select committee on AI has already covered, such as AI-enabled biological weapons and engineered pandemics, this is happening today.

Australian supermarket workers are already being pushed to meet AI-generated productivity metrics that force them to work harder and faster under the threat of punitive repercussions – putting them at risk of injury and workplace accidents.

Remote workers are already being subjected to intrusive surveillance software capable of watching everything they do on their screen – including audio recording conversations they have with their families.

Rideshare drivers are already being penalised for road conditions and customer complaints that are unrelated to their performance, which can result in their account being deactivated and days of work lost.

Workers are being quietly crushed by commonplace AI-powered surveillance tools that have crept into our workplaces and home offices. And the impact is real. Think, for example, of the young woman who reported being sexually harassed by a boss that required her to be on video at all times. Or warehouse workers driven to suicidal ideation due to relentless micromanagement by machine.
Our workplace laws don’t protect workers from unreasonable surveillance. Nor do they give employers clarity about what types of monitoring are lawful.
Unlike existential risks from AI, which are outside the Australian government’s direct control, this problem could be addressed through straightforward law reform.

We urge the government to update the Fair Work Act to require any worker monitoring be “fair and reasonable”. This builds on the government’s commitment to require all personal information covered by the Privacy Act to be handled fairly and reasonably.
Australian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at hand. This is not a hypothetical future risk – let’s address it now.

items.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
paragraphs: Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal.

That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI.

People expect AI to lead to fewer jobs in 34 of the 37 countries surveyed by the Pew Research Center. In wealthy countries like the US, Australia and South Korea, about seven in 10 expect job losses over the next 20 years. And across countries, concern among young people is rising. While fears focus on job numbers, the bigger change will be what jobs become.

The nature of human work will move towards judgment. Experts refer to AI as “jagged”, superhuman at certain tasks but weak at others, with no clear boundary between the two. AI rapidly improves where work can be automatically checked and examples are endless. But it’s shaky where no automated test can determine whether the answer is right. Even if AI is correct a majority of the time on a task, it often doesn’t tell you when it’s inaccurate. If you’ve used AI, you’ve probably experienced how it can be confidently wrong.
Some of these errors will solve themselves as models get better. But jaggedness is a symptom of how these models learn. I see this often as a technology leader building with these systems.

A smarter model still needs a right answer to learn from. When one gap is closed, it shows up somewhere else no one thought to check. But many business decisions don’t immediately have a clear right answer. Whether a choice is good depends on a future no one can see and data no one has. That’s where judgment comes in. So AI will keep mastering tasks that have checkable results but struggle where a person has to decide what a good outcome looks like.

As a result, a new type of work is starting to appear. Someone tests whether the output of AI is correct based on real work, not just on benchmarks. Someone sets limits on what AI is allowed to do before it runs, so the worst mistakes are avoided. Someone runs and manages several agents the way a shift manager runs a crew. Picture an airport control tower. Radar and software track flight paths, with humans judging the few that matter to avoid collisions. No one is manually watching every screen. That would never scale.

Setting AI’s limits is harder than it sounds. In a 2026 study, after an agent was told to protect a secret, it destroyed its own email server, deleting every single email. It was given a goal, without any limits on what it could do. The researchers described it as the right values paired with terrible judgment. Deciding what is off limits and what a mistake would cost takes someone who knows the work and will answer for the result.

Here is the good news for people worried about their own jobs. The people best suited for doing this new type of work aren’t computer programmers. They are the ones who know how the real work is done. Catching what a confident AI left out or got wrong takes someone who knows the complete answer. That knowledge is uncheckable, unwritten and takes the form of judgment honed over years of doing the task and watching it break.

Ford recently learned the value of human expertise. In recent years, it leaned hard on automating its quality control, cutting thousands of jobs. But earlier this year, it had to rehire 350 veteran engineers to oversee the process and hunt for failure points before a part reached the factory floor. They brought the judgment of watching parts fail over years. With humans at the helm, Ford’s quality ranking then hit first among mainstream brands for the first time since 2010.

But we are making a serious mistake with the jobs we’re eliminating due to AI: the entry-level, routine ones. That routine work is how judgment gets built over time. Junior employees work under the supervision of senior experts until their experience turns into instinct. AI eliminates the friction related to learning how to do the job. But the demand for judgment did not go away. We are just destroying the path to developing it.

The real question is not whether machines will take over our work. It is whether we will have the people who can tell when the machines are wrong. Right now, we are automating the training ground where judgment is learned. If you have hard-earned expertise about anything, the next few years will only make you more valuable. And if you are just starting out, the old apprenticeship model will not hand it to you. You have to go and earn it, deliberately, on tasks the machines cannot yet judge.
Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software company

items.title: Watch: Moment fin whale swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding
paragraphs: To avoid causing harm to the whales while recording out at sea, Morgan said: "We do what we can to keep our distance in the boat but unfortunately nature can have a mind of its own sometimes.
"There's been times when we've been anchored up fishing with nothing happening in the area and a whale has popped up next to us.
"The wildlife will approach you sometimes."
Dr Marianna Chimienti is a lecturer in marine top predator ecology at Bangor University and said Morgan experienced a "rare and fortunate encounter".

Chimienti, who specialises in animal behaviour added: "It is normal that the fin whale comes and feeds at the surface, as it is part of the species foraging strategy but being in the coastal water is quite spectacular.
Little is known about fin whale migration but their movements are believed to be quite different from other baleen whales such as blues and humpbacks.
Scientists have found that fin whales are more abundant in higher latitudes in warmer months of the year, and more numerous in lower latitudes during colder months, but this can vary.

items.title: What if an AI bubble bursts — and that accelerates AI job losses?
paragraphs: This article first appeared in the Planet Money newsletter. You can sign up here.
What if an AI bubble bursts, triggering a recession, and that recession ends up accelerating the replacement of workers with AI? Call it the AI double whammy.

I've long been skeptical of sweeping claims about how AI will transform the world. I still am. We don't really know. But as this technology advances, I've found myself worrying more about what it could mean for our livelihoods.

Two strands of economic research have given me reason to take this double whammy seriously. One concerns the history of financial bubbles. The other concerns a surprising relationship between recessions and automation, when businesses use technology to do tasks that were previously done by humans.

First, the bubbles. In 1978, the economist Charles Kindleberger published an influential book titled Manias, Panics, and Crashes: A History of Financial Crises. Drawing on the theoretical work of economist Hyman Minsky, Kindleberger went through centuries of economic history and saw a recurring pattern.

Often the bubble starts with some big potential change to the economy. A revolutionary new technology, for example, that promises to transform industries and create enormous wealth. Investors have a good reason to be excited by it. But they get overly excited. During the upswing, they bet tons of money expecting basically that the sky is the limit. And they often build up debt in the process, borrowing money to make even bigger bets and thereby helping to further fuel the boom. That debt can become a ticking time bomb. When reality sets in, asset prices fall, but those debts remain. Borrowers struggle to repay, lenders suffer losses, and a market crash can spiral into a financial crisis and a painful recession.

One crucial insight is that a technology can truly be revolutionary, yet still fuel a bubble that ends in a financial crash. For example, the railroads. I wrote about that bubble in a previous Planet Money newsletter — and how its collapse triggered "The Panic of 1873." The ensuing economic turmoil helped foment a populist uprising and the first major immigration crackdown in American history.

AI is now basically propping up the U.S. stock market. An analysis from J.P. Morgan earlier this month found that just 42 AI-related companies accounted for around two-thirds of the S&P 500's stock price gains since early 2024. Meanwhile, AI-related companies are borrowing hundreds of billions of dollars to help finance data centers and the energy infrastructure to power them.

None of this proves that what we're witnessing is a bubble or that this debt is a ticking time bomb for the financial system. The bursting of the dot-com bubble helped usher in a relatively mild recession. Debt played a smaller role in that boom, helping to limit the financial fallout. Its collapse did not trigger a systemic financial crisis like the one that followed the housing market bust around 2008.

Even without a financial crisis, though, there could be a painful reckoning. Will all these companies ultimately make enough money to justify all their borrowing and spending? Will each company survive? Technology analyst Benedict Evans has warned that fierce competition between companies offering similarly capable AI models could drive down the prices they can charge and leave little room for profit — even as they're spending ungodly amounts of money to develop and run these models.

If an AI bust triggers a recession, that would be painful enough. But this is where a few studies add to my anxieties. Because they suggest that recessions can be the very moment when businesses turn to new technologies to replace workers.

We tend to imagine automation as a gradual process. Technology improves, businesses adopt it, and jobs slowly change or disappear, theoretically while new jobs appear in other parts of the economy. But this research suggests that automation can happen in bursts, and those bursts tend to cluster around recessions.

One study, by economists Nir Jaimovich and Henry Siu, found that jobs vulnerable to previous waves of automation saw most of their decline around recessions. Between 1990 and 2017, 88% of the decline in the share of Americans employed in these jobs occurred during recessions or in the months immediately before or after them.

And here's the unsettling irony: fierce price competition could keep AI companies from delivering the profits investors expect, while making their technology cheaper for other businesses to use to replace workers. If an AI bust triggers a recession, that downturn could accelerate worker replacement. Investors could lose their money, and workers could still lose their jobs.
It's a nightmare scenario. First, the bust hammers our retirement savings. Then, as businesses scramble to cut costs, many of our jobs are permanently lost.

Of course, we still don't know whether AI will deliver enough profits to justify all the borrowing and spending, whether a bust would trigger a painful recession, or whether the automation patterns found in past recessions will repeat themselves with AI. A downturn could leave businesses with less money to invest in AI. And AI could still prove more useful for helping workers get more productive than outright replacing them.

Whether AI delivers one whammy or two whammies or none, there are policies that can limit the damage when workers lose their jobs. Obviously, unemployment insurance and other policies like that. And people like Bill Gates are proposing that we should tax AI and robots, making it more economical to continue employing humans while generating revenue that the government can spend to enhance the safety net. That idea is something we might explore in a future newsletter.
So, yeah, there are reasons this nightmare might never come true, and there are ways to limit the damage if it does. That, however, hasn't stopped me from worrying about it.
But it felt cathartic writing this down — getting these worries out of my head and onto the page.

Wondering what AI could mean for your livelihood? Join Adrian and friends from The Indicator from Planet Money on Wednesday, Oct. 28, for a virtual Ask an Economist event about AI and jobs. It will feature Daron Acemoglu, a Nobel Prize-winning professor at MIT who's been critical of AI companies, and Ronnie Chatterji, a professor at Duke and chief economist at OpenAI. This is for our NPR+ supporters, join here, and find more details on the event here.

P.S. Charles Kindleberger's life was super fascinating. As we've written before, he worked for the CIA's wartime predecessor and helped design the Marshall Plan. Someone should probably make a Hollywood movie about him.

items.title: Alberta voters reject plan for referendum to leave Canada
paragraphs: Voters in Canada’s Alberta have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to begin a process towards independence, delivering a victory for the prime minister, Mark Carney, and supporters of Canadian unity.
With more than 1.5m votes counted, 76% supported remaining in Canada, while close to 24% backed beginning a process toward separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta.
Carney, who grew up in Edmonton, said: “Albertans made a clear choice. They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other. Above all, Albertans chose Canada.”

He said the result would allow Canadians to move forward together and accelerate efforts to diversify trade, develop major infrastructure projects and make Canada a global energy powerhouse, with Alberta at its centre.

Alberta’s separatists, however, saw a silver lining. “We don’t have the final results. I think the numbers are going to fluctuate, but it is fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better,” said Keith Wilson, a leader of the separatist movement.

The Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, welcomed the early results, saying they showed widespread support for remaining in Canada. “Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada,” Smith posted on social media.

Even though the vote was not explicitly about independence – a point that frustrated separatists – the ballot question nonetheless exposed divisions in Alberta’s politics and raised questions about the durability of national unity.

Delays at roughly 100 of the 1,400 at polling stations across the province pushed results back by more than two hours, but shortly after polls closed on Monday evening the results suggested a decisive win for those looking to remain in Canada.

The separation question – whether to remain in Canada or begin a legal process that could lead to a second vote – was one of 10 put to Albertans on Monday. The others covered issues including immigration, healthcare, education and the province’s constitutional powers. Elections Alberta said the remaining results could take days to count.
In the days leading up to the vote, provincial leaders and federal politicians crisscrossed the province to make the case for a unified country.

Carney warned against a vote from residents of the oil-rich province simply looking to “send a message” to the federal government. “A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he told an energetic crowd last week.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, whose parliamentary seat is in the province, told a crowd of supporters that Albertans were not “quitters”.

“To those people who are thinking about taking out their frustration on the current government by voting for separation in the referendum, I say this: Canada is more than a government,” he said. “It is a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise.”

Data from Elections Alberta indicated roughly 43% of eligible voters – or 1.3 million Albertans – had already cast ballots before Monday’s vote through advance voting and mail-in ballots. That figure pointed to a potentially higher turnout than the province’s last referendum in 2021.

Smith’s tenure as leader of the United Conservative party is due in large part to separatists within the party who ousted her predecessor, Jason Kenney. In recent months she has tried to placate both the separatists and federalists in the party, in a province where a majority is not interested in secession.
The referendum became a political liability for Smith’s party, whose popular support has tumbled in recent months, including with the loss of a one-time conservative stronghold in a byelection.
Still, members of the separatist movement told the Guardian they would continue their push for independence.

In an interview before the results, the Calgary mayor, Jeromy Farkas, a staunch opponent of the independence movement, said the city’s “best future is here, as a Canadian city”, amid fears that uncertainty could lead to capital flight.

“I am Canadian because I’m Canadian, not in a transactional way and regardless of the flavour of prime minister,” Farkas said. “And I’m going to continue to make the case for how our future is strongest together, because no result will permanently put this to bed. “The separatist movement sees this as a long-term project.”
